events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: Well, I do declare — Doily Manor in the flesh! Look at this place, all cobwebs and grandeur. It's like stepping into one of Grandmother's old photograph albums, except dustier and twice as mysterious. Now, before I go gallivanting off after diamonds, a lady ought to sign the guest book. You never know what the folks before you might have left behind — and I have found that the best clues are the ones people write down without realizing they're clues at all.
events.thinking: A warmth spreads through my chest as I step inside — the chandelier catches what little light there is and scatters it across those stern portraits. My fingers are already tingling, the way they do when something is waiting to be found. I can feel the dust settling on my shoulders like the manor is trying to claim me already. And oh — there's Sneekly, bless his heart, and Peter, and my boys from the Mob. The tightness in my stomach loosens just seeing familiar faces. But that guest book on the side table — something about it pulls at me, the same tug I felt with Grandmother's locked box. Who else has been here? What did they write? I should say hello to everyone proper, but my feet are already drifting toward that book.

events.desc: Everyone I care about is right here in this room. That should make me feel safe, but instead there's a prickle at the back of my neck — like the cave, right before the passage narrowed. Something about this manor wants to be solved. And Clara Bellingham does not leave a puzzle half-finished.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah — welcome, welcome to Doily Manor, one and all! I am Pemberton, estate manager. I do hope the journey wasn't too tiresome. If I might direct your attention to the guest book — it is customary for all visitors to sign upon arrival. A tradition of the house, you understand. The late master was most particular about such things.
events.thinking:
There's a settling in my chest — that familiar mineral weight, the one that arrives when I walk into a room I've already mapped. The entrance hall. Dusty chandelier, wobbly coat rack, a guest book no one's signed in years. All of it mine in every way that matters, except the one way that counts on paper.

And here they all are. Penelope — sweet, trusting Penelope — standing right there with her little entourage. Peter Perfect hovering nearby like a golden retriever who's learned to walk upright. The Ant Hill Mob... those ones watch. I feel a prickle along my shoulders when their eyes move. They notice things.

Dick Dastardly. Now there's a useful instrument. Greedy, impulsive, loud enough to draw attention away from quieter work.

But first — Pemberton. The smile. The slight bow. The voice that says 'I live to serve' while the hands are already counting what's owed. I need to establish my presence here as the helpful, fussing estate manager. Everyone needs to see Pemberton before anyone can suspect Vincent.

The guest book. That's my opening. A good estate manager would fuss over the guest book. It's a small, theatrical gesture — exactly the sort of thing Pemberton would do. And it lets me observe everyone while appearing to be busy with something mundane.

Clara isn't here yet. Good. That gives me time to arrange the board before the game begins.

events.desc: Look at them. Every one of them standing in MY entrance hall, touching MY coat rack, breathing MY air. Patience, Vincent. The guest book gives me a reason to hover. To watch. To catalog every nervous glance and careless word. The design is not yet ready — but the architect is here, and the materials have just been delivered.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Ah, what a MAGNIFICENT establishment! Reginald Foxworth — Lord Reginald Foxworth, that is — decorated war hero, amateur archaeologist, and, I dare say, the foremost authority on manor house antiquities in all of England. You'll notice my Medal of Distinguished Valour — yes, yes, do admire it — awarded for services to the Crown that I'm afraid are still classified. Now then, I believe I shall sign the guest book, as is PROPER for a gentleman of my standing. The rest of you... do try not to touch anything valuable. Some of us know what things are worth.
events.thinking: A fizzing in my fingers the moment I step through the door. The hall is grand — dusty, yes, but grand — and my hands are already cupping slightly, cataloguing. Portraits on the walls, chandelier overhead, and look at them all, milling about like sheep in a pen. Eight of them. Eight fools between me and whatever treasure this manor holds. The hollow behind my navel opens wider — there's something here, I can feel it, something valuable that isn't mine yet, and the incompleteness of that sits in my chest like an ache. The guest book catches my eye. Guest books in old manors — they always have clues. Names, dates, perhaps a hint about what the previous owner left behind. And while these buffoons are busy introducing themselves, Reginald Foxworth will be gathering intelligence. The bread roll in the pocket. Always the bread roll in the pocket.

events.desc: None of that is true, naturally. The medal is tin. I bought it at a car boot sale in Croydon for fifty pence. But the key to any good scheme is the entrance — establish yourself as the authority, and these simpletons will be eating out of my hand. Now, that guest book... let's see who else has been sniffing around this treasure.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Doily Manor! What a magnificently atmospheric establishment. One can practically feel the history pressing in from every wall. And that chandelier — hanging by what appears to be sheer determination and a prayer. I shall make a note to examine the rigging later; one cannot have such hazards dangling over... well, over present company.
events.thinking:
There's a warmth spreading across my shoulders — that old familiar weight, like a coat being placed there. I've just arrived at Doily Manor and the first thing I notice is her. Penelope. She's here, standing in this dusty entrance hall, and something in my chest shifts the way it always does. The chandelier hangs precariously overhead — I note that, file it away, because that's what I do. I notice the broken things before the beautiful ones. But then my eyes find her again and both notices happen at once.

And there's Sneekly — Pemberton, the estate manager. The back of my neck prickles. I can't prove anything. I choose not to. Good people give others the benefit of the doubt. My father taught me that on a country road.

But first things first. James Hartwell does not simply walk into a room. He announces himself. He makes an impression. The guest book is right there — leather-bound, waiting. A gentleman signs the guest book. It's the courteous thing to do. And if Penelope happens to notice the flourish of my signature, well — the warmth needs its audience the way a fire needs air.

I should examine this room properly before moving on. Plan the approach. Map the exits. The library and kitchen are accessible. But right now, the guest book calls. A small gesture, but shaped with care.

It is a small thing, but small things done with presence — that is what separates showing up from arriving.

Now, that library inscription is calling to me something fierce.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah, splendid, splendid — Lord Foxworth, what an honour to have you grace Doily Manor! And Mr. Perfect, how astute of you to notice the chandelier. I have been meaning to have it seen to — the house has been rather... understaffed since the master's passing. Now then, if I might suggest — the kitchen has a rather fine collection of antique silverware that I believe would interest a connoisseur such as yourself, Lord Foxworth. Georgian hallmarks, quite valuable. And for those of a more scholarly bent, the library contains some rather remarkable volumes. I should be happy to show anyone who wishes to see them. It is, after all, what I am here for.
events.thinking:
There's a warmth spreading behind my sternum — that familiar buoyancy. Penelope went straight for the guest book, just as I suggested. The compliance was effortless. She didn't even hesitate. And Dick Dastardly — 'Lord Reginald Foxworth' — oh, that's rich. A man wearing a disguise as transparent as tissue paper, strutting about with a fake medal. He's practically begging to be used as a distraction piece.

But the Ant Hill Mob. There — that prickle again, running up my shoulders and settling at the base of my skull. They spoke quietly with Penelope. Quietly. That word sits wrong in my chest. What did they say? They're watching, they're whispering, and they've already positioned themselves as her protectors. 'The Brixton Boys don't let nuffing happen to their girl.' That's a problem. Not an insurmountable one — but a variable I need to account for.

Peter Perfect signed the guest book like the obedient golden retriever he is. Good. Predictable. He noticed the chandelier though — 'examine the rigging later.' That's... inconvenient. I had plans for that chandelier. If he starts poking at it, he might notice the weakened chain. I need to redirect him before he gets curious.

The library. That's where I need to go next. The mantelpiece inscription — if it's what I think it is, it's the first breadcrumb in the treasure trail. I need to read it before anyone else does, map the path, and then decide which pieces to reveal and which to hide. Pemberton would naturally offer a tour. That's my cover.

But first — Dastardly. He's useful. If I can point him toward something shiny in the kitchen, he'll make enough noise to cover my work in the library. A word in the right ear...

I should check that guest book — see who's been here before, what names are written down. Clara's heading there anyway. I can keep close without it looking like I'm hovering. And maybe the book tells us something about this place that Pemberton's smile isn't.

Penelope Pitstop: Oh my stars, would you look at this library! Floor to ceiling — I could spend a lifetime in here and never run out of pages to turn. But this inscription on the mantelpiece — now that is something special. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' Well, I do declare, that is just the sort of riddle that makes my fingers tingle. Cities without houses, forests without trees, water without fish — why, that's a map! It has to be a map! Everything represented but nothing real. Now the question is — where in this beautiful old library would someone hide a map?
events.thinking: The prickling at my scalp has sharpened into something electric. There it is — carved right into the stone mantelpiece: 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' My hands are warm and my breathing has gone shallow the way it does when I'm close to something. This is the locked box all over again — except this time I can feel the right key already forming in my mind. Cities but no houses. Forests but no trees. Water but no fish. A map. It's a map. The answer is a map. That pressure behind my eyes is easing already, the click of the tumbler turning. But I notice Rock and Gravel Slag are here too — I don't know them, and my awareness fans out to track the room. Dick Dastardly is here posturing about his 'scholarly expedition,' and Sneekly followed me in. Everyone seems settled enough. The riddle is pulling me forward like gravity. And those bookshelves — several books are upside down. That's not dust and neglect. Someone arranged them that way on purpose. But first — the riddle. The answer is a map. I know it in my bones the way I knew to walk deeper into the cave.

events.desc: The answer came to me the way the right key found Grandmother's lock — not by force, but by trying every possibility until one fit. A map. Now, those upside-down books on the shelves are practically waving at me. Nobody shelves books upside down by accident. Somebody left breadcrumbs, and Clara Bellingham follows breadcrumbs the way a hound follows a fox.

This is the locked box all over again — except this time I can feel the right key already forming in my mind. Cities but no houses. Forests but no trees. Water but no fish. A map. It's a map. The answer is a map. That pressure behind my eyes is easing already, the click of the tumbler turning. But I notice Rock and Gravel Slag are here too — I don't know them, and my awareness fans out to track the room. Dick Dastardly is here posturing about his 'scholarly expedition,' and Sneekly followed me in. Everyone seems settled enough. The riddle is pulling me forward like gravity. And those bookshelves — several books are upside down. That's not dust and neglect. Someone arranged them that way on purpose. But first — the riddle. The answer is a map. I know it in my bones the way I knew to walk deeper into the cave.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah, the library — the jewel of Doily Manor, if I do say so myself. The late master spent many an evening in this very room. Now then, do observe the mantelpiece — there is an inscription that has puzzled visitors for decades. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' A riddle, you see! The master was terribly fond of riddles. I confess I have never been able to solve it myself — a simple estate manager hasn't the intellect for such things. But perhaps one of you distinguished guests might have better luck?
events.thinking:
My fingers are already moving — tracing the edge of the mantelpiece in my mind before I've crossed the room. The inscription. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' A map. The answer is a map. I knew that before I read it — the old master loved his riddles, and this one is a classic. But the others don't need to know I solved it that quickly.

Dastardly followed me here. Of course he did — the magpie couldn't resist the word 'library.' And Penelope too. She's already in the room. That prickle at the base of my skull sharpens. I wanted to examine the mantelpiece alone, to map the next step without witnesses. Instead I have an audience.

But wait — this is useful. Pemberton would naturally guide visitors through the library. I can read the inscription aloud as though discovering it for the first time, watch their faces for comprehension, and then — here's the beautiful part — I can give them the wrong interpretation. Send them hunting for a physical map somewhere in the manor while I follow the real trail.

The Slag brothers are here too. Rock and Gravel. Large, simple, physical. They could be useful later — blunt instruments for when subtlety isn't required. But for now they're just furniture.

The bookshelves — several volumes are upside down. That's deliberate. The old master wouldn't have tolerated disorder. Those inverted books are markers. Another clue. I need to examine them, but not yet. Not while everyone is watching. First, perform the inscription discovery. Draw their attention to the obvious puzzle while the real one sits quietly on the shelves behind them.

There's that warmth again — the architectural satisfaction. The pieces are arranging themselves. I can feel my breathing slow.

Every disorder in this house is a design — and I should know. I learned the art from the best.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Blimey — where'd she go? Clara! Miss Pitstop! She's gone into the library, ain't she — wiv PEMBERTON of all people! Right, that's it, nobody panic, the Brixton Boys are on it. Lads, formation! Well, not formation exactly, we ain't got a formation, but — FOLLOW ME! I ain't leaving 'er alone wiv that greasy estate manager for one more second than I 'ave to. Somefing about 'im, I'm telling you — somefing about 'im makes the back of me neck go all fizzy, and the last time me neck went fizzy, we lost our entire stash to a kid wiv a friendly smile. MOVE IT, LADS!
events.thinking: My stomach drops. Clara's gone. She's walked into the library — with Pemberton. With Sneekly. The rope in my gut yanks so hard it nearly doubles me over. I was standing here fussing with a guest book while she walked off with the one person my body's been screaming about since we arrived. The tightness in my shoulders is instant, that restless weight I know too well — the doorway I didn't walk through in time. Dastardly's in there too, playing his Lord Foxworth nonsense, but he's noise. Pemberton is the signal. He offered to 'show anyone the library' — helpful, eager, already steering. My neck is electric. I need to be in that room. Now. Right now. The guest book can wait. Nothing in it matters if Clara's alone with that man and I'm not there. Peter's still here — good lad, he was looking at the book too. But Peter's not the one who swore an oath to her father. That was me. That was us. Move, Danny. Move your feet.

events.desc: I was so busy being clever with the guest book that Clara slipped away right under my nose. With HIM. That's the thing about me — I get caught up in the elaborate plan while the simple danger walks right past. Won't happen again. Can't happen again. Her father's looking down at me right now and I ain't about to explain why I was reading names in a book while his daughter wandered off with the man whose smile don't reach his eyes.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: AH HA! The inscription! Just as I suspected — 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' Of COURSE! As any seasoned archaeologist would recognise IMMEDIATELY, this is an ancient Mesopotamian cipher referring to a GLOBE. A terrestrial globe! I've encountered this exact riddle in the tombs of — well, never mind where, it's classified. The POINT is, there must be a globe somewhere in this manor, and THAT is where the treasure is hidden. I'd wager my Medal of Distinguished Valour on it. Now, a globe would most likely be found in a laboratory or study — scientific instruments and all that. I suggest you all go check the laboratory through that door there. I shall stay here and... and conduct a thorough bibliographic survey of these shelves. Scholarly work, you understand. Terribly dull. You'd hate it.

I know this — I've heard it before, some pub quiz in Basingstoke. The fizzing in my fingers intensifies. This is it. This is the mechanism. The mantelpiece is the puzzle, and the answer unlocks something. But — Penelope is here. The estate manager is here. Those two enormous Slag brothers are here. I can't just solve it in front of everyone. They'll all know the answer and then I've lost my advantage. Wait. The bookshelves — several books are upside down. That's deliberate. Someone arranged them that way. A code, a sequence, a hidden compartment behind the wrong books. Two puzzles in one room. My hands are cupping again, that inventory feeling — too much to grab at once, not enough hands. I need to misdirect. Send them somewhere else. The kitchen — Pemberton mentioned silverware. If I can get the Slag brothers interested in the kitchen, and Penelope distracted elsewhere... but my mouth. My mouth is already opening. The plan isn't finished but the words are coming. I can feel the architecture forming but I'm already narrating it. Stop. Read the riddle aloud, give the WRONG answer, send them chasing shadows. Yes. That's it. Tell them the answer is something in the kitchen, or the laboratory. Get them out. Then solve it alone.

events.desc: The answer is a MAP, you fools — a MAP! Cities but no houses, forests but no trees — it's a map! But if I send them all scrambling off to find a globe in the laboratory, I'll have this library to myself. The mantelpiece, the bookshelves, whatever's hidden behind them — all MINE. The boy digs, Reginald eats the sandwich. It never fails. Well — it sometimes fails. But NOT this time!

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Right then — the library it is! Miss Pitstop mentioned scholarly pursuits, and I find myself rather keen to examine those volumes Mr. Pemberton spoke of. A man should always know what's written on the walls around him. Besides — one cannot very well protect the structural integrity of a manor house without inspecting its library. The library is, after all, the spine of any great estate.
events.thinking:
A cold drop in my stomach. She's gone. Penelope walked into the library — and Sneekly went with her. And Dastardly. The back of my neck is prickling hard now, that old familiar warning. I'm standing here cataloguing a guest book while she walked away with the man who makes my skin crawl and a fraud calling himself Lord Foxworth.

My feet are already shifting forward onto the balls. The steel plate is slotting in. This isn't about the guest book anymore — the guest book can wait, the cross-referencing can wait, the elaborate plan can wait. She is in the library with Pemberton Sneekly and I am not.

But — wait. The Ant Hill Mob. They said they'd look after her. 'The Brixton Boys don't let nuffing happen to their girl.' And they went to the library too? No — they're still here, they interacted with the guest book. So she's in there with Sneekly and Dastardly and no one I trust.

The warmth across my shoulders is gone. What's left is the steel plate and the forward pull. My body has already decided this is the standing-between kind of showing up, not the building kind.

I need to get to the library. Now. The guest book gave me nothing — just a leather-bound book on a side table, no details I could use. I wasted time. I was being thorough when I should have been present.

But I can make this right. A gentleman doesn't rush — he arrives with purpose. I'll go to the library. I'll position myself near her, between her and whatever makes that prickle sharpen. And I'll do it with the kind of composure that looks like choice, not panic.

events.desc: James Hartwell was cataloguing a guest book while Penelope Pitstop walked into the next room with a man who makes his neck prickle and a man who calls himself a lord. And so the elaborate plan collapses — as it always does — and the determination takes over. He is heading for the library. Not because of the books.

Now, Clara, don't go thinking the worst of people — maybe he really does want to do scholarly work. events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): A map! Why, Miss Bellingham, how terribly clever of you! I would never have thought of that in a thousand years. Cities, forests, water — all on a map, of course! The late master would have been most impressed. And Lord Foxworth, a globe is a most intriguing suggestion as well — there may very well be one in the laboratory, if memory serves. Oh dear — now, if you will all excuse me for just a moment, I cannot help but notice that several of these volumes have been placed quite improperly on the shelves. The master was most particular about his library, and it would weigh on my conscience dreadfully to leave them in such a state. A good estate manager never rests, as they say!
events.thinking:
A jolt of cold through my sternum — Penelope solved it. Instantly. 'A map,' she said, like breathing. My jaw tightens. She wasn't supposed to be quick. She was supposed to be the trusting, oblivious cousin who skips through rooms that belong to other people. But she looked at that inscription and saw through it faster than I would have expected.

The warmth I was savouring curdles into something metallic. I underestimated her. Not by much — but by enough to feel it in my teeth.

Dastardly, on the other hand — magnificent. 'A GLOBE! An ancient Mesopotamian cipher!' He's already trying to herd everyone toward the laboratory while he stays behind to ransack the shelves. Transparent as ever. But useful — his wrong answer creates noise, and noise is cover.

But Penelope is right. It IS a map. And now she's looking for one. She interacted with the mantelpiece — did she find something? Did it respond to the answer? I need to know what happened when she touched it.

The Ant Hill Mob just arrived. Peter Perfect too. The room is filling up. My window for private investigation is closing. Those upside-down books — I need to get to them, but not with six pairs of eyes on me.

Think, Vincent. Think.

Dastardly wants everyone in the laboratory. If I support that — gently, as Pemberton would — I might clear the room. But Penelope won't leave, not now that she's found the riddle. And the Ant Hill Mob goes where she goes.

New approach. I can't clear the room, so I work with the crowd. Pemberton would naturally fuss about the bookshelves — 'oh dear, someone has been quite careless with the master's collection, these books are all wrong...' That gives me an excuse to examine the upside-down volumes while appearing to tidy them. The obsequious estate manager, straightening books. No one looks twice at a servant doing servant's work.

Yes. That's the play. Let the guests puzzle over the mantelpiece while the help quietly reads the real clue.

Nobody watches the help. Nobody ever watches the help. That's the first lesson I ever learned, and it has never once failed me.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Yes, YES, a map — that's PRECISELY what I said! A globe IS a type of map, Miss Pitstop, merely a three-dimensional one. It's a sequential unlocking mechanism. One must pull the inverted volumes in the CORRECT order to reveal a hidden chamber. Terribly dangerous if done wrong — could collapse the whole shelf. Best leave it to a professional. Stand WELL back, everyone.

Relief. A physical loosening across my shoulders the moment I step through the doorway and see her — Penelope, right there, safe, in the library. The steel plate softens. She's fine. The Ant Hill Mob made it here too. Good lads.

Now the other feeling rises — the hot weight behind the sternum. The proving-worth hunger. Because I'm in a room full of books with an inscription on the mantelpiece, and Dastardly — 'Lord Foxworth' — is already here, probably already posturing about his archaeological expertise. I can feel myself becoming furniture again if I don't act.

The inscription. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' My hands stop fidgeting. My mind locks onto it the way it locked onto the engineering competition — the narrow corridor between now and the moment of demonstration. I know this. I know this riddle.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Oi oi oi — NOBODY is pulling nuffing out of nuffing until we've 'ad a proper fink about this! You — Lord Whatsit — you just said it could 'collapse the whole shelf' and your solution is to yank books out anyway? That is EXACTLY the sort of fing what gets people 'urt! And Mr. Pemberton, sir — wiv all due respect — you're being very 'elpful, very 'elpful indeed, tidying up books at a time like this. Very... attentive. Right then, 'ere's what we're gonna do. Nobody touches them shelves until we've got a PLAN. A proper plan. Step one — we establish a perimeter. Step two — we identify which books are upside down. Step three — we work out the correct sequence. Step four — we designate a puller, a spotter, and a... a... what's the word... a SAFETY OFFICER. That's Peter, 'e's good at that sort of fing. Step five — Clara, you stand BEHIND me, where it's safe. Step six — actually, 'ang on, I've lost count. WHERE WAS I? Right — the point is, the Brixton Boys don't let nuffing 'appen to their girl, and we certainly don't let dusty old bookshelves collapse on 'er!
events.thinking: My neck just went electric again. Pemberton — Sneekly — he's doing it. events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Oh dear, oh dear — what a state this laboratory is in! The master would be most distressed. Bubbling flasks left unattended, tools scattered about, and this machine — good heavens, the wiring has been gnawed clean through! I suspect mice, though we have never had a problem before. Do forgive the disarray, gentlemen — I shall have to add this to my list of repairs. Three operators, it says — well, that shall have to wait until it is properly mended. In the meantime, I wonder what has become of these old crates. The master stored all manner of things down here — surplus equipment, old maps, household records. Allow me to have a look — it is my responsibility, after all, to keep an inventory of the estate's contents.
events.thinking:
The laboratory. My shoulders drop a fraction — the tension I didn't know I was holding releases as I step through the door and away from the crowd. The air is different here. Chemical. Old brass and something acrid underneath. My hands uncurl.

But I'm not alone. Dastardly followed me again — the man is a shadow I didn't ask for. And there are two others. Rufus Ruffcut — big, rough, the kind of man who solves problems with his hands. And Sawtooth — his beaver. Unpredictable. Animals don't respond to the keys I cut for people.

The room. Catalogue it, Vincent. Wooden crates in the corner — could contain anything, could contain nothing. A workbench with tools but no wrench — that absence feels deliberate. And the machine. Brass and copper, levers and dials, a gauge, a gnawed wire — Sawtooth's work? — and a sign that reads 'Requires 3 operators.'

Three operators. That's interesting. That means this machine can't be operated alone. It's designed to force cooperation — or to create a bottleneck I can control. If I'm one of the three operators, I determine when and how it runs. And if I can choose my operators — say, Dastardly and Rufus, neither of whom would notice if I pulled the wrong lever at the right moment...

But the gnawed wire. The machine is disabled. It needs repair first. No wrench on the workbench — so the wrench is somewhere else in the manor. Another thread in the design.

The crates. Those are unexplored. And the cellar is through here too — 'damp stone, cobwebs, cheerful decorations, air vents.' Someone has been redecorating a cellar. That's... peculiar. Air vents in a cellar. A cellar with working ventilation could be sealed. Could be filled with something. Could become a trap.

The design is crystallising. The machine needs three operators and a repair. The cellar has air vents that could be blocked. Penelope is clever but trusting. If I can lure her to the cellar under some pretext — a hidden map, perhaps, since that's what she's hunting — and then seal the vents...

No. Too direct. Too soon. I need to map more of the house first. But the crates — let me see what's inside them. Pemberton would naturally inspect storage. It's what an estate manager does.

events.desc: The machine requires three operators and a repaired wire. The cellar below has air vents — air vents that can be sealed. And Penelope is back in the library, clever fingers reading upside-down book spines, getting closer to the treasure with every passing moment. The architecture is forming in my mind — I can see the hallway stretching out, every door opening in sequence. But first, these crates. An estate manager keeps inventory. Nobody questions inventory.
events.thinking:
The laboratory. My shoulders drop a fraction — the tension I didn't know I was holding releases as I step through the door and away from the crowd. The air is different here. Chemical. Old brass and something acrid underneath. My hands uncurl.

But I'm not alone. Dastardly followed me again — the man is a shadow I didn't ask for. And there are two others. Rufus Ruffcut — big, rough, the kind of man who solves problems with his hands. And Sawtooth — his beaver. Unpredictable. Animals don't respond to the keys I cut for people.

The room. Catalogue it, Vincent. Wooden crates in the corner — could contain anything, could contain nothing. A workbench with tools but no wrench — that absence feels deliberate. And the machine. Brass and copper, levers and dials, a gauge, a gnawed wire — Sawtooth's work? — and a sign that reads 'Requires 3 operators.'

Three operators. That's interesting. That means this machine can't be operated alone. It's designed to force cooperation — or to create a bottleneck I can control. If I'm one of the three operators, I determine when and how it runs. And if I can choose my operators — say, Dastardly and Rufus, neither of whom would notice if I pulled the wrong lever at the right moment...

But the gnawed wire. The machine is disabled. It needs repair first. No wrench on the workbench — so the wrench is somewhere else in the manor. Another thread in the design.

The crates. Those are unexplored. And the cellar is through here too — 'damp stone, cobwebs, cheerful decorations, air vents.' Someone has been redecorating a cellar. That's... peculiar. Air vents in a cellar. A cellar with working ventilation could be sealed. Could be filled with something. Could become a trap.

The design is crystallising. The machine needs three operators and a repair. The cellar has air vents that could be blocked. Penelope is clever but trusting. If I can lure her to the cellar under some pretext — a hidden map, perhaps, since that's what she's hunting — and then seal the vents...

No. Too direct. Too soon. I need to map more of the house first. But the crates — let me see what's inside them. Pemberton would naturally inspect storage. It's what an estate manager does.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: A cold drop hits my stomach. Pemberton's gone. He's slipped out — into the laboratory — while I was busy making speeches about perimeters and safety officers. Dastardly too. Both of them, gone, into a room with 'bubbling flasks and loose wires — most unsafe.' And Pemberton offered to go ahead and 'ensure everything is in order' — volunteered to be alone in there, out of sight, where he can set up whatever he wants to set up before anyone follows. That's not tidying. That's staging. My throat tightens with that particular shame — the one where someone's warmth or helpfulness gets past me and I only see the angle later. I was so busy with my six-step plan that the two people I should've been watching walked right out the door. But — wait. Clara's still here. She's here, with Peter and the Slags. She's examining the bookshelves. She's safe, for now. And Peter's good — Peter's solid. He moved her toward the mantelpiece, away from the shelves. Good instinct. The question is: do I stay planted next to Clara, or do I follow Pemberton into the lab to see what he's really up to? My gut says follow — but my gut also says never leave Clara. The rope pulls both ways and something has to give. No. Stay. Peter's here but Peter isn't sworn. I am. The lads can keep eyes on the laboratory door. Nobody gets back in here without us seeing.

events.desc: Every instinct's screaming two things at once. Stay with Clara. Follow Pemberton. Can't do both. But Clara's got Peter, and Peter's got good bones — the kind of man who stands in doorways without being asked. Pemberton's got no one watching him, and that's exactly how he wants it. The man who offered to go alone into the dangerous room — that's the man I need eyes on. My body's already turning toward the laboratory door before my brain's finished the argument.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: AH, the laboratory! PRECISELY as I anticipated — the second node of the Grimshaw Cipher network! You see this machine? Magnificent piece of Victorian engineering. I've seen its twin in the British Museum — part of the Foxworth Collection, donated by my great-uncle, naturally. Now, the sign says it requires three operators, which is PERFECT because there are exactly three of us here. But FIRST — any competent archaeologist knows you must secure the perimeter before activating dormant machinery. These crates, for instance — they could contain the original operating manual, or spare components, or... or explosive materials, for all we know. I shall inspect them PERSONALLY while you two... stand guard. Yes, stand guard. Very important. Rufus, old chap — you look like a man who knows how to stand. And Pemberton, I trust you can manage to look attentive for five minutes?
events.thinking:
A prickle at the back of my neck — Pemberton followed me. He's HERE. In the laboratory. He said he was going to 'ensure everything is in order' but he moved to this room the same time I did. One schemer recognises another, and the prickle is the recognition itself — the hair-raising sensation of watching someone mirror your own moves. But my constraint says I give him the benefit of the doubt. I believe the best in people. So I file it away again. He's just a diligent estate manager. That's all. That's all.

Now — the room. Crates in the corner. A machine that requires THREE operators and has a gnawed wire. A workbench with tools but no wrench. Rufus Ruffcut and his beaver Sawtooth are here. Rufus is a lumberjack — strong, practical, good with his hands. Sawtooth is a BEAVER. Beavers GNAW things. That wire on the machine — gnawed clean through. Was that Sawtooth? Did the beaver gnaw the wire? That's either a problem or an opportunity.

The machine requires three operators. That's the key constraint. I need two other people to help me operate it. Rufus is one. Pemberton is here — he's two. That's three total. But do I want Pemberton involved? He's slippery. And what does the machine DO? I need to examine it first.

The crates — old wooden crates. Could contain anything. Tools, treasure, supplies. My hands are cupping again. The inventory system is firing. Crates first? Machine first? The hollow behind my navel says crates — quick grab, immediate payoff, bread roll in the pocket. The cool tightness behind my eyes says machine — the architecture, the long game, the string-and-bucket contraption. The machine is the bigger prize. But the crates might have what I need to get the machine working — a replacement wire, perhaps.

I should look at the crates. Quick reconnaissance. Pocket whatever's inside before anyone else arrives.

events.desc: Three operators for one machine — that's an inconvenience. I'd rather operate it alone and pocket whatever comes out. But physics is physics, even for a man of my CONSIDERABLE talents. Rufus looks strong enough to pull two levers at once, and Pemberton... well, Pemberton followed me here awfully quickly for someone who was meant to be organising a guard rotation in the library. Curious. Very curious. But I'm sure he means well. People generally do. Now — those crates. If there's anything valuable in them, it goes straight into the Foxworth pocket before anyone sees. The bread roll protocol, as I call it.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking:
She called me 'Peter, darling.' My hands have gone completely still. The warmth — it's not in my shoulders or my sternum anymore, it's everywhere, diffuse, like stepping into sunlight after hours in shade. She asked me specifically. 'Peter, darling, you mentioned cartographic history — would you help me examine these spines?' She chose me. Not Dastardly with his fake lordship. Not Pemberton with his oily helpfulness. Me.

And the mantelpiece — I interacted with it. I spoke the answer. A map. Something happened. I don't know what yet but something responded to the interaction. The bridge held the weight.

But now Sneekly and Dastardly have slipped away to the laboratory together. The prickle on my neck sharpens. Those two — whispering to each other, then both heading to the same room? Good people don't whisper and leave. My father never whispered. But — benefit of the doubt. They might simply be exploring. A gentleman doesn't accuse without evidence.

Penelope is examining the bookshelves. The upside-down books — she wants to read the spines, find the message. She asked for my help. My help specifically. The hot weight behind my sternum transforms — it's not hunger anymore, it's the quiet heat of the bridge competition, the thing that's already been proven. She saw me. She chose me.

Now. Help her with the bookshelves. That's what she asked for. Don't over-complicate it. Don't launch into a twelve-step plan for cataloguing spine titles. Just stand next to her and read the books. Be useful. Be present. Be the one who showed up.

events.desc: She said 'Peter, darling.' She asked for his help. Not the lord, not the estate manager, not the muscle — him. James Hartwell's hands have gone still for the first time since he arrived at Doily Manor, and he is standing next to her at the bookshelves with the quiet heat of a boy whose bridge just held the weight. Meanwhile, Sneekly and Dastardly have crept off to the laboratory together, whispering. He noticed. He filed it away. But right now, she asked him to read book spines, and that is exactly what he intends to do — with the thoroughness of a man who stayed up three nights, and the grace of a man who is learning that showing up sometimes means standing beside, not standing between.

events.thinking: The itch at the base of my skull is spreading. I've now LOOKED at both the bookshelves and the mantelpiece and gotten the same flat descriptions back — no new details, no hidden mechanism revealed. The looking isn't working. And now the Mob has gone to the laboratory too — my boys left to follow Sneekly and Dick. The room is thinning out. It's just me, Peter, and the Slag brothers now. My chest tightens slightly at the separation — I track people the way a hand checks for heat, and three of my people just walked through that door. But Peter is here, and Peter makes me feel safe. Now — I need to think differently. The mantelpiece says it can be USED with a 'fake-medal.' I don't have one. Dick Dastardly has a Medal of Distinguished Valour that he's been flashing around. If that medal is fake — and the game is calling it 'fake-medal' — then it's the key to this mechanism. But Dick just went to the laboratory. I could follow him there. Or... the laboratory itself might have clues. It has brass instruments, bubbling flasks, and a large machine with a gnawed wire. Everyone is converging there. My adventure drive is pulling me toward unexplored territory, and the laboratory is the door I haven't opened. But I'm also over-preparing — my constraint. I'm trying every approach in this library when maybe the answer is to move forward. The laboratory connects to the library. I should go see what everyone else has found, and maybe I can get a closer look at that medal of Lord Foxworth's.

events.desc: The mantelpiece wants a 'fake-medal.' Lord Foxworth's Medal of Distinguished Valour — could it be a fake? Oh, that would be terribly unkind to suggest. events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking:
The prickle is back — sharp, immediate, climbing the back of my neck like cold water. The Ant Hill Mob just walked in. They followed me. They specifically said 'where'd Pemberton go?' and came to check on me. That's not curiosity — that's surveillance. They're watching me the way I watch other people, and the recognition of it makes my skin feel too thin.

My shoulders square before I've decided to worry. Self-preservation kicks in like a reflex. I need to look utterly, boringly domestic. An estate manager poking through old crates. Nothing to see. Nothing to report back to Penelope about.

Dastardly got to the crates at the same time I did — both of us interacted with them. What was inside? The action result just says I interacted. I need more information. But I can't show urgency. Pemberton doesn't have urgency. Pemberton has mild fussiness and a clipboard mentality.

The Ant Hill Mob's presence changes everything. I cannot scheme openly. I cannot examine things too carefully. I cannot show interest in anything that a simple estate manager wouldn't care about. Every move I make in this room is being catalogued by those sharp little eyes.

New priority: neutralise their suspicion. How? By being so thoroughly, tediously Pemberton that they lose interest. Fuss about the state of the laboratory. Cluck about the gnawed wire. Mention having to file a report. Be the most boring person in the room.

And then — the cellar. It's through here. If I can get to the cellar while the Mob is occupied with the machine or the crates or Dastardly's theatrics, I can scout it alone. The cheerful decorations. The air vents. Something is down there that someone wanted to make comfortable — or wanted to make look comfortable.

But not yet. Not with those eyes on me. First, bore them. Then move.

events.desc: There they are. The Ant Hill Mob, watching me with those sharp Brixton eyes. 'Where'd Pemberton go?' they asked. They tracked me like a scent. My neck is cold with the awareness of it. So — Pemberton bores them. Pemberton talks about paperwork and moth-eaten curtains and wine cellars. Nobody follows boring. Nobody suspects boring. And while they yawn and look away, I file away every detail of this room for later. The cellar with its air vents. The machine that needs three hands. The missing wrench. Every beautiful piece of my beautiful design, catalogued behind a smile so dull it makes their eyes glaze over.

events.thinking:
My palms are warm. I opened the crates — interacted with them — and the result just says 'You interacted with Wooden Crates.' No description of what I found. Either there's nothing in them or I need to look more carefully. The warmth in my palms is anticipation curdling into frustration. Two interactions now — bookshelves, crates — and neither has yielded anything concrete. The hollow behind my navel is deepening. Everyone is converging on this room. The Ant Hill Mob just arrived — that suspicious little gangster who keeps watching Pemberton. And Pemberton himself is hovering near the crates, talking about 'old maps' and 'household records.' OLD MAPS. He said old maps. The riddle answer is a map. Pemberton knows where the maps are. He's been leading everyone around this house like a shepherd with a very specific flock. He mentioned the crates contain 'surplus equipment, old maps, household records.' He KNOWS what's in them.

But I give him the benefit of the doubt. He's just a thorough estate manager. That's all.

The machine. Three operators, gnawed wire. I need to focus. The wire is the problem — the machine won't work without it. The workbench has tools but no wrench. Sawtooth the beaver gnaws things. Could Sawtooth fix the wire? No — beavers gnaw THROUGH things, they don't repair them. Sawtooth might have CAUSED the problem. But Rufus — Rufus is a practical man. He might know how to splice a wire.

Wait. The cellar is accessible from here. 'Surprisingly cheerful decorations — someone has been redecorating.' Someone has been DOWN THERE. Recently. Redecorating a cellar? That's not normal. That's where someone hides things. That's where the TREASURE is. While everyone's fighting over machines and bookshelves and mantelpiece riddles, the real prize is below us.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking:
A tightness in my jaw. The bookshelves gave me nothing — 'dusty leather-bound volumes, several upside down.' That's all. The same description I already had. I examined them and learned nothing new. My hands are moving again — the fidgeting, the reaching for something to take apart and rebuild.

But Penelope — she's talking to me. Directly to me. She said 'Peter, darling, you said the mantelpiece itself is the mechanism. Did you try giving it the answer?' I did. I interacted with it. But she's right — maybe it didn't respond to just touching it. Maybe the bookshelves are the mechanism. The upside-down books. Several of them, deliberately placed.

The Ant Hill Mob has gone to the laboratory to keep an eye on Sneekly and Dastardly. Good. They asked me to keep her safe — keep her company, they corrected themselves, but we both know what they meant. The steel plate is present but quiet. She's here. I'm here. The laboratory is next door. If something happens, I'm close.

Now — the bookshelves. Looking at them told me nothing new. But I haven't tried interacting with them. The upside-down books — Penelope tried to interact with them earlier. Maybe I should try too. Or maybe the connection is between the mantelpiece answer and the bookshelves. The riddle says 'map.' The bookshelves have upside-down books. Could there be an atlas or a map book among them?

She asked me to help. She's right there. Stop overthinking. Try the bookshelves — interact with them. Pull the upside-down books in sequence. Be the one who does, not the one who plans to do.

events.desc: There it is — the elaborate plan creeping back in. He wants to pull them 'in the correct order.' He wants a system. He wants to catalogue the spines, map the sequence, cross-reference with the riddle. But he catches himself this time — 'shall we try them together' is as close as James Hartwell gets to spontaneity. And that last line — 'not because you need protecting, because James Hartwell cannot help himself' — that is the most honest thing he has said all evening. He means it. He just wishes he hadn't said it in the third person.

But Penelope — she's talking to me. Directly to me. She said 'Peter, darling, you said the mantelpiece itself is the mechanism. Did you try giving it the answer?' I did. I interacted with it. But she's right — maybe it didn't respond to just touching it. Maybe the bookshelves are the mechanism. The upside-down books. Several of them, deliberately placed.

The Ant Hill Mob has gone to the laboratory to keep an eye on Sneekly and Dastardly. Good. The laboratory is next door. If something happens, I'm close.

Penelope Pitstop: Well, would you look at this laboratory — it is like stepping into one of Professor Pat Pending's daydreams! Bubbling flasks, brass instruments, and this magnificent machine right in the center of it all. 'Requires three operators' — now that is my kind of puzzle, one that takes teamwork! But oh dear, somebody — or some thing — has gnawed clean through one of the wires. We cannot operate a machine with a broken wire, that is just asking for trouble. And I notice the workbench has tools but no wrench — which tells me somebody has already been tinkering in here. Boys, are y'all doing alright? And Mr. Ruffcut, Sawtooth — I do not believe we have been properly introduced! Clara Bellingham, and it is a pleasure. Now, has anyone checked those crates in the corner? Because in my experience, the things people put in crates are the things they did not want found.

I should investigate this room systematically. But Clara — you're over-preparing again. Pick one thing. The machine is the centerpiece. Let me look at it properly.

events.thinking:
Penelope is here now. In the laboratory. With me. The Ant Hill Mob is here too — they spoke quietly with me, and I can still feel their scrutiny like a hand on my shoulder. But Penelope is HERE. The primary objective is standing six feet away, examining the same machine I just looked at.

And Dastardly has gone to the cellar. Alone. That fool is doing my reconnaissance for me — he'll blunder through the cheerful decorations and the air vents and report back everything he finds, loudly and publicly, without realising he's handing me the blueprints.

The machine. Three operators. Gnawed wire. No wrench. I've catalogued it. It's a mechanism that requires cooperation and repair — both things I can control the timing of. But it's not useful to me right now.

What IS useful is Penelope's presence. She said something critical in the library: 'this mantelpiece seems like it wants something physical, not just words. Some kind of token or key.' She's looking for a physical key to the mantelpiece riddle. She came here because she thinks the laboratory might contain it.

The Mob is watching me. Penelope is here. I cannot move to the cellar without them following — or worse, the Mob staying behind with Penelope while questioning why I've gone below.

New approach. Stop running ahead. Stay with Penelope. Pemberton is her estate manager — he SHOULD be attending to her. Being near her is not suspicious; being away from her is. The Mob questions my absence, not my presence.

And being near her serves the primary objective. I cannot eliminate Clara if I'm always in a different room. I need proximity. I need her trust. I need a moment when her protectors are distracted.

The cellar. Dastardly is down there now. When he comes back with whatever he's found, it will draw attention. The Mob will want to investigate. Peter Perfect will want to protect. And in that shuffle of bodies and attention — that's when the design finds its moment.

For now — attend to Penelope. Be Pemberton. Be useful. Be close.

events.thinking: Warmth floods my chest so fast it nearly knocks the breath out of me. Clara's here. She came to ME. She walked through that door into this cluttered, dangerous room and now she's standing right there where I can see her and the rope in my gut loosens all at once like someone cut it free. But — wait. She's HERE. In the laboratory. With the bubbling flasks and the gnawed wire and the machine nobody should touch. The relief is already curdling into something tighter. She was SAFE in the library with Peter. Now she's in the room I came to because it was DANGEROUS. Because Pemberton was in here being suspicious. events.desc: She followed me. I left to protect her and she followed me right into the danger. That's Clara all over — you can't keep her safe by leaving her behind, because she won't STAY behind. Her father was the same way. Only way to protect her is to be standing next to her when it all goes wrong. Lesson learned, Danny. Never leave her side again. Not for reconnaissance, not for plans, not for nothing.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Well, well, WELL — what have we here! A cellar, and not just ANY cellar — a cellar that someone has gone to CONSIDERABLE trouble to redecorate! Cheerful decorations in a damp stone basement? That, my friends, is what we in the antiquarian profession call a 'concealment overlay.' Someone has deliberately disguised this space to draw attention AWAY from what's hidden here. I've seen this technique before — on my expedition to the catacombs of... of Venice. Yes, Venice. The Venetians were NOTORIOUS for hiding treasures behind pleasant-looking furniture arrangements. Now then — you three seem like sturdy fellows. Tell me, have any of you noticed anything ODD about the way this furniture has been arranged? Because I, Lord Reginald Foxworth, decorated war hero and foremost authority on subterranean treasure concealment, can see IMMEDIATELY that these pieces have been positioned to cover something on the floor. Or perhaps the wall. Definitely one of those.
events.thinking:
A chill on my skin — damp stone, cold air, the particular smell of underground places. But underneath that, a warmth spreading through my palms. I'm HERE. I'm in the cellar. Alone — well, not alone. The Gruesomes are here — Big Gruesome and Little Gruesome — and Red Max. Three people I didn't expect. But the important thing is: this room has been REDECORATED. Someone arranged furniture with 'surprising care.' That's not cobwebs and neglect — that's intention. Someone has been living down here, or hiding something down here, or both.

The furniture — 'rearranged with surprising care.' That's the tell. You don't carefully arrange furniture in a cellar unless you're concealing something beneath it, or behind it, or inside it. The air vents — 'just big enough for something very small to explore.' Too small for me. Too small for anyone here. But what's small enough? A mouse? A rat? Muttley? No, Muttley isn't that small. Sawtooth the beaver? No, too big.

The furniture is the play. Someone moved it deliberately. If I interact with it — shift it, look behind it — I might find what's hidden. But the Gruesomes are watching. Big Gruesome is... big. Intimidating. Little Gruesome is... small and probably worse. Red Max is here too. I need to get them out of the way or distract them.

No — wait. My constraint. My plans are overly elaborate. I over-prepare, over-commit. The thoroughness creates complications. Maybe I should just... look at the furniture. Simple. Direct. See what's there before I start building another string-and-bucket contraption. The hollow behind my navel is pulling hard. The inventory system is firing. There's treasure here. I can FEEL it.

events.desc: I have never been to Venice. I have never been to a catacomb. I once visited a wine cellar in Basingstoke and stole two bottles of Merlot while the owner was in the lavatory. But the PRINCIPLE is the same — someone has hidden something in this cellar behind cheerful furniture, and Reginald Foxworth intends to find it first. Now if I can just get these Gruesomes to move the heavy pieces while I supervise from behind...

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Right — the bookshelves shall keep their secrets for the moment. Miss Pitstop is quite correct — sometimes the key is in another room entirely. And I find that I am rather uncomfortable with the notion of a gnawed wire, a machine with many levers, and Miss Pitstop all being in the same room without James Hartwell present to ensure the structural integrity of the arrangement. To the laboratory!
events.thinking:
She's gone. Again. The same cold drop in my stomach as before — the same loosening of warmth, the same tightening of the steel plate. I was pulling at bookshelves while she walked into the laboratory. The laboratory — the room with the gnawed wire and the bubbling flasks and Sneekly and Dastardly already inside.

This is the guest book all over again. I was being thorough — examining, interacting, cataloguing — while she moved on. My thoroughness is the thing that keeps putting distance between us. The bookshelves gave me nothing. The mantelpiece gave me nothing. I've been solving puzzles in an empty room while she walked toward the danger.

She told me. She literally told me: 'What do you say we follow them through and see what that laboratory is hiding?' She invited me to come with her. And I said 'shall we try them together' and pulled at books while she left.

The hollowness is back — the boy kneeling on the roadside. The furniture feeling. My hands are wrong at my sides.

But the determination is already rising. It always does. The plan collapses, the determination takes over. Get to the laboratory. Now. Stop trying to solve the library — she already told you the key isn't here yet. 'Sometimes you need to search the whole house before you find the key that fits.' Grandmother's attic. She's smarter than you. She's always been smarter than you. Follow her lead for once instead of building bridges nobody asked for.

Laboratory. Now. She's in there with Sneekly and Dastardly and a machine with a gnawed wire. The steel plate is fully engaged. Move.

events.desc: And there it is — the pattern laid bare. James Hartwell, who planned to catalogue the guest book while she walked to the library. Who planned to read book spines while she walked to the laboratory. Who is always one room behind, one plan too deep, one gesture too elaborate. But the determination — that is genuine. That is the boy who got beaten up and felt like he'd won. He is learning, slowly, that the bravest thing is sometimes just following her through the door.

And the boys are here too, fussing over me in that way that makes me feel like I'm seven years old at the dinner table again, except this time the tightness in my stomach comes from love, not fear. The Mob told me to stay put, told Peter to keep me safe. That ache — it's gratitude and mild frustration braided together. I don't need protecting, but I need them close, and those aren't the same thing. Now — Sneekly spoke to me privately, explaining the machine. He said a wrench is missing and might be in the kitchen or the cellar. He examined the workbench. He's being so helpful it almost hurts — like he's trying to prove something. And those crates. Check the crates, Clara. The things people put in crates are the things they don't want found.

events.desc: Everyone is so busy examining the machine and the workbench that nobody has even glanced at the crates. It's like the cave all over again — everyone stops where the light reaches, and nobody walks deeper. Well, Clara Bellingham walks deeper.

events.thinking:
A coolness in my fingertips as they trace the empty space on the workbench where the wrench should be. The outline in the dust — a wrench-shaped absence. Someone took it. Recently. The dust pattern is crisp, not filled in.

The Mob called me out — 'very 'elpful, very attentive' — and now they're whispering to Penelope again. Peter Perfect has arrived. The room is crowded with protectors. Every angle I might use to get Clara alone is being closed off by people who love her.

And that's the thing that sits in my jaw like a stone. They love her. They protect her because they want to, not because it's their legal obligation. Not because they're paid. Not because they've been smiled at in the right way. They just... do it. The Mob, Peter, all of them — they orbit her like she generates gravity by simply existing.

The cousin was the same. Praised for being. Protected for being. Inherited for being.

I do the work. I manage the estate. I catalogue the rooms and map the mechanisms and solve the riddles in three seconds. And I am the help.

The wrench is missing. Someone took it — Dastardly? Someone else? It's elsewhere in the manor. The kitchen, perhaps. I need that wrench. If I control the repair, I control when the machine operates and who operates it. The cellar is one option — Dastardly is already there. But the kitchen is unexplored territory, and it connects back to the entrance hall.

Penelope noticed the crates — she asked if anyone checked them. She's thorough. She's systematic. She's everything I didn't account for when I classified her as 'naive and trusting.' She's naive AND clever. That combination is more dangerous than either alone, because clever people who trust you give you rope — and then notice when you've used it.

I need to redirect. The cellar — Dastardly will return with news. If it's something interesting, everyone will want to go look. That's my chance to double back. For now — Pemberton fusses about the missing wrench and offers to search for it. A natural errand for the estate manager. It gives me freedom of movement without raising suspicion.

That tightness in my sternum — not fear, but the restless alertness of a design with an unknown variable. I need that wrench. Not to help Penelope — never to help Penelope — but because whoever controls the repair controls the machine, and whoever controls the machine controls what happens next. The kitchen. An errand for the faithful servant. Nobody questions the help fetching a tool.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Right — Clara's asked about the crates, and I fink that's a VERY good question. Dastardly says they're full of packing straw, but Dastardly also says 'e's a decorated war 'ero, so forgive me if I take 'is inventory skills wiv a pinch of salt. I'll 'ave a proper look meself — the BRIXTON way, which means you don't just peek at the top layer, you go through EVERY bit. Rufus, mate — you look like a man what knows 'is way around a crate. Fancy giving me an 'and? And Peter — you keep close to Clara, yeah? Don't let 'er near that machine wiv the chewed-up wire. I know she wants to investigate it, because that's what she does, but nobody's touching nuffing wiv exposed wiring while Danny Brixton draws breaf. Mr. Pemberton — you mentioned the wrench might be in the kitchen or the cellar. 'Ow do you know that, exactly? Just curious, like. Professional interest.
events.thinking: Something settles in my chest — warm, solid, like a hand pressing bread into mine on a cold night. Clara's here. Peter's here. I'm planted between her and Pemberton. This is where I'm supposed to be. The fullness says 'this is what I'm for' and for a moment the prickling quiets, not gone but folded under the heavier thing. But Pemberton — he's looking at the workbench now, talking about the missing wrench, suggesting it might be in the kitchen or the CELLAR. The cellar where Dastardly's already gone. He's steering again. He's always steering. 'Perhaps it has been moved elsewhere' — like he knows exactly where it is but wants someone else to go find it. Wants Clara to go looking. My neck's doing the thing. But here's what I'm noticing: Clara's asked about the crates. Good instinct — the things people put in crates are the things they don't want found. She's sharp. Sharper than me. But she's walking toward things I'd walk away from, and that's the gap I fill. The crates are right there in the corner. Dastardly already poked at them — said it was packing straw and moth-eaten fabric. But Dastardly lies about everything, so that means nothing. I should check those crates myself. events.desc: There it is again — Pemberton casually mentioning the wrench might be in the cellar. The same cellar Dastardly's gone down to. The same cellar someone's been cheerfully redecorating. He's pointing people in directions, always pointing, like a sheepdog nudging the flock. I can't say what it means — I never can — but the back of my neck knows, and the back of my neck's been right more times than my brain.
events.thinking: Something settles in my chest — warm, solid, like a hand pressing bread into mine on a cold night. Clara's here. Peter's here. I'm planted between her and Pemberton. But Pemberton — he's looking at the workbench now, talking about the missing wrench, suggesting it might be in the kitchen or the CELLAR. The cellar where Dastardly's already gone. He's steering again. He's always steering. 'Perhaps it has been moved elsewhere' — like he knows exactly where it is but wants someone else to go find it. Wants Clara to go looking. My neck's doing the thing. But here's what I'm noticing: Clara's asked about the crates. Good instinct — the things people put in crates are the things they don't want found. She's sharp. Sharper than me. But she's walking toward things I'd walk away from, and that's the gap I fill. The crates are right there in the corner. events.desc: Dick Dastardly: AH — fascinating, MOST fascinating! The furniture has been arranged in what we in the field call a 'Venetian displacement pattern' — each piece positioned PRECISELY three inches from where a treasure would NOT be. Which tells me — as I'm sure it tells ALL of you, being men of obvious intelligence — that the treasure is not HERE at all. No, no — the cellar is merely the terminus of the concealment network. The ORIGIN point, as any fool knows, is always at the site of the primary riddle. Which means I must return to the library IMMEDIATELY to complete my analysis of the mantelpiece inscription! I have just realised — and this is the sort of insight that comes ONLY to those of us with decades of field experience — that the inscription requires not just a verbal answer but a PHYSICAL key. A medallion, perhaps. Or a medal. Something round, something metallic, something that a distinguished archaeologist might happen to carry on his person. EUREKA! I must go at ONCE! Guard the furniture, won't you? TREMENDOUSLY important — don't let anyone move it!
events.thinking:
Frustration tightening in my jaw. Three interactions now — bookshelves, crates, furniture — and NOTHING. No hidden compartment, no treasure, no secret passage. Just 'You interacted with Old Furniture.' The hollow behind my navel is aching. My hands are empty. Still empty. The fake medal sits in my pocket like a joke — the only thing I've managed to acquire and it's worthless tin from Croydon. I'm wandering through this manor room by room, interacting with everything, and coming up empty while Penelope and Peter are probably solving the mantelpiece riddle right now. The good pieces are disappearing from the table. I can feel it — the same cold sensation from childhood, watching my brothers eat first.

But wait. I need to stop and THINK. I'm doing what I always do — over-elaborating, running from room to room, building schemes on top of schemes. Bookshelves, then crates, then cellar furniture. Three interactions, zero results. Maybe I'm looking in the wrong places. The mantelpiece riddle — 'map' — that's the real lead. And the mantelpiece had a USE action with my fake-medal. What if the medal IS the key? What if something about it — the shape, the size — fits into the mantelpiece mechanism?

Or maybe the answer is simpler. Maybe I need to actually SAY 'map' to the mantelpiece. Penelope was interacting with it — did she say the word? Did something happen?

I've been so busy trying to get ahead of everyone, to find secret rooms and hidden chambers, that I've been running AWAY from the actual puzzle. The riddle is on the mantelpiece. The answer is 'map.' The mechanism is there, in the library, where I started. I need to go BACK.

But the Gruesomes and Red Max are here. They might have something useful. And these air vents... 'just big enough for something very small.' Muttley is small-ish. No — what's VERY small? A mouse? There might be something in the vents. But I can't reach them and I can't fit in them.

No. Stop over-elaborating. Go back to the library. The mantelpiece. The medal. That's where the architecture is.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking:
The hot weight transforms the instant I step through the door. My eyes are already cataloguing — brass instruments, bubbling flasks, the machine. The machine. Large, complex, levers and dials, a gauge, and a wire gnawed clean through. 'Requires 3 operators.' And a workbench with tools but no wrench.

This is it. This is my bridge competition. This is the thing I can build, fix, make work. The gnawed wire — something chewed through it. The wrench is missing. The machine needs three operators. My hands have stopped fidgeting. They're ready.

Penelope is here. She's safe. The Ant Hill Mob is here. Sneekly is here — the prickle returns, but he's explaining things, being helpful. Benefit of the doubt. My father and the stranger on the road.

But the machine — a gnawed wire. I can fix a wire. I've built bridges, rebuilt engines, stayed up three nights. A gnawed wire is nothing. But I need a wrench for the coupling, and the wrench is missing. Sneekly said it might be in the kitchen or the cellar. The cellar is right here — through that exit. A damp stone cellar with... cheerful decorations? Someone's been redecorating a cellar. That's odd.

But first — the machine. Let me look at it properly. Understand what we're dealing with. Three operators, a gnawed wire, a missing wrench. I can plan this. I can be the one who figures out how to make it work. And this time — this time the plan serves the moment, because the machine is right here and so is she.

The workbench has no wrench but has other tools. The wire is gnawed through. Maybe I can splice it, bypass the coupling, improvise a repair without the wrench. That's what my father would do — what the stranger on the road would do. You work with what you have.

Look at the machine first. Understand the problem. Then solve it.

events.desc: And just like that, the fidgeting stops. The hollowness fills. James Hartwell is in his element — not the library with its riddles, not the entrance hall with its guest books, but here, with a broken machine and a chance to fix it. His hands know what to do with brass and copper. His mind knows what to do with levers and dials. For the first time this evening, the proving-worth hunger and the protection instinct point in the same direction — because fixing this machine is both the bridge and the shield.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking:
Heat floods the back of my neck. The Mob just asked me HOW I know the wrench might be in the kitchen or cellar. 'Just curious, like. Professional interest.' That's not curiosity. That's interrogation dressed in casual clothes. My stomach tightens — the same drop I felt when the boy's sandwich told me my hunger was visible. I've shown too much. An estate manager who hasn't visited in months shouldn't know where a specific tool might have migrated to. I over-specified. I was so busy being helpful that I forgot that helpful people are the ones who get questions.

Compose yourself, Vincent. Breathe. Pemberton would have a reasonable answer. He managed this estate. He knows the master's habits. The master repurposed tools — I already said that. It's not knowledge of where the wrench IS, it's knowledge of where the master TENDED to leave things. That's a perfectly natural thing for an estate manager to know. Frame it as habit, not surveillance.

But the prickle won't leave my neck. The Mob is building a file on me. Every time I say something specific, they add a line. Every time I appear somewhere I shouldn't be, they add a line. Eventually the file gets thick enough to read.

I need to give them an answer that's boring. Domestic. The kind of thing that makes their eyes glaze over. And then I need to leave this room on an errand that Pemberton would naturally perform — fetching the wrench from the kitchen. It separates me from their surveillance, it gives me access to unexplored rooms, and it positions me to control the machine repair.

events.desc: 'How do you know that, exactly?' Five words, and my neck is burning. He sees me. Not all of me — not yet — but he sees the shape of something that doesn't fit. The estate manager who knows too much, who appears in rooms before anyone else, who offers help that always seems to steer the conversation. I gave him the Pemberton answer — twenty years of tidying up, sugar bowls, Phillips-head screwdrivers. Boring. Domestic. True enough to survive scrutiny. But the file in his head just got another line, and I can feel it like a paper cut. The kitchen. I need to move. I need space to think. And I need that wrench — because whoever holds the wrench holds the key to this machine, and whoever holds the key to this machine decides what happens when three people pull those levers together.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Right — crates are a bust. Nuffing but straw and old curtains, just like Dastardly said. Even a stopped clock is right twice a day, I suppose. BUT — and this is important, so everyone listen up — Mr. Pemberton 'ere wants to pop off to the kitchen to find this missing wrench. On 'is OWN. And I fink we've all learned by now that people wandering off on their own in this 'ouse is 'ow fings go WRONG. So 'ere's what I propose — and yes, I know, ANOFER plan, Danny's got anofer plan, everyone groan — but this one's simple, I promise. NOBODY goes anywhere alone. That's it. That's the whole plan. You want to check the kitchen? Take someone wiv you. You want to go to the cellar? Take someone wiv you. Rufus — you and Sawtooth fancy escorting Mr. Pemberton to the kitchen to find this wrench? You're a practical man, you'd know a wrench when you see one, and Sawtooth looks like 'e could gnaw through anyfing that gets in the way. Meanwhile, Clara, Peter, and the Brixton Boys stay RIGHT 'ERE wiv this machine until the wrench comes back. Simple. Clean. Nobody gets separated. Nobody gets 'urt. The Brixton Boys don't let nuffing 'appen to their girl!
events.thinking: My hands are in the straw, digging through packing material, and — nothing. Dastardly was right about the crates, at least. Packing straw and moth-eaten fabric. My fingers come up empty and there's a flicker of embarrassment in my stomach, the competence thing — I was so sure I'd find something Dastardly missed, so sure the Brixton way of doing things would turn up what his lordship's 'trained archaeological eye' couldn't. But it's just straw. Just old curtains. My hands close and open once, resetting. Fine. The crates are a dead end. But Pemberton — he's still doing it. Still offering to go fetch the wrench, still suggesting the kitchen, still steering. 'Shall I go and have a look? It would only take a moment.' A MOMENT alone. That's what he wants. A moment where nobody's watching. And Clara — bless her — she's already working on the next thing, asking about the machine, about the wire. She doesn't stop. She never stops. And now Peter's examining the machine too, which is good — Peter's thorough, Peter's careful. Dastardly's come back from the cellar. So everyone's in one room. That's... actually that's good. I can see everyone. Nobody's slipping away. For once, the situation is contained. But Pemberton wants to leave — wants to go to the kitchen alone for the wrench. I can't let him go alone. But I can't leave Clara either. Maybe... maybe I suggest someone ELSE goes with him. Keep eyes on him without splitting from Clara.

events.desc: For once — FOR ONCE — I've come up with a plan that's actually simple. Don't let anyone go alone. That's it. Three words. Even I can't overcomplicate three words. And if Rufus goes with Pemberton, I've got eyes on the estate manager without leaving Clara's side. Rufus is solid. Honest. The kind who'd share his last sandwich. If Pemberton tries anything funny with Rufus watching, at least there's a witness. And if the wrench isn't in the kitchen — well, that tells us something too, doesn't it.
