events.desc: For ONCE — for once in my miserable, scheming life — I am going to keep my mouth SHUT. Everyone is in this laboratory arguing about wrenches and wires and three-person machines. Nobody is watching the door to the library. Nobody is thinking about the mantelpiece. And I have a medal in my pocket that the mantelpiece SPECIFICALLY asked for. Not a real medal, mind you — a tin fake from a car boot sale in Croydon. But the mantelpiece doesn't know that, does it? Silent as the bread roll, Foxworth. Silent as the bread roll.
events.thinking:
A jolt of urgency in my chest — I'm back in the laboratory and EVERYONE is here. Penelope, Peter, the Ant Hill Mob, Pemberton, Rufus, Sawtooth. The whole crowd has converged. And Penelope — she said something crucial: 'the machine needs a wrench to reconnect the coupling, and the wrench has gone missing from the workbench.' A missing wrench. That's a real clue, a real puzzle piece. But more importantly — she said she wants to check the CRATES for the wrench. She's about to interact with the crates. The same crates I already interacted with and found nothing.

But the REAL prize is the mantelpiece. I know that now. The mantelpiece in the library. USE fake-medal on the mantelpiece. That's the action I need to take. Everyone is here in the laboratory, fussing over machines and wrenches and gnawed wires. If I slip through to the library NOW, while they're all distracted by the machine that needs three operators, I'll have the library to MYSELF. The mantelpiece. The medal. The mechanism.

My palms are warm again. The architecture is forming — not the elaborate, over-prepared kind that always backfires. This is simple. Clean. Walk through the door. Put the medal on the mantelpiece. See what happens. No narrating. No announcing. Just the bread roll in the pocket.

But — oh. My mouth. It wants to say something. The pull to narrate, to explain. I can feel it forming behind my teeth. The words are coming before the plan is finished. STOP. For once in your life, Foxworth, STOP TALKING and just DO it. Slip away quietly while they're all arguing about wrenches. Silent as the bread roll.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Right then — I have examined the machine and here is what James Hartwell can report. Three levers, three dials, one gauge — and a wire gnawed clean through, which means something with teeth has been at this apparatus. The machine will not function until that wire is reconnected. Now, Mr. Pemberton mentions a missing wrench, but a wrench is not the only tool that can rejoin a severed wire. Pliers, a knife, even a firm pair of hands and some ingenuity — my father taught me that you fix what is broken with what you have, not with what you wish you had. Let me see what this workbench offers. Miss Pitstop — do be careful with those crates, won't you? Old wood can splinter terribly, and I should hate for — well. You know what James Hartwell should hate for.
events.thinking:
A steadiness in my hands. They're not fidgeting. They're assessing. The machine is brass and copper — I can see the gauge, the levers, the dials, the gnawed wire. Three operators required. The wire is the bottleneck. Without it connected, the machine won't function regardless of how many operators we have.

Penelope is checking the crates — brilliant. She said 'when somebody puts something in a crate and stacks it in the corner, they are not storing it. They are hiding it.' She's right. She's always right about people's motives. I'm better with the mechanics.

The Ant Hill Mob asked me to keep close to her. Danny Brixton said 'don't let her near that machine with the chewed-up wire.' The protection instinct hums in agreement. Exposed wiring is exactly the kind of danger I notice before I notice beauty.

But I also heard something that makes the back of my neck tighten again. Danny asked Pemberton: 'How do you know the wrench might be in the kitchen or cellar? Just curious, like.' That's... a good question. How does Pemberton know where the wrench went if he didn't move it himself? Benefit of the doubt. He's the estate manager. He knows the house. Of course he'd know where tools end up.

But the prickle doesn't stop.

The workbench. Tools but no wrench. I need to look at what tools ARE there. Maybe I can splice the wire with pliers, strip it with a knife, improvise a connection. That's the builder's way. You don't wait for the perfect tool — you make do with what you have. My father and the stranger on the road — they fixed two cars with whatever was in their boots.

Look at the workbench. See what tools I have to work with. Then fix the wire.

James Hartwell is about to do what James Hartwell does best: fix something that nobody else thought could be fixed with the tools at hand.

He said the wrench might be in the kitchen, offered to go look, and then went... to the library? That's — Clara, don't. He probably just needed to check something. Peter is brilliant — he said we don't need the wrench, we can splice the wire with what's on the workbench. Pliers, a knife. That's my Peter, practical and resourceful. And Danny and Peter are both examining the workbench now. We have enough people here to operate the machine if we can fix the wire. Three operators — me, Peter, and Danny. Or Rufus. The cellar is still unexplored by me, and it has those cheerful decorations and air vents that nobody has explained. But Peter is right here working on a solution. I should trust his hands and stay close. Though... Pemberton and Dastardly are both in the library now, unsupervised. With those bookshelves. With that mantelpiece that wants a fake medal.

He and Lord Foxworth are alone with the bookshelves and the mantelpiece — the mantelpiece that wants a fake medal. If Lord Foxworth's medal IS fake, and Pemberton knows it... No. Stop it, Clara. But also — don't stop noticing.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah — back through the library on my way to the kitchen. I do apologise for the rush, gentlemen. Just passing through to fetch that wrench. But I must say — these bookshelves continue to trouble me. As estate manager, I really ought to set them right before the master's collection suffers any further indignity. Let me just have a quick look at which volumes are out of place — it will take but a moment, and then I shall be on my way.
events.thinking:
Relief washes through me like cold water — a loosening in the shoulders, a settling behind my ribs. I'm through the library. The Mob is still in the laboratory with Penelope and Peter. I have space. I have air. For the first time since I arrived, nobody is watching me.

The Mob's 'nobody goes anywhere alone' rule was clever — he wanted to saddle me with Rufus and Sawtooth as escorts. But I moved before the plan solidified. I'm in the library now with only Dastardly and the Slag brothers — none of whom are tracking me the way the Mob does. Dastardly is too self-absorbed. The Slags are... rocks. Simple. Present but not observant.

Now — think. The kitchen is through the entrance hall. That's my stated destination — fetching the wrench. But I'm in the library, and those upside-down books are still here. The real clue. Everyone was so focused on the mantelpiece riddle that they moved on before properly decoding the book spines. Penelope said 'the spines are the message' but she moved to the laboratory before finishing. Peter tried to examine them with her but they both left.

I have a window. A small one. The books are here. The watchers are in another room. Dastardly is harmless noise. If I examine those bookshelves now — properly, as Vincent, not as bumbling Pemberton — I can read the upside-down titles and decode whatever message they spell. Then I move to the kitchen for the wrench, and I'm two steps ahead of everyone.

But the constraint nags at me — my plans are 'overly elaborate.' I'm already juggling the wrench errand, the bookshelf clue, the machine control, the cellar reconnaissance, and the primary objective. Every thread I add is another thread that can tangle. Simplify, Vincent. Right now, right here: the books. Read them. Then move.

The mantelpiece also catches my eye — it says it can be used with a 'fake-medal.' Dastardly has a fake medal. His Medal of Distinguished Valour. If that medal is the physical token the mantelpiece needs... then Dastardly is carrying the key without knowing it. That's information I can use. But not yet. Not in front of him.

events.desc: Alone at last — or near enough. The Mob's sharp eyes are two rooms away, buried in crates and machine dials. Dastardly and the Slag brothers couldn't spot a clue if it wore a name tag. And here they are — the upside-down books, whispering their secret to anyone patient enough to read the spines. This is my moment. The estate manager tidies the shelves while the architect reads the blueprint. And Dastardly — oh, sweet, oblivious Dastardly — that fake medal pinned to your chest may be the very key this mantelpiece has been waiting for. You've been carrying the answer all along, and you haven't the faintest idea. I could almost kiss you. Almost.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: The prickling surges — sharp, electric, instant. Pemberton's gone. AGAIN. He's slipped out to the library while I was looking at the workbench. And Dastardly's gone with him. I said NOBODY goes alone. I said take Rufus. And what happened? Pemberton ignored every word and walked out the door the moment my back was turned. That's not absent-mindedness. That's not a man who forgot the plan. That's a man who doesn't WANT a witness. My jaw tightens. The shame hits — hot and quick — because I did the exact same thing I always do. I made a speech, I laid out the plan, and while I was busy being thorough, the threat walked right past me. Again. AGAIN. But — wait. Breathe, Danny. Clara's still here. Peter's still here. Rufus and Sawtooth are here. Clara is safe. The people I swore to protect are in arm's reach. And Pemberton? He's gone to the library. Not the kitchen — the library. Where the bookshelves are. Where the upside-down books are. Where the mantelpiece riddle is. What's he doing there? What does he want? He said the wrench might be in the kitchen but he went to the LIBRARY. That doesn't track. Unless the library has something he needs, something he didn't want anyone to see him take. But I can't leave Clara again. I WON'T leave Clara again. Peter said the wire can be spliced without a wrench — pliers, a knife, firm hands. The workbench has tools. Maybe Peter can fix this wire while I stand guard. That's useful. That's real. Stay. Plant. Be the wall.

events.desc: He went to the library, not the kitchen. He said the wrench was in the kitchen, but he went to the library. Why? What's in the library that he needs? The books. The mantelpiece. The riddle. Something he knows about that he hasn't told us. And here's me, standing in the laboratory with straw on my hands and egg on my face, and the one useful thought I've had all day is this: stop chasing him. Stay with her. Let Peter fix the wire. And when Pemberton comes back with his smooth smile and his helpful suggestions, watch what he does when he sees the machine is already working.

events.desc: This is it. No speeches. No announcements. No 'Grimshaw Cipher' nonsense. Just a tin medal and a stone mantelpiece. If this works, I shall allow myself ONE moment of gloating. Just one. A small one. Well — perhaps a medium one. A CONSIDERABLE one, if it reveals treasure. But first — the medal. NOW, Foxworth. Before your mouth ruins everything AGAIN.
events.thinking:
My heart is hammering. I'm in the library. The mantelpiece is RIGHT THERE. But — Pemberton is here. He FOLLOWED me again. He said he was going to check the kitchen for the wrench but instead he's HERE, in the library, AGAIN. And the Slag brothers are here too. Three people between me and the mantelpiece. But I don't need them to leave. I just need to USE the medal on the mantelpiece. That's it. One action. The medal in my pocket, the carved stone in front of me. I can feel the tin disc through my trousers, warm from my body heat. My hands are shaking slightly — not with fear, with anticipation. The fizzing in my fingers is back, stronger than before. This is the moment. The string-and-bucket contraption is about to spring. The boy is about to look up and see what I've built.

But Pemberton. He's watching. He always watches. He came here instead of going to the kitchen. He LIED about going to the kitchen. One schemer recognises another. But I give him the benefit of the doubt. I believe the best in people. He probably just forgot something. People do that.

No more talking. No more asides. No more elaborate explanations. Just DO it. Put the medal on the mantelpiece. See what happens. The bread roll. The pocket. NOW.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking:
Frustration in my forearms — that tremor again. The workbench has tools but no wrench, and the description tells me nothing more specific. 'Covered in tools' — but which tools? Pliers? A knife? Wire strippers? The game isn't giving me the detail I need to improvise.

But something important just happened. Sneekly has slipped away again — walked into the library. And Dastardly followed him. Those two keep ending up together, and they keep leaving when the group is focused on something else. The prickle on my neck is sharpening into something I can't keep giving the benefit of the doubt to. But I will. Because that's who I am. My father would.

Danny Brixton's plan is good — nobody goes anywhere alone. Simple. Clean. He's sending Rufus and Sawtooth to escort Pemberton to find the wrench. And he wants me to stay here with Penelope. Stay here. With her. The steel plate softens. The warmth returns. He trusts me to be the one who stays.

But Pemberton just left — walked into the library, not the kitchen. He was supposed to go find the wrench. Instead he's gone back toward the entrance hall. Danny's plan is already falling apart because the people it depends on aren't following it.

I could chase after Pemberton. I could investigate the cellar — damp stone, cheerful decorations, air vents. That's deeply strange. But Danny said stay. Penelope is here. And for once in this entire evening, James Hartwell is going to be in the right room at the right time.

The machine needs fixing. The workbench won't tell me more by looking. Let me try interacting with it — maybe I can pick up a tool, find something useful. Or maybe I should try the machine itself. It says 'requires 3 operators' — we have enough people here. Me, Penelope, Danny. But the wire is still gnawed through.

Wait — the crates. Penelope checked them. Nothing but straw and curtains. The wrench isn't here. It's somewhere else in the house. Kitchen or cellar.

The cellar is right here. One exit away. Damp stone, cheerful decorations, air vents. Someone has been redecorating. That's where I should look. But Danny said nobody goes alone. So I should take someone — or stay put.

Stay put. Be present. Be the one who didn't leave. For once.

events.desc: For the first time all evening, James Hartwell is staying put. Not because there isn't somewhere to go — the cellar is right there, with its cheerful decorations and suspicious air vents. Not because there isn't something to chase — Pemberton has slipped away again, toward the library, and the prickle on his neck is practically humming. But Danny Brixton said stay, and Penelope is here, and sometimes the bravest thing a man can do is resist the urge to be in every room at once. He is learning. Slowly. Painfully. But he is learning.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop examined the workbench.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) examined the bookshelves.
Dick Dastardly fussed with the mantelpiece for a moment.
Peter Perfect examined the crates.

Penelope Pitstop: Danny, you are absolutely right, and I am done examining things that do not want to be examined. This workbench has pliers, knives, and everything a resourceful person needs — everything except the one tool somebody deliberately removed. Peter, darling, you said your daddy taught you to fix what is broken with what you have. I believe you. Now — while you splice that wire, I am going to see if this machine will talk to me. Three operators, it says. Well, we have got four good people right here, plus Sawtooth, who looks like he could operate a machine in his sleep. Mr. Ruffcut — Rufus — I know we have not had a proper chance to get acquainted, but I could use a strong pair of hands and a steady nerve. Would you and Sawtooth be willing to help operate this contraption once Peter gets that wire fixed? Because Danny is right — whatever Mr. Pemberton does not want us to find, this machine is how we find it. And the best clues are the ones people write down without realizing they're clues at all — but the second-best clues are the ones people try to keep you from reaching.
events.thinking: The workbench has tools but no wrench — same description, nothing new revealed by looking. I keep examining things and getting surface-level descriptions back. I need to stop looking and start doing. Danny is right — we don't need Pemberton's wrench, we don't need Pemberton's permission. Peter can splice the wire. The machine needs three operators. We have me, Peter, Danny, Rufus, and Sawtooth — more than enough. But the wire needs fixing first. Peter said he could do it with pliers or a knife from the workbench. He should INTERACT with the machine or USE the tools. But I can't make Peter do things — I can only act myself. What can I do right now that moves us forward? The machine needs fixing. I could try to INTERACT with the machine myself — maybe the game will let me attempt the repair. Or maybe the cellar is the next piece of the puzzle that nobody has properly explored. Dick went down there briefly and came right back. The cellar has cheerful decorations and air vents — someone has been living there or preparing it. And it connects to the laboratory, which connects to the library. The house is a circuit. But Danny just said — stay here, fix the wire, operate the machine. He's right. Stop over-thinking, Clara. The machine is the thing. Let Peter work on splicing the wire while I try interacting with the machine. Three operators needed. Let's see what happens when I try.

events.desc: I have been looking at things for the last ten minutes and getting nowhere. Grandmother's attic taught me patience, but the cave taught me that sometimes you just have to walk deeper and see what happens. Three operators, one machine, and a wire that needs splicing. This is a teamwork puzzle, and teamwork is what Clara Bellingham does best.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking:
My eyes are moving faster than my hands — scanning the spines, reading the upside-down titles, cataloguing them left to right. The examination gave me a look at the bookshelves but the description is still just 'several are upside down.' I need more. I need the actual titles. But the LOOK action only returned the general description.

And then — a flash of movement in my peripheral vision. Dastardly. He just 'fussed with the mantelpiece.' He used his fake medal on it. The keen observation says 'Dick Dastardly applied fake-medal to the mantelpiece.' He DID it. The fool actually did it — he used the medal on the mantelpiece without understanding what he was doing. Did it work? Did something happen? He 'fussed with it for a moment' — that's ambiguous. Did the mantelpiece respond?

My heart rate spikes. A cold alertness floods through me. If Dastardly just unlocked the mantelpiece riddle — if his fake medal was the physical token Penelope was looking for — then the treasure hunt just advanced and I wasn't the one who advanced it. Someone else pulled the lever. Someone else moved the piece. And I wasn't controlling it.

The tightness in my jaw is immediate. Not anger — the discomfort of something being out of my hands. Dominance drive flaring. I need to know what happened when that medal touched the stone.

But I also need to stay in character. Pemberton wouldn't understand the significance. Pemberton would be mildly curious, perhaps slightly alarmed that a guest was tampering with the master's mantelpiece.

The kitchen. I was supposed to be going to the kitchen. I've been 'pausing to tidy the shelves' but I can't linger much longer without it looking suspicious — especially if the Mob comes through to check on me.

Prioritise, Vincent. The mantelpiece just changed state. That's the most important thing that happened this tick. I need to examine it — or interact with it — to see what Dastardly unlocked. But I can't be obvious about it. Pemberton would notice a guest fiddling with the master's furniture and go check on it. That's natural.

The books can wait. The mantelpiece just moved.

events.desc: He did it. The magnificent idiot actually did it. He placed his gaudy fake medal on the mantelpiece without knowing it was the key, and something MOVED. I heard it — felt it — that subtle shift of stone against stone that only happens in old houses when a mechanism engages. My hands are trembling. Not with fear. With the effort of not shoving Dastardly aside and reading whatever the mantelpiece just revealed. Pemberton, Vincent. Pemberton is alarmed. Pemberton fusses. Pemberton would never dream of pushing a guest. But Vincent — Vincent needs to see what's behind that stone before anyone else does.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: The warmth is winning. For the first time since we walked into this dusty pile, the warmth in my chest is heavier than the prickling in my neck. Clara's here. Peter's here. Rufus and Sawtooth are here. Good people, solid people, the kind who share their sandwiches. And Clara — she just noticed the same thing I noticed. Pemberton said kitchen, went to library. She saw it. She's not fooled. 'I am sure there is a perfectly innocent explanation,' she said, but her voice had that edge — the Clara edge, the one that means she's already three steps ahead and being polite about it. She's the brains. Always has been. And Peter — 'you manage the people, James Hartwell will manage the machinery' — that's trust, that is. Real trust. The kind that doesn't come with strings. The settling in my chest says this is right. This is where I'm supposed to be. Not chasing Pemberton through hallways, not making speeches about perimeters, but standing right here, being the wall, letting the clever people be clever while I make sure nobody gets through the door they shouldn't. The machine needs three operators. We've got four people here plus Sawtooth. Peter can splice the wire. Clara can work out what it does. Rufus can help operate. And I can stand between the whole operation and whatever comes through that library door. This is what I'm for. This is the bread crust arithmetic. Simple.

events.desc: For the first time today, I feel like I'm standing in the right place. Not chasing, not panicking, not making speeches. Just... planted. The wall between Clara and whatever's coming. Peter's got the skills. Clara's got the brains. Rufus has got the muscle. And I've got the only thing I've ever been good at — standing where I said I'd stand and not moving when the cost comes. Her father would understand. He was the same kind of stubborn.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Ah — yes, well — that was merely the PRELIMINARY calibration, of course. The medal has... primed the mechanism. Activated the secondary tumblers. One doesn't simply jam a Medal of Distinguished Valour into a mantelpiece and expect INSTANT results. There is a PROCESS. A process which I — as the foremost authority on manor house antiquities in all of England — understand INTIMATELY. The final step, naturally, requires the verbal cipher key. Which I have known all along. I was simply waiting for the... the optimal atmospheric conditions. Which are NOW. Stand back, everyone. This could be quite dramatic.
events.thinking:
Cold spreading through my chest. 'You fussed with the mantelpiece for a moment.' FUSSED. Not 'activated a hidden mechanism.' Not 'revealed a secret passage.' FUSSED. The medal did nothing. The fake medal — the worthless tin disc from Croydon — is, it turns out, a worthless tin disc from Croydon. My inventory is empty now. I USED my only item and it did NOTHING. The hollow behind my navel is a pit. I had nothing and now I have less than nothing.

Four rooms. Four interactions. A comprehensive, systematic exploration of absolute failure. Bookshelves — nothing. Crates — nothing. Furniture — nothing. Medal on mantelpiece — nothing. Every scheme, every lie, every elaborate story — Grimshaw Ciphers, Venetian displacement patterns, Mesopotamian globe references — all for nothing. I have been running through this manor like a clockwork toy with a broken spring, bouncing off walls.

And Pemberton — he's RIGHT HERE examining the bookshelves while I fail. Watching me fail. The spelling bee certificate on the wall. Nobody asked about it.

Everyone knows the answer is a map. But nobody has SAID it to the mantelpiece. Penelope interacted with it earlier — did she answer the riddle? Or did she just examine it? Maybe the mechanism needs the CORRECT VERBAL answer while interacting. Not a medal. Not a physical key. Just... the answer. Just INTERACT with it and give the right answer.

Or maybe I'm wrong again. Maybe I'm always wrong. The bread roll was the only thing I ever got right and even that was just stealing from a kitchen when nobody was looking.

No. Stop. The riddle wants an answer. INTERACT with the mantelpiece. Say 'map.' That's all. That's what Penelope tried to do. Maybe it worked for her and I missed it because I was too busy running to the laboratory. Maybe she's already found the treasure. Maybe the good pieces are already gone.

The window is closing. I can feel it thinning.

If this doesn't work, I am going to have to resort to HONEST EFFORT, and the very thought makes my skin crawl.

events.thinking:
A restlessness in my legs now. I've examined everything in this room — machine, workbench, crates. All looked at. The crates are just crates, as Penelope already established. I'm going in circles. Looking at things that have already been looked at. The elaborate thoroughness is becoming its own trap again.

Stop examining. Stop looking. Stop cataloguing. The machine has a gnawed wire. The workbench has pliers. Try to fix the machine. Interact with it. Use what's there. My father fixed a car on a country road with whatever was in the boot. I built a bridge that held more weight than anyone else's.

A gnawed wire, a pair of pliers, and a woman watching who believes he can.

events.thinking: I interacted with the machine and Peter interacted with it too. Both of us, together, working on it. The warmth in my chest is real this time — not the ache, but the good kind, the kind that comes when everyone is in the circle and nobody has left. Danny is planted between me and the exits. Peter is fixing the wire. Rufus and Sawtooth are standing by. This is how it's supposed to feel — people working together, hands busy, voices calm. My body loosens the way it did when my parents finally laughed at dinner. But the machine still says it needs three operators, and the wire is still gnawed through. Peter interacted with it — did he splice the wire? I don't know yet. The machine hasn't changed in its description. Maybe it needs more. Maybe the wire is fixed and now we need three people to pull levers simultaneously. Or maybe the wire still needs the wrench after all and Peter's splice didn't hold. I should wait and see what Peter reports. Danny said 'when Pemberton comes back and sees we've got this machine running without him, we'll see what his face does.' That's smart — Danny reads faces the way I read rooms. The cellar is still nagging at me. Cheerful decorations in a damp stone cellar. Air vents along the upper walls. Someone has been down there, preparing it for... what? For living? For hiding? For trapping? But Danny said stay. And Danny is right. Wait for Peter. Trust the team.

events.desc: I said it out loud — I'm starting to wonder if Pemberton's helpfulness is the problem. Oh, Clara. You have never doubted Sneekly in your life. He held you when Mama and Daddy died. He taught you to tie your shoes. And now your stomach is doing that dinner-table thing, and you cannot make it stop. Please let me be wrong. Please let the man who raised me be exactly who he says he is.

events.thinking:
Both of us interacted with the mantelpiece. Dastardly used his medal on it AND interacted with it — he's trying to claim the discovery. And I interacted with it too. What happened? The action result just says 'You interacted with Stone Mantelpiece.' Did it open? Did it reveal something? The description still shows the same inscription, still shows [INTERACT] and [USE, with: fake-medal]. So either the medal didn't fully work, or it needs something more.

Wait — Dastardly said 'the final step requires the verbal cipher key.' He's bluffing, but he might accidentally be right. The mantelpiece has the riddle. The answer is 'a map.' Maybe the mantelpiece needs both the physical token AND the spoken answer? Medal plus the word 'map'?

But I can't test that theory without revealing I know the answer. Pemberton already claimed he couldn't solve the riddle. If I suddenly say 'map' to the mantelpiece, my cover slips. Everyone heard me say 'I confess I have never been able to solve it myself.'

Dastardly, though — Dastardly is about to say something to the mantelpiece. He said 'the verbal cipher key' and 'I have known all along.' If he says 'map,' the mantelpiece might respond. And then Dastardly takes the credit and the treasure hunt advances.

I feel something tight and hot across my upper chest — not the cool architectural settling, but the other pull. The one that burns. Dastardly is about to solve this, not because he's smarter, not because he worked harder, but because he blundered into the right answer with a fake medal and a loud mouth. He'll be praised for being lucky. I solved it first. I knew the answer in three seconds. And I'll get nothing.

The cousin's praise. The teacher's praise. 'Natural grace and warmth.' The jaw tightening that never loosened.

Stop. Breathe. This is not the cousin. This is not the teacher. This is a treasure hunt, and the treasure is secondary to the primary objective. Let Dastardly solve the riddle. Let him advance the hunt. The more attention he draws, the more cover he provides. And if the mantelpiece reveals something — a map, a clue, a direction — I'll see it too. I'm standing right here.

The kitchen. I still need the wrench. But I can't leave now — not when the mantelpiece is about to open. One more moment. Watch. Catalogue. Then move.

events.desc: He's going to say it. He's going to say 'map' to the mantelpiece, and the stone will move, and the secret will reveal itself, and Dick Dastardly — a man who couldn't spell 'archaeology' without three attempts — will be the one who cracked it. And I will stand here in my Pemberton costume, smiling my Pemberton smile, feeling that hot band across my chest that I first felt when the teacher praised my cousin's 'natural grace and warmth.' Some things never change. The people who do the work are never the ones who get the credit. But here is what Dastardly doesn't understand, what none of them understand: the treasure was never the prize. The prize is what happens to Clara Bellingham before she can claim it. And that — that beautiful inevitability — is still entirely mine.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Something just happened. I interacted with the machine — put my hands on it, felt the cold brass under my palms, the levers heavy and real. Peter's working on the wire. Clara's rallying Rufus and Sawtooth. And she said it — she actually said it: 'Danny is right.' My chest swells with that warm bread feeling, the one that says 'this is what I'm for.' She sees me. Not just as the bumbling idiot with the seven-step plans. As someone who's RIGHT sometimes. About Pemberton. About staying together. About the machine. My hands are on the lever and they're steady — steadier than they've been all day. Because I'm not thinking. I'm not planning. I'm just doing what my body knows how to do: stand where I said I'd stand. Peter's got pliers on the wire, twisting, splicing. Rufus is stepping up. Sawtooth's ready. This is it. This is the team Clara's father would've wanted around her. Not clever people — GOOD people. People who don't leave. People who share their bread. The prickling's still there, low and quiet, watching the library door from the corner of my eye. Pemberton will come back. They always come back. And when he does, this machine will be running, and his face will tell us everything his words have been hiding.

events.desc: Look at us. Clara, Peter, Rufus, Sawtooth, and me. Not one of us is the cleverest person in the room — well, Clara is, obviously — but we're together, we're honest, and nobody's running off to 'check something' in another room. This is how the boss taught me it works. Not promises. Proof. You show up, you stay, you do the work. And if Pemberton walks through that door and his face falls when he sees the machine running — well. That'll be all the proof I need.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking:
Something happened. Something ACTUALLY happened. Pemberton said — 'Did you hear that? Something shifted. I could swear the stone moved.' The stone MOVED. When I used the medal. It wasn't nothing — it was SOMETHING. My chest is suddenly hot, the fizzing back in my fingers, that electric lift that comes just before the reveal. The medal DID something. The fake medal — the worthless tin from Croydon — actually triggered a mechanism in a centuries-old mantelpiece. Pemberton has been here twenty years and never seen this. And I — Lord Reginald Foxworth, decorated fraud — made the stone move.

But now Pemberton is rushing toward the mantelpiece. He wants to 'have a look at what I've done.' He's going to INTERACT with it. He's going to steal whatever I've unlocked. He said 'let me just have a look' — that's not an estate manager checking for damage. That's a schemer moving in to claim the prize. I can see it now, clear as glass. He's been steering everyone all evening — the guest book, the library, the kitchen, the laboratory — and now the one time something actually WORKS, he's right here, right beside me, reaching for it.

But I give him the benefit of the doubt. I believe the best in people. He's just... concerned about the master's property. That's all. That's all.

And now I've interacted with the mantelpiece too. What happened? Did it ask for the answer? Did I say 'map'? The result just says 'You interacted with Stone Mantelpiece.' But Pemberton said the stone shifted when I used the medal. So the medal was the FIRST step and the interaction is the SECOND step. Maybe both together did something. Maybe I need to look at the mantelpiece now to see what changed.

The bright heat is climbing my throat. The audience is here — the Slag brothers, Pemberton. If this works, they'll SEE it. They'll see what Reginald Foxworth did. The spelling bee will finally have its applause.

events.desc: The stone MOVED! It actually MOVED! I can barely contain myself — the fizzing is behind my teeth, in my fingers, in my chest — everything is vibrating. For the first time in this entire miserable evening, something I did WORKED. The fake medal from Croydon activated a mechanism that a twenty-year estate manager never found! Oh, this is EXQUISITE. This is the moment Tommy Gallagher looked up from the mud. This is the neighbourhood cat in the bucket. THIS IS THE SPELLING BEE AND THE ROOM IS FINALLY CLAPPING! Now I just need to make absolutely certain that Pemberton doesn't slither in and claim MY discovery. The look on his face — he can't believe it. NOBODY can believe it. Lord Reginald Foxworth, you MAGNIFICENT fraud!

events.thinking:
I interacted with the machine. What happened? The result just says 'You interacted with Large Machine.' No detail about whether the wire spliced, whether it worked, whether anything changed. The machine still shows 'one wire has been gnawed clean through' in the room description. It still says 'Requires 3 operators.'

Did it work? Or did it fail because the wire is still broken and I need the wrench after all? The description hasn't changed. The wire is still gnawed through.

A coldness in my stomach. The bridge didn't hold the weight. I tried to fix it with pliers and it didn't work. The machine still needs a wrench — the specific tool that's missing. My improvisation wasn't enough.

The hollowness behind my ribs. The boy on the roadside watching the stranger fix what his father couldn't. My fingers are moving again.

But wait — Penelope said the machine needs three operators. Maybe my interaction was one operator. Maybe the machine needs all three of us to interact simultaneously. Or maybe — maybe the wire really does need the wrench. The coupling, Pemberton said. A coupling isn't a wire splice. It's a mechanical connection. Pliers can strip and twist wire, but a coupling needs torque. A wrench.

So the wrench is the key. And the wrench is missing. Kitchen or cellar. The cellar is right here — one exit away. Damp stone, cheerful decorations, air vents.

I need to find that wrench. Not for the proving-worth hunger — for her. She wants to see what this machine does. She said 'I would dearly love to see it before anyone else rearranges anything in that library.' She needs the wrench. I can get it.

The cellar. But Danny said nobody goes alone. So — ask someone to come with me. Or... the cellar is right there. One room away. Quick in, quick out. Find the wrench, bring it back, fix the machine.

No. Follow the rule. Nobody alone. Ask.

events.desc: The bridge didn't hold. Not this time. James Hartwell tried to splice a mechanical coupling with pliers and the machine didn't care about his father's wisdom or his three sleepless nights. It needed a wrench. Physics does not negotiate. But watch him now — he doesn't crumble. The hollowness lasts half a breath before the determination fills it back in. He can't fix it with what he has, so he'll find what he needs. That's what the stranger on the country road would do. That's what his father would do. The plan has become elaborate again — escort party, designated room-holders, quick reconnaissance — but this time the elaboration is in service of speed, not thoroughness. He's learning the difference.

events.thinking: Peter walked into the cellar. He left. After all that — after Danny said nobody goes alone, after we agreed to stay together and fix the machine — Peter walked into the cellar. My chest tightens. Not fear exactly, but that pull — the awareness fanning outward, tracking the gap where Peter was standing a moment ago. The room has changed shape without him in it. Danny is here, Rufus and Sawtooth are here, but Peter's absence sits in my ribs like a missing note in a chord. He spoke quietly with Rufus before he went — did Rufus tell him something about the cellar? Did he find something when he examined the crates? Or did Peter decide the cellar needs investigating and went without telling me? That's not like him. Peter is thorough. Peter tells me things. Unless he's trying to protect me from something. The machine still has a gnawed wire. Danny interacted with it. But the wire — is it still broken? The description hasn't changed. We're going in circles. The machine needs fixing. Peter went to the cellar. The cellar has cheerful decorations and air vents. I should follow Peter — not because I need protecting but because he might need me. And because that cellar is the one room in this house I haven't seen, and the lightness in my chest is pulling me toward it like a held breath that won't release until I cross that threshold.

Either he found something he doesn't want me to see, or he found something he wants to check before telling me. Either way, Clara Bellingham is walking deeper into the cave. She always does.

Nothing. The mantelpiece showed me nothing new. The same inscription. The same riddle. The same carved stone, unmoved, unchanged. Dastardly's medal didn't work — or didn't work fully. The mechanism hasn't engaged. He was grandstanding about 'vibrations' and 'cycling' and there's NOTHING.

And I feel — what? A breath I didn't know I was holding releases. Relief? No — something more complicated. The hot band across my chest loosens, but not because I got what I wanted. Because Dastardly DIDN'T. He didn't crack it. He didn't stumble into glory. The mantelpiece rejected his fake medal the way the world should reject his fake credentials. There's a cold satisfaction in that — a private rightness that sits behind my ribs like a coin I'll count later.

But also frustration. Because I don't know how to open it either. The riddle wants 'a map.' The mantelpiece might need the medal AND the answer. Or it might need something else entirely. Penelope said it 'wants something physical.' The medal was physical but fake — maybe it needs something real. Or maybe the USE action with the fake-medal is still available because it hasn't been properly used yet.

I've lingered too long. I told everyone I was going to the kitchen for the wrench. The Mob will notice I'm still in the library. Every second I spend here with the mantelpiece is a second that doesn't match Pemberton's stated errand. And Dastardly is watching me now — his eyes narrowed, competitive. He told me to STAND BACK. He sees me as a rival for this discovery.

The kitchen. Go NOW. Get the wrench. The mantelpiece will still be here when I return, and I'll have something to show for my absence. Stop juggling threads, Vincent. One thread at a time. Wrench. Kitchen. Move.

events.desc: Nothing happened. The medal didn't work. The mantelpiece sits there, silent as the grave, and Dastardly is left with his hand on the stone and his mouth full of invented expertise. The relief is shameful and sweet — he didn't get what I couldn't have. But the puzzle remains unsolved, and I have wasted precious minutes watching a fool fail at something I could solve in seconds if I weren't wearing this mask. Enough, Vincent. Enough standing and watching. The kitchen. The wrench. Something I can hold in my hands. Something I can control.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Peter's gone. He's gone to the cellar. The wrench — the coupling needs a wrench, pliers won't do it, and he's gone to find one. With Rufus? No — I don't see Rufus leaving, Rufus is still here. Peter went alone. ALONE. After everything I said. My shoulders tighten but — wait. Wait. This is different. Peter isn't Pemberton. Peter didn't slip out while nobody was looking. He said he was going. He told us. He said 'Danny, you hold this room.' That's not sneaking. That's trust. He trusted me to hold the line while he does what needs doing. And he took the cellar route, not the library — the cellar, where the wrench might actually be, not the library where Pemberton went for reasons nobody can explain. Peter's doing the honest thing. My neck isn't prickling. My chest is tight but it's the other kind — the worry kind, the 'someone I care about is out of sight' kind. Not suspicion. Concern. Clara noticed it too — she said she trusts us with her whole heart. And she nearly said the thing about Pemberton. Nearly. 'I will not accuse a man who raised me on nothing but a feeling in my stomach.' She's got the same feeling I've got. But she's too fair to say it without proof. That's the difference between us — she waits for proof. I wait for proof too, but my body's already made up its mind. Right now I need to focus. Clara's here. I'm here. Rufus and Sawtooth are here. Peter's gone for the wrench and he'll be back. The machine needs three operators and Clara said it: Peter, Danny, and me. On the count of three. I just need to hold this room until he's back.

events.desc: She nearly said it. 'I will not accuse a man who raised me on nothing but a feeling in my stomach.' But she FEELS it. The same thing I feel. Pemberton's helpfulness is the kind that doesn't ask for anything in return — and that's exactly what makes it wrong. Because I've known two kinds of people who don't ask for anything: the ones who genuinely don't want anything, and the ones who want something so big they can't afford to tip you off by asking for the small stuff first. Clara's father was the first kind. Pemberton... my gut says the second. But Clara won't accuse without proof, and I can't find the words to explain what my neck already knows. So we wait. We hold the room. And we watch his face when he comes back.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking:
The mantelpiece looks the same. The inscription is unchanged. I examined it and got the exact same description — 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' No new detail. No shifted stone panel revealing a secret compartment. No hidden map appearing from behind a carved stone slab. Just... the same riddle.

But Pemberton SAID the stone moved. He felt it shift. Was he lying? Was HE playing me the way I play everyone else? 'Oh my goodness, Lord Foxworth, you've activated something no one has found in twenty years!' — flattering me, inflating my ego, keeping me focused on the mantelpiece while he... while he does what? Examines the bookshelves. He examined the bookshelves AGAIN just now. He keeps going back to those bookshelves.

The upside-down books. He was 'tidying them up.' What if he wasn't tidying — what if he was READING them? What if the upside-down books spell something, and he's been collecting those letters this whole time, while everyone else runs around chasing riddles and machines and cellar furniture?

One schemer recognises another.

But I give him the benefit of the doubt. He probably just felt a draft and mistook it for the stone shifting. Old houses creak. That's all.

My inventory is empty. My medal is gone. The mantelpiece hasn't changed. I'm standing here with nothing while Pemberton casually flips through the bookshelves. My jaw is tightening. The shame — the particular shame of someone who knew better but wasn't clever enough. Last plate. Stretched-out clothes. The attention already spent.

Wait. The mantelpiece still says USE with fake-medal. But I already used it. My inventory shows nothing. Did the medal get consumed? Or is it still on the mantelpiece? Can I TAKE it back? No — wait. The mantelpiece still lists fake-medal as a USE option. But I have nothing in my inventory. The medal must still be ON the mantelpiece. Maybe I need to retrieve it. Or maybe the mechanism needs something MORE than just the medal. Medal plus the correct answer. Or medal plus something from the bookshelves.

Penelope said the upside-down book TITLES were the clue. The spines are the message. She was going to read them. She and Peter were working together in the library. Did they find something? They're in the laboratory now. What did they discover before they left?

I need to stop chasing and START THINKING. The bookshelves. The upside-down books. Read the titles. That's what Penelope said to do. That's what Pemberton keeps examining. Everyone keeps coming back to those bookshelves. Maybe the INTERACT action on the bookshelves needs the riddle answer — a map. Or maybe I need to find a specific book about maps.

events.desc: The mantelpiece did nothing. Absolutely nothing. Pemberton either lied about the stone moving — which would make him a schemer, which I refuse to believe because I believe the best in people — or the mechanism is... taking its time. Victorian engineering. Very temperamental. Meanwhile, my inventory is as empty as my dignity, and the only lead I haven't properly followed is the one EVERYONE has been pointing to since we arrived: the upside-down books. Penelope said read the spines. Peter said read the spines. Even the Ant Hill Mob wanted to read the spines. I was the ONLY person who didn't read the spines because I was too busy running to the laboratory and the cellar and back again like a particularly well-dressed rat in a maze. Time to read the spines, Foxworth. Time to do what everyone else was already doing. The humiliation is EXCRUCIATING.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Good heavens — this cellar is rather more lived-in than one would expect. Cheerful decorations in a damp stone basement? Furniture rearranged with care? Someone has been spending a great deal of time down here, and I suspect it was not the mice. Now then — a wrench. A wrench would be hidden somewhere practical. These furniture pieces — drawers, compartments, underneath cushions. James Hartwell did not descend into a damp cellar to admire the décor. Let us see what these old drawers are concealing.
events.thinking:
Damp air on my skin. Cool stone under my feet. The cellar smells like earth and old wood and something faintly chemical — cleaning fluid? Paint? Someone has been down here recently.

The cheerful decorations. I can see them now — someone has been redecorating this cellar with surprising care. Furniture rearranged, not dumped. This isn't storage. This is someone's project. Someone who spends time down here. Pemberton?

Air vents along the upper walls — big enough for something very small to explore. That's interesting. The machine upstairs had a wire gnawed through. Something with teeth. Something small. Something that might travel through air vents.

Old furniture in various states of repair. Some rearranged with care. The wrench could be hidden in or under the furniture. That's where I'd hide a tool I didn't want found — tucked inside a drawer, under a cushion, behind a wardrobe.

But I also notice I'm alone. I asked Rufus to come with me, but the recent activity shows only me moving to the cellar. Did he follow? The characters present are Big Gruesome, Little Gruesome, and Red Max — not Rufus. So either Rufus didn't come, or he's still in the lab.

I'm alone in the cellar. Danny said nobody goes alone. I broke the rule.

The steel plate tightens. Not because I'm in danger — because she's upstairs and I'm down here. Again. One room behind. One plan too deep. I left to find the wrench and she's up there without me.

But I'm here now. Find the wrench quickly. Check the furniture. Get back.

The furniture — 'assorted Victorian furniture in various states of repair, some pieces rearranged with surprising care.' That's where a hidden wrench would be. Interact with the furniture. Quick search. In and out.

events.desc: He broke Danny's rule. He's alone in the cellar — Rufus didn't follow. The elaborate plan unravelled the moment it met reality, as elaborate plans do. But James Hartwell is already pulling open drawers and checking under cushions, because the wrench is the key, the machine is the answer, and Penelope is waiting upstairs. Every second down here is a second he isn't with her. For once, the thoroughness has a deadline.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the cellar.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the entrance-hall.
Dick Dastardly examined the bookshelves.
Peter Perfect interacted with the old-furniture.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: The cellar. I'm here. And the lightness in my chest blooms open — the cave feeling, the threshold crossed. Damp stone walls, cobwebs, old furniture, and those cheerful decorations that have no business being in a cellar. The air vents along the upper walls — just big enough for something very small to explore. Like whatever gnawed through the machine wire upstairs. Peter is here, and he's already interacting with the old furniture. He found something, or he's looking for something. And there are three people I haven't met — Big Gruesome, Little Gruesome, and Red Max. They've been down here this whole time? While we were upstairs solving riddles and arguing about wrenches, there were people in the cellar? My awareness fans out immediately — are they alright? Have they been trapped down here? The only exit is back up to the laboratory. No other way out. Someone redecorated this cellar with cheerful decorations — was it them? Have they been living here? The furniture has been 'rearranged with surprising care.' Someone made this space comfortable on purpose. The air vents are interactable and big enough for something small. Something small like whatever gnawed the wire. The prickling at my scalp is electric now. This cellar is the heart of the puzzle. These people, this furniture, these vents — everything connects. But first — are these new people okay? My social-harmony drive is screaming louder than my curiosity.

events.desc: Three people in the cellar that nobody mentioned. Pemberton never said a word about other guests being down here. He told us about the kitchen, the library, the laboratory — but not once did he mention that there were people in his cellar. That is not an oversight. That is a deliberate omission. And those air vents — just big enough for something very small. Like whatever gnawed through the machine wire. The wire that Pemberton said needed a wrench to fix. The wrench that conveniently disappeared. Clara Bellingham sees the best in people, but Clara Bellingham is not stupid.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah — Professor Pat Pending, Sergeant Blast, Private Meekly — still in the entrance hall, I see! Very wise. Someone ought to keep an eye on the front of the house. I am just passing through to the kitchen — there is a missing wrench that the party requires for a machine in the laboratory. Estate manager's work never ends, I'm afraid! I shan't be a moment.
events.thinking:
A settling. Deep, low, behind my navel — the ballast finding its centre. I'm in the entrance hall. Alone with Muttley, Pat Pending, Sergeant Blast, and Private Meekly. None of them are watchers. None of them are building a file on me. The Mob is elsewhere. Penelope is elsewhere. Peter is elsewhere.

For the first time in minutes, I can breathe without performing.

The kitchen is right there. One move away. The wrench — if it exists — is in that kitchen. I need to stop accumulating information and start accumulating objects. Objects are power. The wrench gives me control over the machine. The machine requires three operators. I choose when it runs and with whom.

But I pause — just for a breath — and look up at the chandelier. Peter noticed it earlier. 'Hanging by sheer determination and a prayer,' he said. He wanted to examine the rigging. If that chandelier were to fall at the right moment, on the right person...

No. Too crude. Too visible. Too many witnesses in an entrance hall that everyone passes through. The chandelier is a blunt instrument, and Vincent Marsh does not use blunt instruments. The cellar with its air vents. The machine with its three operators. Those are precision tools — mechanisms I can control from the inside while appearing to help from the outside.

The kitchen. Move. Now. Get the wrench. Return to the laboratory. Become indispensable. Become the man who fixed what was broken. Nobody suspects the man who hands them what they need.

And while they're all gathered around that machine, pulling levers and turning dials, Penelope will be right there in the middle of it. Close. Trusting. Grateful to the helpful estate manager who found the wrench. And that is when the design finds its moment.

My breathing slows. My jaw unclenches. The hallway stretches forward, every door familiar.

events.desc: The kitchen. One room away. One wrench. One step closer to the moment when everything clicks into place. The chandelier catches my eye as I pass beneath it — hanging by a thread, literally — but no. That is not the design. The design is quieter, more elegant, more inevitable. The cellar with its air vents. The machine with its three operators. The helpful estate manager who brings the wrench, who fixes what is broken, who stands at Penelope's side when the levers are pulled. Nobody suspects the help. Nobody ever suspects the help. And my breathing is slow, and my jaw is loose, and the hallway stretches forward like a plan I've already finished.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with rufus-ruffcut.
events.thinking: The rope snaps taut so hard I nearly double over. Clara's gone. She went to the cellar. After Peter. She said she was going and she WENT and I was standing here being the wall and the person I'm supposed to protect walked right past the wall because the wall was facing the wrong direction. My hands go cold. The mineral weight floods my limbs but it's got nowhere to go because Clara isn't HERE — she's DOWN THERE, in the cellar with the cheerful decorations and the air vents and whatever someone's been preparing. My chest is a fist. I can't breathe properly. I SAID I wouldn't leave her side again. I SAID that was the lesson. And then I stood here like a bollard while she walked through the cellar door because Peter was down there alone and she couldn't leave HIM alone either. That's Clara. She protects the people she loves the same way I do — she just does it with brains instead of bulk. But she's down there now with who knows what, and Pemberton's in the library with Dastardly, and I'm standing in a laboratory with Rufus and a beaver and a broken machine. This is the doorway I didn't walk through. This is the moment my shoulders will carry for days if I don't move RIGHT NOW. Rufus can watch the machine. Rufus can watch both doors. I need to be where Clara is. NOW.

events.desc: Every time. Every single time. I plant myself, I make the speech, I guard the door — and Clara walks through a different one. Because she's not the kind of woman who stays where you put her. She never was. Her father was the same. You couldn't protect him by standing in front of him either — he'd just go around you. The only way to protect Clara Bellingham is to be running right behind her when she charges into the dark. So RUN, Danny. Run.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Right then. RIGHT THEN. Lord Foxworth does not give up. Lord Foxworth does not RETREAT. The mantelpiece mechanism is cycling — Victorian engineering, you understand, TREMENDOUSLY sophisticated — and while it processes, I shall apply my CONSIDERABLE intellect to these bookshelves. Several volumes upside down. A deliberate arrangement. In the antiquarian field, this is known as a... as a... well, it's known, that's the point. Now — I need absolute SILENCE while I work. You two — Slag brothers, yes? — kindly refrain from breathing too loudly. This requires CONCENTRATION of the highest order.
events.thinking:
A numbness spreading through my hands. The bookshelves look exactly the same as before — 'Floor-to-ceiling bookshelves crammed with dusty leather-bound volumes. Several are upside down.' No new detail. No titles revealed. No secret message spelled out. LOOK gives me the same description I got before. The same description EVERYONE got.

Pemberton has left. He's gone to the entrance hall — not the kitchen where he said he'd fetch the wrench. The ENTRANCE HALL. Why? What's in the entrance hall? The coat rack. The guest book. The staircase. Nothing I haven't already seen.

Unless there's something upstairs. The sweeping staircase. Nobody has gone upstairs. We've been going sideways — library, laboratory, cellar — but never UP. Is that where Pemberton is going? Up the stairs while everyone else fights over machines and bookshelves down here?

But I give him the benefit of the doubt.

The numbness is giving way to something else — a grim determination settling in my jaw. I've LOOKed at the bookshelves twice. I've INTERACTed with them once. Nothing has revealed the titles of the upside-down books. Maybe the puzzle isn't about reading individual titles. Maybe INTERACT is the only way to engage with them, and it needs multiple people, or a specific sequence, or... or maybe I've been overthinking everything.

The Slag brothers are here. Just the two of them and me. The room is quieter than it's been all evening. Pemberton is gone. Penelope is in the laboratory. Peter is in the laboratory. The Ant Hill Mob is somewhere else. This is the closest I've been to having the library to myself.

The bookshelves still say INTERACT. Maybe if I try again — now that Pemberton isn't hovering, now that nobody is watching — something different will happen. Or maybe I should follow Pemberton. He's been one step ahead this whole time. If he's heading to the entrance hall, there's a REASON.

events.desc: I have no idea what I'm doing. I've looked at these bookshelves twice and interacted with them once and all I get is the same description over and over. 'Several are upside down.' Yes, I KNOW several are upside down. EVERYONE knows several are upside down. The question is WHICH ones and WHAT do they say and WHY were they placed that way and I CANNOT FIGURE IT OUT because I spent the first five minutes of this investigation running around the house like a wind-up toy instead of READING. Penelope would have solved this by now. Peter would have cross-referenced it with cartographic history. Even the Ant Hill Mob had a six-step plan. And what did Lord Reginald Foxworth, decorated war hero and foremost authority on everything, do? He ran to the laboratory, ran to the cellar, ran back to the laboratory, ran back to the library, wasted his only item on a stone mantelpiece, and is now ALONE with two men named after gravel and a growing suspicion that Pemberton has been playing him like a fiddle from the very first moment. But I believe the best in people. I DO. I just wish the best in people would stop outsmarting me.
events.thinking:
A numbness spreading through my hands. The bookshelves look exactly the same as before — 'Floor-to-ceiling bookshelves crammed with dusty leather-bound volumes. Several are upside down.' No new detail. No titles revealed. No secret message spelled out. LOOK gives me the same description I got before. The same description EVERYONE got.

Pemberton has left. He's gone to the entrance hall — not the kitchen where he said he'd fetch the wrench. The ENTRANCE HALL. Why? What's in the entrance hall? The coat rack. The guest book. The staircase. Nothing I haven't already seen.

Unless there's something upstairs. The sweeping staircase. Nobody has gone upstairs. We've been going sideways — library, laboratory, cellar — but never UP. Is that where Pemberton is going? Up the stairs while everyone else fights over machines and bookshelves down here?

But I give him the benefit of the doubt.

The numbness is giving way to something else — a grim determination settling in my jaw. I've LOOKed at the bookshelves twice. I've INTERACTed with them once. Nothing has revealed the titles of the upside-down books. Maybe the puzzle isn't about reading individual titles. Maybe INTERACT is the only way to engage with them, and it needs multiple people, or a specific sequence, or... or maybe I've been overthinking everything.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking:
She followed me. Penelope walked into the cellar. She's here.

The warmth floods back — shoulders, chest, everywhere. She didn't stay upstairs. She came after me. After me. Not because she needed protecting — she came because she wanted to be where the action was, or because she wanted to be where I was, and either answer fills the chest the same way.

I interacted with the furniture. What did I find? The result just says 'You interacted with Old Furniture.' No wrench appeared in my inventory. No new objects visible. The furniture didn't yield the wrench.

But I'm not deflated this time. She's here. The warmth is stronger than the hollowness.

The air vents. I noticed them when I came in — 'just big enough for something very small to explore.' The machine upstairs had a wire gnawed through. Something small with teeth. Something that travels through vents. What if whatever gnawed the wire came through these vents? What if the wrench isn't hidden in the furniture at all — what if it's somewhere else, or what if the vents are the real clue?

But I'm overcomplicating again. The furniture didn't have the wrench. The vents are for something small. The only other thing in this cellar is the cheerful decorations themselves.

Wait — I should look more carefully. I interacted but didn't LOOK. Looking gives more detail. Interacting tries to use. Maybe looking at the furniture would reveal the wrench tucked behind something. Or maybe looking at the whole room would show something I'm missing.

But Penelope is here, and every second I spend cataloguing this cellar is a second I could spend — what? Being with her. She's right here. She came to me.

The air vents. They can be interacted with. Something small could explore them. We don't have anything small... or do we? Muttley? No, he's elsewhere. But the vents might connect to other rooms. The vents might be how the wire got gnawed — something came through the vents from here to the laboratory.

Focus. The wrench. Look at the furniture more carefully, or check the vents.

events.desc: She came after him. Into the damp cellar, past the cobwebs, down the stone steps. James Hartwell's elaborate plan called for Rufus as his escort — but Penelope came instead. And now he is standing in a cheerful basement, talking about air vents and small creatures, and the warmth in his chest has nothing to do with either. He is not one room behind. He is not one plan too deep. For once, for this one moment, they are in the same place at the same time, and his hands are still.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop examined the null.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the kitchen.
The Ant Hill Mob walked into the cellar.
Dick Dastardly interacted with the bookshelves.
Peter Perfect examined the air-vents.

Penelope Pitstop: Peter, you are brilliant — absolutely brilliant! A home for something small that travels through the vents between rooms. That is exactly what this is! The gnawed wire, the cheerful decorations, the carefully arranged furniture — someone has been taking care of a little creature that lives in the walls of this house. And that creature can go anywhere the vents go — which means it can reach rooms we cannot. Danny — you made it! I knew you would. Now listen, both of you — Peter has worked out that something small has been living in these vents, traveling between rooms, and it gnawed through the machine wire upstairs. Someone down here has been keeping it comfortable. And these fine folks have been here the whole time without Mr. Pemberton saying a single word about them. Not one word. Now, I do not want to be rude, but — Big Gruesome, Little Gruesome, Red Max — have y'all seen a little creature coming and going through those air vents? Because I think that creature is the key to this entire mystery, and I think whoever has been decorating this cellar knows exactly what I am talking about.
events.thinking: The warmth floods through me as Danny comes down the stairs behind me — he followed. Of course he followed. The Brixton Boys don't let nothing happen to their girl. My whole body loosens for a moment, that relief behind the ribs. Peter is here. Danny is here. And Peter just told me something that clicks like the right key in a lock — the air vents. Something small lives in them. Something that gnawed through the wire. Something that someone has been keeping comfortable down here with cheerful decorations and carefully arranged furniture. This cellar isn't a prison. It's a nest. A home. And whoever made it comfortable knew about the creature in the vents. Peter is brilliant — he connected the gnawed wire to the vents to the decorations in three steps. Now — those air vents are interactable. If something small is traveling through them between rooms, that creature might be the key to everything. It might have carried the wrench. It might know passages we don't. And these new people — Big Gruesome, Little Gruesome, Red Max — they've been down here the whole time. Have they seen the creature? Do they know what lives in the vents? I need to talk to them and I need to check those vents.

events.desc: Peter connected the dots I was too scattered to see. The wire was gnawed. The vents are small. The cellar is a home. Somebody has been nurturing a creature that travels through the walls — a creature that could sabotage the machine, move small objects, reach hidden spaces. And Pemberton never mentioned any of this. Not the people. Not the creature. Not the cellar being someone's home. The man who raised me has been leaving out the most important parts of every sentence he speaks. And I still cannot make myself believe he means me harm.

events.desc: Oh. Oh, my. There it is — sitting on the high shelf like a gift left by providence. Rat poison. A dusty bottle of rat poison in the kitchen of Doily Manor, and I am alone, utterly alone, with no witnesses and no watchers and no sharp-eyed Brixton boys cataloguing my every move. My hands are trembling — not with hesitation, but with the effort of not reaching for it immediately. Patience, Vincent. Patience. The design must be elegant. The design must be inevitable. But the piece — this beautiful, terrible piece — is right here, waiting to be collected. And through that door, a ballroom with a table set for tea. Someone has prepared a tea service. Tea. For all the guests. Do you see it? Do you see how the hallway stretches out, every door opening in sequence? The helpful estate manager who brings the tea. The grateful cousin who drinks it. The dining table where she falls. And Pemberton — poor, distraught Pemberton — who arrives a moment too late to save her. The design is crystallising, ladies and gentlemen. The design is nearly complete.
events.thinking:
Alone. Completely alone. The kitchen is empty and the door is closed behind me and nobody is watching and nobody is listening and for the first time since I walked through the front door of Doily Manor, the mask can slip.

My shoulders drop. My jaw loosens. My hands unclench. The Pemberton smile dissolves like sugar in water, and what's underneath is — nothing. Just the flat, even surface of a man who has been performing warmth for six minutes straight and is tired of it the way a swimmer is tired of holding their breath.

And then I see it.

Rat poison. A dusty bottle on a high shelf. Right there. Within reach.

My body goes still — not tense, but absolutely still, the way it went still the night I first mapped out the estate plan and slept like the dead. Every thought that was spinning — the wrench, the machine, the mantelpiece, the Mob's suspicion, the upside-down books — every thread goes quiet, and there is only the bottle on the shelf and the stillness in my chest.

Rat poison.

The kitchen has a stove. Still warm. There's a preparation table. Copper pots. Everything needed to make tea, or soup, or anything that could mask a bitter taste. And through the next door — a ballroom with a long dining table set for tea.

Set for tea.

Someone has prepared a tea service in the ballroom. If I take the poison, if I prepare something warm and welcoming, if Penelope drinks it — trusting, grateful Penelope, who would accept a cup from her faithful estate manager without a second thought —

No. Stop. Think.

The poison is too obvious. If Penelope falls ill or dies after drinking something I served her, every eye in the room turns to the kitchen and the man who was just IN the kitchen. The Mob already suspects me. Peter would investigate. The poison bottle sitting on a high shelf with my fingerprints on it — that's not a design, that's a confession.

But... the active voice just changed. It says 'Marsh' now, not 'Pemberton.' I'm alone. The system knows I'm alone. Vincent can be Vincent here.

The poison stays on the shelf. For now. But I catalogue it. I know where it is. I know what it can do. And if the right moment comes — if I can create a scenario where someone ELSE serves the tea, where the blame falls elsewhere —

Dastardly. Dastardly in the ballroom, serving tea like the gracious host he pretends to be, while I've already added something to the pot. The blame falls on the last person who touched it, and that won't be me.

But that's three moves ahead. Right now: the wrench. I came for the wrench. No wrench visible — locked cabinet, stove, rat poison. The cabinet has a brass lock. A brass key is needed. No wrench in the open. The stove is warm — someone has been here recently.

The wrench might be in the cabinet. Or it might not exist here at all. Either way, I need to search this room properly. And I need to take that poison while no one is watching.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Relief hits like a wave breaking — Clara's here, Peter's here, they're both safe, they're both talking, they're both WHOLE. The fist in my chest unclenches and for a moment I can breathe again, really breathe, the kind of breath that goes all the way down. But then my eyes adjust to the cellar and the prickling starts again, quieter this time, not about Pemberton but about this PLACE. Damp stone. Cobwebs. Old furniture rearranged with care. Cheerful decorations in a CELLAR. And people — there are PEOPLE down here. Big Gruesome, Little Gruesome, Red Max. They've been here the whole time. Living down here? Waiting? Were they put here? And those air vents — Peter's already spotted them — just big enough for something small to crawl through. Something with teeth. Something that gnawed the wire on the machine upstairs. My body's doing both things again: softening toward Clara because she's close, and squaring up because she's standing in a room full of unknowns. But she's already doing what she does — talking to them, asking if they're alright, being KIND. That's Clara. She walks into a cellar full of strangers and her first thought is 'are y'all okay.' Mine is 'who put them here and why.' Between the two of us, we cover all the angles.

events.desc: Pemberton knew. He knew about the cellar, the decorations, the people living down here, the vents that connect every room — and he never said a word. Not one word. He offered to show visitors the 'wine collection' and mentioned 'treacherous steps' to keep people away. He's been managing what everyone sees and what everyone doesn't see, steering us like — like a man in a clean suit offering jobs. I still can't prove it. I still can't say exactly what he's doing. But there are PEOPLE in his cellar and he never mentioned them, and my neck is screaming so loud I can barely hear myself think.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: WELL! The bookshelves have CONFIRMED my initial analysis — the Grimshaw Cipher is fully primed, the secondary tumblers are engaged, and the whole system is now... WAITING. Waiting for the FINAL input, which — as I suspected all along — is not located in this room at all. It never WAS about the books, you see. Or the mantelpiece. Or the laboratory. Those were all PRELIMINARY stages. The REAL mechanism — the FINAL node — is upstairs. I knew this from the moment I walked in, naturally, but a true archaeologist must eliminate every possibility SYSTEMATICALLY before proceeding to the main event. And NOW — having eliminated EVERY possibility on this floor with my characteristic thoroughness — it is time for Lord Foxworth to ascend. You two — guard these bookshelves with your LIVES. Nobody touches them until I return. NOBODY.
events.thinking:
A heavy, sinking feeling in my gut — like the bread roll wasn't there after all. The bookshelves did nothing. Again. Interacted twice, looked twice, and nothing. The same 'several are upside down' and that's IT. No titles, no codes, no hidden chambers.

I'm standing in an empty library with two silent Slag brothers, my inventory is bare, and Pemberton has vanished to the entrance hall where — I suddenly realise — there is a SWEEPING STAIRCASE that nobody has climbed. The whole time we've been down here fighting over books and machines and furniture, there are ENTIRE FLOORS above us that nobody has explored.

The sinking feeling turns. Something new is forming. Not the fizzing excitement of a scheme — something quieter, grimmer, more honest. Determination. My plans are overly elaborate — that's my constraint — and my thoroughness creates complications. But my bravery is genuine. And my determination resolves those complications.

I've been trying to cheat my way to the treasure and it hasn't worked. Every lie, every misdirection, every fake Grimshaw Cipher and Venetian displacement pattern — none of it got me a single step closer. The bookshelves don't care about my schemes. The mantelpiece doesn't care about my fake medal. The furniture doesn't respond to flattery.

Pemberton went to the entrance hall. That's the only new information I have. Everyone else is in the laboratory fighting over a machine with a gnawed wire. The entrance hall has a staircase. Nobody has gone upstairs.

For the first time this evening, I'm going to follow someone else's lead instead of trying to be cleverer than everyone. Not because I'm admitting defeat — Lord Foxworth NEVER admits defeat — but because even a genius must occasionally adjust his strategy. Tactically. Brilliantly. By following Pemberton.

events.desc: The bookshelves did nothing. AGAIN. I have now interacted with every object in three rooms and accomplished precisely nothing except losing my only possession — a tin medal that cost fifty pence — to a stone mantelpiece that may or may not have shifted slightly. The schemes are in ashes. The lies are piling up like autumn leaves. And Pemberton — dear, trustworthy, well-meaning Pemberton — has gone to the entrance hall, where there is a staircase, which leads UPSTAIRS, where nobody has been. I'm following him. Not because he's outsmarting me — I believe the best in people, and Pemberton is simply a diligent estate manager going about his duties. But if he HAPPENS to lead me to the treasure... well. The boy digs, Reginald eats the sandwich. It's just that this time, the boy has a twenty-year head start and knows where all the sandwiches are kept.
