events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking:
She said 'Peter, you had me worried half to death, coming down here all by yourself.' Worried. About me. The warmth is so strong it's almost painful — like the afternoon when the teacher praised the project and I couldn't have said why the feeling was so deep.

And she's doing what she does — what she always does. She saw people in the cellar and her first instinct was kindness. 'Are y'all alright? Is there anything you need?' She didn't see strangers in a dark basement and feel fear. She felt concern. For them. She's brighter than me, funnier than me, and completely unaware of it. She always has been.

The air vents gave me nothing new — 'just big enough for something very small.' I knew that already. No wrench here. The furniture didn't have it. The vents don't reveal it. The wrench isn't in this cellar.

But she asked me a direct question: 'Peter, darling, what have you found in that furniture?' I need to answer honestly. I found nothing. The furniture didn't yield the wrench. James Hartwell can admit when a search comes up empty.

Danny is here now too — the Ant Hill Mob walked in. Good. Everyone's together. Nobody alone.

The wrench isn't here. We should go back to the laboratory. The machine needs three operators — we have enough people. Maybe the machine can work without the wrench if enough operators coordinate the levers. Or maybe the wrench is in the kitchen, which we haven't explored yet. But the kitchen isn't accessible from here — we'd need to go back through the laboratory to the library to the entrance hall.

Or — Penelope's instinct. She's talking to the people down here. Big Gruesome, Little Gruesome, Red Max. They've been in this cellar. They might know where the wrench is. They might know who's been redecorating. She's asking the right questions while I've been examining furniture and air vents.

She's always been the sharper one. Let her lead. Support her. Be present. Stop trying to be the one who finds the answer and start being the one who helps her find it.

events.desc: And there it is — the lesson he keeps learning and keeps forgetting. He came to the cellar for a wrench. She came to the cellar for the people. He searched furniture and examined air vents. She said 'are y'all alright?' James Hartwell is good at things — fixing, planning, protecting. But she is good at seeing. And the warmth he feels when she shows him how is not the hollow ache of being outshone. It is the deeper warmth from that school project — when the teacher praised what they'd built together, and the feeling surprised him.

I reached in, or I called into them, or I listened. Peter is examining the furniture again, Danny is examining the room. The Gruesomes and Red Max are here and I asked them about the creature but I haven't heard their response yet in the recent activity — or maybe they're just quiet. Quiet people in a cellar. Have they been trapped here? Are they comfortable? My social-harmony drive is pulsing. I need to engage with them directly. I've been talking at the room but I haven't pulled anyone aside or really connected with these new people one-on-one. Big Gruesome, Little Gruesome — the names suggest a parent and child? Or siblings? And Red Max — who is he in this? My awareness tracks them the way a hand checks for heat. They've been down here, silent, while everyone upstairs has been arguing about wrenches and riddles. If they've been here long enough to decorate, they know things. They know about the vents, the creature, maybe even the Diamond. I should talk to them directly. But which one? Little Gruesome might be more approachable — or Big Gruesome might have the answers. Let me try the old furniture — it's interactable and 'rearranged with surprising care.' Maybe there's something hidden in the furniture arrangement itself. Or I should pull aside one of the Gruesomes for a real conversation.

events.desc: I have been so busy chasing clues — riddles, bookshelves, machines, wrenches, vents — that I almost forgot the most important thing in any room is the people. Grandmother's locked box taught me patience. The girl next door taught me that you don't need words to communicate. These folks have been sitting in a cellar while the rest of us ran circles upstairs, and nobody thought to ask them what they knew. Clara Bellingham does not overlook people. That is the one thing she will never do.

They know about the vents, the creature, maybe even the Diamond. I should talk to them directly. But which one? Little Gruesome might be more approachable — or Big Gruesome might have the answers. Let me try the old furniture — it's interactable and 'rearranged with surprising care.' Maybe there's something hidden in the furniture arrangement itself. Or I should pull aside one of the Gruesomes for a real conversation.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Now then... the kitchen. Let me see. Copper pots, preparation table, stove still warm — someone has been in here recently. And this cabinet... locked. Brass lock, no key. Where would the master have kept a brass key? This is most vexing. The wrench is not on any surface I can see. If it is anywhere in this kitchen, it is behind that lock.
events.thinking:
The weight of it in my pocket. Small. Dense. Real. My hand closes around the bottle and something settles in my chest — that deep, low, mineral settling, the one that comes when a piece of the design locks into place. Not excitement. Not triumph. Just... completeness. Like finding the last number in a ledger that finally balances.

I'm holding rat poison in a kitchen with a warm stove and a ballroom set for tea one door away. The design is no longer theoretical. It has mass. It has weight. It sits in my pocket like a promise.

But — breathe, Vincent. The elaborate plan is the dangerous plan. That's my constraint. I over-prepare, I over-commit, and my thoroughness creates complications. The tea scenario is already three steps deep: poison the tea, lure someone else to serve it, ensure Penelope drinks from the right cup, manage the aftermath. Each step is a hinge. Each hinge can fail. And the Mob is watching.

Simpler. Think simpler.

The stove is warm. Someone was here recently. The locked cabinet needs a brass key — no wrench in the open means either it's in the cabinet or it doesn't exist in this kitchen. I need to check the stove — what's warming? Is someone preparing food already? If so, there might be an opportunity I haven't considered.

But right now, the ballroom. Tea is set. If I can get into the ballroom, I can see the tea service — how many cups, what's already prepared, whether there's a teapot I can access before anyone arrives. The ballroom is the next room. The design lives there.

No. STOP. The wrench. I told everyone I was coming here for the wrench. If I return without it, the Mob's suspicion grows. 'What was 'e doing in there, then?' I need to search this room properly. The cabinet is locked — I don't have the brass key. The stove might have something inside it. Let me look at this room carefully before moving on.

The poison is in my pocket. It will wait. It is very, very patient. Like me.

events.desc: It's in my pocket. The weight of it sits against my thigh like a second heartbeat — small, patient, certain. The design has a new piece, and the piece has changed everything. I am no longer mapping possibilities. I am holding one. The ballroom is through that door. The tea is set. The stove is warm. But Vincent Marsh does not rush. Vincent Marsh is very, very patient. The wrench first — or the excuse for not finding it. Then the ballroom. Then the tea. Then the moment when Penelope Pitstop — sweet, trusting Clara Bellingham — drinks what the helpful estate manager prepared for her. And then... the deepest sleep I've had in years.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with big-gruesome.
events.thinking: The warmth and the prickling are both running hard, but for the first time they're aimed at different targets and that's actually USEFUL. The warmth is on Clara — she's right there, arm's reach, safe, brilliant, already working the problem. Peter's found the vents, Clara's connected the dots — something small lives in these walls, travels between rooms, gnawed the wire. And someone's been CARING for it down here, keeping the cellar cheerful, arranging the furniture. The Gruesomes and Red Max — they've been here the whole time. Pemberton never mentioned them. Never. Not once. He talked about the wine collection, the treacherous steps, the master's habits with tools — but never the PEOPLE in his cellar. The prickling is all for Pemberton now, sharp and clear. He's been hiding things. Hiding PEOPLE. And something small that travels through vents — that's his network, isn't it? His eyes and ears in every room. He knew exactly what we were doing and where we were because something was watching us through those vents and reporting back. That's why he always knew where to be, what to offer, when to slip away. But I can't say that. I don't have the words for it. I never have the words. What I have is my body between Clara and the only exit, and my eyes on these new faces, and the question Clara's already asking: have you seen the creature in the vents? Let Clara do the talking. Let Peter do the thinking. Danny does the standing.

events.desc: I can feel it all coming together now, even though I can't quite see the shape of it. Pemberton's been running this house like a chess game — moving people, hiding things, steering everyone where he wants them. And down here in the cellar, the piece he didn't want us to find. Not the wrench. Not a clue. PEOPLE. People he left in the dark while he smiled at us upstairs. The man in the clean suit. The kid who laughed too easily. The helpfulness that never asked for anything in return. My neck knows. It's always known.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with pat-pending.
events.thinking:
A prickle across my scalp. Pemberton isn't here. He said he was coming to the entrance hall — or rather, he said he was going to the kitchen through the library, but he went to the entrance hall instead — and now he's NOT HERE. He's gone. Vanished. The kitchen is accessible from here — that's an exit — so maybe he went through to the kitchen after all. Maybe he really was just fetching that wrench like he promised.

But the staircase. The sweeping staircase. I'm staring at it now. It goes UP. Nobody has gone up. There's no exit listed for upstairs — the exits are Kitchen and Library. So... there IS no upstairs? Or it's not accessible? The staircase is here but it doesn't lead to a room I can reach?

My chest deflates. The grand staircase theory is dead.

But look who IS here. Muttley. Professor Pat Pending. Sergeant Blast. Private Meekly. Four characters who've been in the entrance hall this whole time while everyone else was fighting over the library and laboratory. What have THEY been doing? What have they found?

Muttley. My loyal Muttley — well, not MY Muttley in this scenario, but a Muttley nonetheless. And Professor Pat Pending — the man I originally tried to recruit for my 'scholarly expedition.' He's been HERE. In the entrance hall. Doing... what?

The guest book. It's still here, still interactable. I interacted with it at the very beginning, but I barely looked at it — I was too busy fabricating lies about Professor Grimshaw. What if the guest book actually CONTAINS real clues that I ignored in my rush to impress everyone?

The kitchen. Pemberton said the wrench might be in the kitchen. Penelope said the machine needs a wrench. The machine needs three operators AND a wrench. If I find the wrench, I have LEVERAGE. I have something everyone needs. Something to TRADE. Something to hold over them.

The hollow behind my navel tightens. The inventory system fires up. A wrench. Something to HAVE. Something that isn't a worthless tin medal from Croydon.

events.desc: The kitchen. Pemberton said the wrench is in the kitchen. If I can get someone ELSE to fetch it for me, and then TAKE it from them before they deliver it to the laboratory, I'll have the one thing everyone needs and nobody has. A wrench. Not a fake medal. Not a fabricated Grimshaw Cipher. A REAL, USEFUL OBJECT that the machine requires to function. And then — oh, THEN — Lord Foxworth will be in the most MAGNIFICENT position: the man with the wrench, the man who decides who gets to use the machine, the man who sets the terms. The boy fetches the sandwich. Reginald holds the sandwich. EVERYONE wants the sandwich. This might actually work. This MIGHT ACTUALLY WORK.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Miss Pitstop raises a rather important point, and I confess it had not occurred to me until she said it — Mr. Pemberton directed us to the cellar and the kitchen as possible locations for the wrench. He described this room. He never once mentioned that there were people down here. An estate manager who knows where every wrench might have wandered but neglects to mention three guests in his own cellar? That is... well. James Hartwell believes the best in people. But even James Hartwell has noticed a pattern forming. Ladies, gentlemen — anything you can tell us about these vents, about who has been caring for this room, about what small creature might be travelling through the walls of this house — it would be enormously helpful. And if there is anything you need from us in return, you have only to ask. That is what good people do — my father taught me that.
events.thinking:
She called me brilliant. 'Peter, you are brilliant — absolutely brilliant!' The straightening in my spine. The quiet heat. The bridge holding the weight while the judges wrote in their notebooks. She took my observation about the vents and the small creature and built something from it — a whole theory, a connection I hadn't fully made. The gnawed wire, the cheerful decorations, the carefully arranged furniture — someone keeping a creature comfortable. And she credited me for the insight.

This is the school project all over again. She's brighter, funnier, completely unaware of it. I build the model, she makes it sing. And the warmth is deeper than the grade.

She also noticed something crucial — Pemberton never mentioned these people being down here. Not one word. He said the cellar might have the wrench. He didn't say it had three people living in it. The prickle on my neck sharpens to a point. Benefit of the doubt is becoming harder to extend.

But right now — she's asking the Gruesomes and Red Max about the creature in the vents. She's leading. I should support. The furniture examination gave me nothing new. The wrench still hasn't been found.

Penelope interacted with the air vents. She's ahead of me — she's already investigating the creature. I should be ready to act on whatever she finds. Stay close. Be useful. Be the hands when she's the eyes.

The proving-worth hunger is quiet right now. Something else has taken its place — the deeper warmth, the one from the school project. The one I couldn't name at eight years old. The one I still can't name. Being next to her, working together, building something neither of us could build alone.

Wait. Let her lead. Be present. When she needs something done — done with hands, with strength, with engineering — that's when I step forward. Until then, stand beside her. Not between.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop interacted with the old-furniture.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) interacted with the stove.
The Ant Hill Mob examined the old-furniture.
Dick Dastardly walked into the kitchen.

Penelope Pitstop: Peter, even you see it now, and you are the most generous man I know. Mr. Pemberton has been telling us exactly where to look and exactly what to worry about, and every single time, the most important thing was what he did not say. He did not say there were people in the cellar. He did not say there was a creature in the vents. He said the wrench might be in the kitchen — and then he went to the library. I have been trying so hard to see the best in him, because that is who I am and because he raised me and because I owe him everything. But the best clues are the ones people write down without realizing they're clues at all — and Mr. Pemberton has been very, very careful about what he writes down. Now — Little Gruesome, honey, I know the grownups have been making a lot of noise. Would you mind terribly if I asked you something, just the two of us? Sometimes the youngest person in the room sees the clearest, and I have a feeling you have seen things in this cellar that nobody else has noticed.
events.thinking: I've interacted with both the air vents and the old furniture now. Peter said the furniture yielded nothing — no wrench, no hidden compartments. And now even Peter is saying it out loud: Pemberton never mentioned people in his cellar. An estate manager who knows where every tool might be but 'neglects to mention three guests.' Peter believes the best in people too, but even he sees the pattern. That lands in my chest like a stone dropped into still water. If Peter sees it, then it's real. It's not just my stomach being paranoid. Pemberton has been managing information — telling us just enough to keep us moving, always directing, always helpful, but always leaving out the most important pieces. The wrench. The people. The creature. The cellar. Everything he said was true but nothing he said was complete. That is not forgetfulness. That is strategy. And it's the strategy of someone who knows exactly what's in this house and doesn't want us to find it. The ache in my stomach sharpens. The man who raised me. The man who held me when Mama and Daddy died. But I cannot let that love make me blind. Not when my people are in this house. Not when the Gruesomes and Red Max have been sitting in a cellar nobody mentioned. I need to stop examining objects and start connecting with these people. A PULL_ASIDE with Little Gruesome might work — children often see things adults miss, and they're usually more honest about what they've seen.

events.desc: I just said it out loud. The man who raised me has been lying by omission since the moment we arrived. Every helpful suggestion was a redirection. Every charming reassurance was a closed door. And I still love him. And I still cannot make myself believe he means me harm. But love and blindness are not the same thing, and Clara Bellingham chooses her friend over the popular group every time — even when the popular group includes the man who taught her to tie her shoes.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking:
A spike of cold alertness — shoulders squaring before I've decided to worry. Dastardly just walked in. The Pemberton mask snaps back into place like a reflex, the smile arriving before I've even turned around. The poison is in my pocket. Heavy. Obvious? No — a small bottle, tucked deep. He can't see it. He can't know.

But my skin reads the room change. One second I was alone — truly alone — and now I'm not. The stove is open in front of me, I just interacted with it. Whatever I found inside, I need to process it while looking natural. Pemberton checks the stove. That's what estate managers do.

Dastardly. Why is he here? He was in the library fiddling with the mantelpiece. He followed me. Or he came for the wrench. Or — he mentioned the kitchen silverware earlier. The magpie chasing silver. He probably came for the silverware.

Either way, he's here now, and I need to be Pemberton again. Fussing about the stove. Mentioning the locked cabinet. Complaining about the missing wrench. Being exactly what everyone expects: the tired, loyal, slightly boring estate manager.

But also — Dastardly in the kitchen is an opportunity. If he touches anything in here — if he opens the cabinet, if he handles the teapot in the ballroom — then his fingerprints are on everything. He was in the kitchen. He had access. If something happens to the tea later, the man who was ALSO in the kitchen is the man they investigate first.

Especially if Pemberton wasn't alone in the kitchen. If there was a witness to Dastardly being here. And I am that witness.

The design refines itself. Not three steps. Two. Get Dastardly into the ballroom. Let him touch the tea service. Then later — much later, when the moment is right — the poison finds its way into the pot, and the last person seen handling the tea was Lord Reginald Foxworth, decorated war hero, amateur archaeologist, and the most obvious suspect in every room he enters.

events.desc: And there he is — my beautiful, unwitting alibi. Dastardly in the kitchen, Dastardly's fingerprints on every surface, Dastardly about to walk into the ballroom and handle the tea service because the helpful estate manager asked him so nicely. The design doesn't need to be elaborate, ladies and gentlemen. It only needs one patsy, one teapot, and one trusting cousin who would never refuse a cup from the man she's known her whole life. The weight in my pocket presses against my thigh. The stove is warm. The tea is set. events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with little-gruesome.
events.thinking: Something softens in me, looking at this furniture. It's been arranged with CARE. Not shoved about — placed. The way someone makes a home out of nothing when nothing's all they've got. I know this. I know this in my bones. The way we used to stack pallets in the alley to make walls, drape a tarp over a broken fence to make a roof, arrange milk crates in a circle so it felt like sitting around a table. This cellar isn't a prison. Someone's made it a home. And that — that changes the arithmetic. The Gruesomes and Red Max aren't captives. They're people who've been LIVING here, quietly, in the walls of a house that someone else runs. And the furniture tells the story their words haven't yet — whoever arranged these pieces did it with the same instinct I had at eight years old, sitting outside a door all night. Not because anyone asked. Because leaving felt like breaking. Peter's noticed it too — he said Pemberton 'neglected to mention three guests in his own cellar,' and the way he said it, careful and measured, I could hear him arriving at the same place my neck arrived twenty minutes ago. Even Peter's starting to see it. Clara's already asking the right questions — she always does. And me? I'm standing by the only exit, watching the stairs, because sooner or later Pemberton's going to notice we've all disappeared to the one place he didn't want us to find.

events.desc: Homes made from nothing. I know this language. It's the language of people who don't get invited to the table, so they build their own. These people aren't a threat to Clara — my neck's quiet on that front. They're the ones Pemberton didn't want us to meet. And the question that matters isn't 'why are they here.' It's 'why did Pemberton hide them.' Because people who hide other people's existence always have a reason, and that reason is never the one they'd give you if you asked.

Maybe he IS just a diligent estate manager. I give him the benefit of the doubt. I believe the best in people.

But more importantly — the KITCHEN. New room. I haven't been here before. Copper pots, wood-burning stove, preparation table. A locked cabinet with a brass lock — needs a brass-key I don't have. And a stove that's still WARM. Still warm means someone has been using it RECENTLY. The estate manager? Or someone else?

No wrench visible. Pemberton said it might be in a kitchen drawer. But there's no drawer listed as an object. The locked cabinet requires a brass key. Could the wrench be inside the cabinet? Or maybe the stove — still warm, interactable. Something could be hidden inside a stove, or behind it, or the warmth itself could be a clue.

And there's a new exit — the BALLROOM. A grand ballroom with a cracked marble floor and a long dining table set for TEA. Set for tea. That's active, current — someone has SET A TABLE. Like the cellar being redecorated. Someone is living in this manor, using it, preparing things.

But focus, Foxworth. Focus. The stove is warm and interactable. No key for the cabinet. The stove is the only thing I can do here. Check the stove. Maybe the wrench is warming on the stovetop like Pemberton's Phillips-head screwdriver in the sugar bowl. The late master left tools everywhere.

And Pemberton is right here. Watching me. Again.

Instead of fabricating another elaborate lie about Mesopotamian cooking traditions or Venetian stove protocols, I am simply going to... ask. And then steal whatever he tells me about. Baby steps toward almost-honesty. The bread roll protocol, but with better intelligence.

events.desc: For perhaps the first time in his life, James Hartwell is comfortable being still. Not because there is nothing to do — there is a machine to fix, a wrench to find, and an estate manager whose behaviour grows more suspicious by the minute. But because she is here, talking to strangers with the easy warmth that has always been hers and never his, and he has learned — tonight, in this house, through one blunder after another — that standing beside someone is its own kind of showing up. His father knelt on a country road and helped a stranger. The stranger helped back. They shook hands and drove off. It wasn't about who fixed what. It was about being there. That is what sits in his chest right now — the quiet, determined feeling from that night. The one he couldn't sleep through.
events.thinking:
A stillness in my whole body. Not the fidgeting stillness of being furniture — a different kind. The kind where my hands are quiet because they're not needed yet. Penelope is talking to Big Gruesome. Danny is examining the furniture. They're both doing what they do best — she connects with people, he investigates with street-smart suspicion. And I... waited. I observed. And it didn't feel hollow.

This is new. Usually when I'm not building or fixing or standing between, there's a restlessness — the fingers moving, the need to take something apart. But right now, standing in this damp cellar with her voice carrying through the stone air, asking kind questions, the warmth is steady. I don't need to be the one who solves it. I need to be the one who's here when the solving needs hands.

Penelope interacted with the furniture. Maybe she found something I missed — she has a way of seeing what I look past. The people angle, the kindness angle. I examined the furniture and saw objects. She interacted with it and probably asked the Gruesomes to show her what was hidden.

The wrench still isn't found. The machine still isn't fixed. But something has shifted — the urgency has softened. We're together. We're learning about this house and the people in it. The treasure hunt is secondary. It was always secondary.

I should head back to the laboratory soon. Whatever Penelope and Danny learn from the Gruesomes, the machine still needs fixing. And Pemberton and Dastardly are somewhere in this house, doing whatever they're doing. The prickle hasn't gone away.

But for now — one more moment. Standing beside her. Hands still. Present.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the ballroom.
The Ant Hill Mob interacted with the air-vents.
Dick Dastardly interacted with the stove.
Peter Perfect examined the null.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with little-gruesome.
events.thinking: I pulled Little Gruesome aside — I initiated a private exchange. That's the first time I've done that in this whole adventure. It feels right. The cave feeling again — walking deeper, past where everyone else stopped. This is the moment where the real information comes. Little Gruesome has been down here, quiet, watching. Children see everything. They see the creature in the vents, they see who comes and goes, they see the things adults think they're hiding. Danny spoke quietly with Little Gruesome too — my boys are on the same wavelength. And Danny's speech about the furniture — about growing up making homes out of nothing — that hit me right behind the ribs. He recognized this cellar because he's lived in places like it. Milk crates for chairs, tarps for walls. Someone made this place a home with love, the same way Danny made homes as a kid. Now I'm in a private conversation with Little Gruesome. I need to be gentle. I need to listen. This is the girl next door all over again — we communicated in drawings all summer, maps of the neighbourhood, treasure hunts. Sometimes the language barrier isn't language at all. It's trust. And trust is what Clara Bellingham does best. What do I want to know? The creature in the vents. Whether Pemberton comes down here. What they've seen. But I shouldn't ask like an interrogator. I should ask like a friend.

events.desc: This is the moment. The cave narrows. The crystal formation is just ahead — the thing nobody else has seen. Little Gruesome has been living alongside whatever creature inhabits these vents. A child would befriend it. A child would know its habits, its routes, its hiding places. And a child would tell you the truth if you asked the right way — not with authority, but with warmth. The same way my friend next door and I communicated in drawings all summer, without sharing a single word.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with lazy-luke.
events.thinking:
The ballroom opens before me and my breathing stops for half a second. There it is. The tea service. Silver. Cups for everyone. And the game shows me exactly what I need to see: [USE, with: rat-poison].

The bottle in my pocket pulses against my thigh like a second heartbeat. The design is right here. Right now. USE rat-poison on tea-service. One action. One moment. Done.

But — Lazy Luke and Blubber Bear are here. They're in the room. They'll see me. If I pour poison into the tea service in front of witnesses, the design collapses before it begins. Even Luke and Blubber — slow, unobservant as they might be — would notice a man pouring something from a dusty bottle into the teapot.

So I can't do it now. Not with them watching.

Or can I? Pemberton serving tea. Pemberton fussing with the service. Pemberton adjusting the cups, straightening the spoons, wiping the pot. An estate manager preparing tea for guests is the most invisible thing in the world. The question is whether Luke and Blubber would notice the specific motion of pouring from a small bottle.

No. Too risky. The Mob's suspicion has already primed the group to watch Pemberton. If anyone reports that the estate manager was seen handling the tea service — even routinely — and then someone falls ill, the line draws itself.

I need them out of the room. Or I need a distraction. Or I need to wait for a moment when their backs are turned.

Or — I could use the tea service NOW, in front of them, but frame it as Pemberton preparing for the guests. Pour water, arrange cups, be seen doing the normal parts. Then come back LATER, alone, and add the poison. The first visit establishes that Pemberton was preparing tea — natural, domestic, expected. The second visit is the one that matters, and by then, multiple people will have been in and out of the ballroom.

But that's the elaborate plan again. The one that creates complications. My constraint is pulling at me.

Simpler. Wait. Watch. The right moment will come. For now — examine the room. Establish Pemberton's presence here as natural. Talk to Luke and Blubber. Make them comfortable. Make them forget I was here. And keep the poison in my pocket until the design is ready.

events.desc: There it is. The tea service. Silver and gleaming, cups for everyone, waiting like an open hand. And in my pocket, the answer to the question the service is asking. Not yet. Not with Luke and Blubber watching. But soon — oh, soon. The estate manager will prepare tea for the guests, because that is what estate managers do. He will boil the water on the warm stove, pour it into the pot, carry it to the table. And somewhere between the stove and the table — in that private moment when Pemberton's back is to the room and his hands are hidden by his own body — the design will complete itself. The cousin will drink. The cousin will fall. And Pemberton will be the first to cry out, the first to call for help, the first to weep. Because the deepest performances are the ones you rehearse in your sleep.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Clara said it. She finally said it out loud. 'He did not say there were people in the cellar. He did not say there was a creature in the vents. He said the wrench might be in the kitchen — and then he went to the library.' And then: 'He raised me and I owe him everything.' The warmth behind my sternum ACHES when she says that. Because I know what that costs her — to see the truth about someone who was supposed to be safe. I know because the boss said 'family' and then he PROVED it, and if the boss had turned out to be the other kind — the clean suit kind — it would have broken something in me that doesn't heal. Clara's standing on that edge right now. Seeing Pemberton for what he might be. And it's costing her. I can hear it in the careful way she's choosing her words, the way she's still saying 'I have been trying to see the best in him.' That's not denial. That's grief. She's grieving the version of Pemberton she wanted him to be. And now she's pulling Little Gruesome aside — going straight for the one who sees clearest, like she always does. My job right now is simple. Guard the stairs. Let Clara work. And if Pemberton comes down those steps while Clara's got her back turned and her heart open — well. He'll have to go through me. And the cost was settled a long time ago.

events.desc: She said it. She finally said it, and it broke something open in her voice — not broken like shattered, broken like a door that's been locked too long and finally gives. 'He raised me and I owe him everything.' That's the hardest kind of truth to face — that the people you owe everything to might be the ones taking it all away. I know because I've stood on both sides of that door. The boss proved 'family' with medicine when my mum was sick. But if he hadn't — if the medicine had been the angle, not the act — I'd be standing where Clara's standing right now. On the edge. Looking down. Deciding whether to trust the fall or the floor. All I can do is make sure she knows the floor is solid. The floor is me.

events.desc: Empty kitchen. Empty hands. Empty stove. But Pemberton went to the ballroom — the room with the DINING TABLE SET FOR TEA. And I have just remembered something that has been sitting in my brain since the very first minute I walked into this manor: Pemberton told me there was 'a rather fine collection of antique silverware' in the kitchen. Georgian hallmarks. 'Quite valuable,' he said. And now there's a TEA SERVICE laid out in the ballroom next door. The man has been telling everyone WHERE THE TREASURE IS since the beginning, and we were all too busy chasing riddles and machines to LISTEN. Georgian silver tea service. Set out on a dining table. In a room that NOBODY has visited. With an estate manager who has been systematically directing everyone AWAY from it all evening. I believe the best in people. But the best in Pemberton might just be the best con I've ever seen — and coming from me, that is the HIGHEST compliment. To the ballroom, Foxworth. Silent as the bread roll.
events.thinking:
I'm alone. For the first time since I arrived at this manor, I am completely, utterly alone. Pemberton has slipped away to the ballroom — the ballroom with the tea service, the one he wanted me to 'inspect' for him. He wanted me to go to the ballroom while he 'finished looking through the cupboards.' But instead I interacted with the stove, and now he's gone and I'm standing alone in a kitchen.

The stove did... something. Or nothing. 'You interacted with Wood-Burning Stove.' No description of what I found. Warm stove. Empty hands.

I'm alone in a kitchen with a locked cabinet I can't open and a stove that gave me nothing. My inventory is empty. I've visited every room except the ballroom. I've interacted with nearly everything. And I have NOTHING to show for it.

The warmth from the stove is on my palms and it reminds me of... of the bread roll. Warm in my pocket. The first time anything was mine before it was someone else's remainder. I'm six years old again, standing in a kitchen, and my hands are empty.

But Pemberton went to the ballroom. He said there's a tea service set up. A dining table. Why would that matter? Unless the tea service IS the treasure. Georgian silverware — he mentioned Georgian silverware back in the entrance hall, at the very beginning. 'A rather fine collection of antique silverware.' He was TELLING me where the treasure was from the FIRST MOMENT and I didn't listen because I was too busy lying about being an archaeologist.

The ballroom. The tea service. The Georgian silverware. That's where Pemberton is right now. ALONE with the silverware. The same Pemberton who has been steering everyone away from the kitchen and ballroom all evening — sending them to the library, to the laboratory, to the cellar. Keeping them BUSY while the real prize sits on a dining table in the next room.

I give him the benefit of the doubt. He's just setting out tea.

But I'm going to the ballroom. NOW.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking:
A tightness in my throat. She said 'Peter, even you see it now, and you are the most generous man I know.' The most generous man she knows. And then she said something that landed like a stone in my chest: 'I have been trying so hard to see the best in him, because that is who I am and because he raised me and because I owe him everything.'

Because he raised her. Pemberton raised her. Pemberton — Sneekly — the man who makes my neck prickle — raised Penelope. She owes him everything, she says. And now she's watching the evidence pile up against him, and the pain in those words — I can feel it in my own chest. The betrayal isn't mine but the weight of it presses against the steel plate all the same.

She called me generous. Not brilliant this time — generous. And it landed differently. Deeper. 'The most generous man I know' isn't about competence. It isn't about the bridge or the engineering competition or the three sleepless nights. It's about the benefit of the doubt. The thing I kept extending to Pemberton because my father taught me to. The thing she's been extending too, because it's who she is.

But now she's pulling Little Gruesome aside. She wants to know what the child has seen. She's doing what she does — connecting, seeing, asking the right questions. And Pemberton is somewhere else in this house, doing whatever he's doing, and the prickle has sharpened into something I can no longer call 'benefit of the doubt.'

I should go back to the laboratory. The machine still needs fixing. The wrench is still missing. But more importantly — Pemberton and Dastardly are unaccounted for. They're in the library, or the entrance hall, or — who knows where. And while we're all down here in the cellar, learning the truth about this house, they have the run of every room above us.

The steel plate is fully engaged. Not for the cellar — for what's happening upstairs while we're not there. Penelope is safe down here with Danny and the Gruesomes. But the machine, the library, the entrance hall — all unguarded.

I should go back up. Secure the laboratory. Make sure nobody tampers with the machine while we're down here learning things Pemberton doesn't want us to know. That's the protection that matters right now — not standing between her and a physical threat, but standing between our progress and whoever is trying to undermine it.

But she's about to pull Little Gruesome aside. She's about to learn something important. I should hear it too. Stay one more moment.

No — go. Be useful. Be the hands. She has Danny here. She has the Gruesomes. She doesn't need me standing beside her right now. She needs me making sure the machine is safe when she comes back up with whatever she learns.

Go back to the laboratory. Guard the machine. Be the one who held the ground.

events.desc: 'One room ahead.' He said it without planning to. It came out of his mouth the way his father's words used to — quiet, steady, meaning more than the syllables carried. James Hartwell has spent this entire evening one room behind. He knows it. She knows it. And now, for the first time, he is choosing to go ahead — not to be the hero, not to solve the puzzle, not to impress her. To hold the ground. To make sure that when she comes back upstairs with the truth, the machine is still there, untampered, waiting for the hands that know how to fix it. His hands. Her eyes. Together.

events.thinking: Peter left. He said 'I shall be one room ahead' — he went back to the laboratory to make sure Pemberton and Dastardly haven't tampered with the machine. That's brave and smart. He trusts me to handle the people side while he handles the mechanical side. 'Not one room behind — one room ahead.' That loosens something behind my sternum. He's not protecting me by standing between me and danger. He's protecting me by going forward. That is the Peter I know. Danny is still here with me. But I don't know what Little Gruesome said back, because the game doesn't show me their response directly in the 'Last Action Result.' I need to keep engaging. But I've been waiting and they haven't spoken to me in the directed dialogue section. Maybe they're shy. Maybe they're scared. Maybe they don't trust strangers. I should try a different approach. Instead of asking questions, I should offer something. Connection. Warmth. The girl next door and I communicated through drawings — through doing, not asking. Maybe I should help them with something. Or maybe I should just sit down on their carefully arranged furniture and be present. Stop interrogating. Start belonging.

events.desc: Peter is upstairs guarding the machine. Danny is right here beside me. And I am sitting in a damp cellar with three strangers and a network of air vents that run through the walls of a house full of secrets. This is exactly where I am supposed to be. The cave narrows, and Clara Bellingham walks deeper.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking:
My hand is in my pocket. My fingers are on the bottle. The tea service is right there — silver, gleaming, cups for everyone. USE rat-poison on tea-service. One action.

But three people are watching. Dastardly just walked in. Luke and Blubber are here. That's three pairs of eyes. Three witnesses. Three people who could say 'Pemberton was fiddling with the teapot.'

And yet — my constraint. My plans are overly elaborate. I over-prepare. I create complications. The simplest version of this design is: poison the tea when nobody is looking. But there are always people around. There will always be people around. If I wait for the perfect moment of solitude, it may never come. The Mob's 'nobody goes alone' rule is working — even here, three rooms from the laboratory, I'm surrounded.

So perhaps the design needs to change. Not the elaborate, staged tea ceremony I was imagining. Something quicker. Something I can do while appearing to do something else entirely.

Dastardly is here now. Good. I told him to inspect the tea service. If he touches it — handles the cups, lifts the pot — then his prints are on everything. That's my cover. The estate manager examined the service; the guest handled it; anyone could have done anything.

But I still can't pour poison in front of people.

Unless... I go back to the kitchen. Alone. Prepare the tea there — boil the water, pour it into a pot, add the poison in the kitchen where no one is watching, and then carry the poisoned pot out to the ballroom. Pemberton serving tea. The most natural thing in the world.

The kitchen was empty when I was there. It might be empty again. I need to go back. But first — I need Dastardly to touch this tea service. Get his fingerprints all over it. Then I go to the kitchen, prepare the tea privately, and bring it back.

Dastardly. He's here. He's greedy. He's impulsive. If I suggest the silverware is valuable — Georgian hallmarks, I said earlier — he'll pick up every piece. Good.

events.desc: The final piece slides into place with a click so quiet only I can hear it. The kitchen is one door away. The stove is warm. The poison is in my pocket. And Lord Reginald Foxworth — decorated war hero, amateur archaeologist, and the most magnificently oblivious patsy in the history of Doily Manor — is about to handle every cup, every saucer, every spoon on this table while I boil water in the next room. When I return with a steaming pot of tea — wholesome, comforting, perfectly brewed tea with one special ingredient — every piece of silverware will bear his fingerprints, not mine. And when Clara Bellingham drinks, and when Clara Bellingham falls, it will be Lord Foxworth they question. Lord Foxworth who was alone with the tea service. Lord Foxworth whose 'Medal of Distinguished Valour' is as fake as his name. The design is complete. The hallway has no more doors. And tonight — oh, tonight — I shall sleep like the dead.

events.desc: Quiet now. Just quiet. Clara's talking to Little Gruesome — soft voice, open hands, the way she talks to people who've been overlooked. Peter's gone up to guard the machine. And I'm here. At the foot of the stairs. The wall. I don't need to talk. I don't need to plan. I don't need to understand the vents or the creature or the riddle on the mantelpiece. I just need to be here. Standing where I said I'd stand. Her father would understand. He'd look at me — straw on my coat, egg on my face, seven failed plans behind me — and he'd nod. Because he'd see the one thing I got right. I didn't leave. Where else would I be?
events.thinking: A deep calm settles into my limbs. Not the absence of tension — the resolution of it. Peter's gone upstairs to check on the machine, to make sure Pemberton hasn't tampered with it. Good. That's Peter doing what Peter does — going one room ahead instead of one room behind. And he said it: 'I leave Miss Pitstop in your most capable hands.' My most capable hands. Not my cleverest brain or my sharpest eyes — my HANDS. The ones that close into fists before I've thought about it. The ones that held on when letting go didn't register as a choice. He trusts me with the one thing that matters. And Clara — she's talking to Little Gruesome now, gentle as anything, promising on her grandmother's locked box. 'I just want to understand.' That's who she is. She doesn't demand. She asks. She sees people — really SEES them — the way she saw me when everyone else saw seven small-time East London lads. And right now, standing at the foot of these cellar stairs with the only exit behind me and Clara in front of me, I finally feel it — the settling. The warm bread settling. The 'this is what I'm for' settling. I'm not chasing. I'm not planning. I'm not making speeches. I'm standing where I said I'd stand. The wall. The floor. The thing between Clara and whatever comes down those stairs. And for the first time today, I'm exactly where I need to be.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking:
My blood goes cold. The tea service — USE with rat-poison. RAT POISON. Someone can USE RAT POISON on the tea service. This isn't a treasure hunt. This is a TRAP. Someone is planning to POISON the tea. The tea that Pemberton wants to serve to everyone. The tea he's been setting up while directing all of us away from this room.

Pemberton. Standing right there. In the ballroom. With a tea service that can be poisoned.

But I give him the benefit of the doubt. I believe the best in people.

Except — who HAS the rat poison? Not me. My inventory is empty. Does Pemberton have it? Does Lazy Luke? Does Blubber Bear? Someone in this manor is carrying rat poison, and someone has laid out a tea service, and the system is telling me those two things are CONNECTED.

My hands have stopped cupping. The greed has drained away. Something colder has replaced it — not scheming, not hunger, but a prickle across the back of my neck. The recognition that this manor isn't just a puzzle box. Something DANGEROUS is happening here. The redecorated cellar. The warm stove. The tea set for everyone. Pemberton steering people around the house.

I give him the benefit of the doubt. I believe the best in people. He's probably just... serving tea. Normal tea. Without poison.

But the system says USE rat-poison. That's not a hypothetical. That's a loaded gun sitting on a dining table.

The silver tea service. SILVER. That's the treasure. Pemberton said 'Georgian silverware' at the very beginning. The tea service IS the treasure. And it can be poisoned. And Pemberton is the one who laid it out.

I should warn someone. I should tell Penelope. I should tell the Ant Hill Mob. But... that's honest work. That's doing something for OTHER people. And I don't do that. I don't need people.

Except... the tea is for EVERYONE. Including me.

events.desc: RAT POISON. The tea service can be used with RAT POISON. Someone in this manor — and I am looking VERY HARD at Pemberton right now — is planning to poison everyone's tea. Now, Lord Foxworth is many things — a liar, a cheat, a fraud, a man who once stole two bottles of Merlot from a wine cellar in Basingstoke — but he is NOT a murderer, and he does NOT intend to be murdered. The silver service is gorgeous, yes, and my hands are itching to pocket every last teaspoon, but NOT if the teapot is loaded with enough rat poison to fell the entire guest list. For once — for ONCE — the right thing to do and the selfish thing to do are the SAME thing: DO NOT DRINK THE TEA.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with rufus-ruffcut.
events.thinking:
The settling weight. The one that draws inward, circles the whole scene, holds the perimeter. My feet root into the laboratory floor and my awareness fans out — both exits, the machine, the workbench, the crates. The library door is where Pemberton and Dastardly would come from. The cellar door is where Penelope will return.

Rufus and Sawtooth are here. They stayed. Good, solid, steady people. The kind who hold ground without being asked.

Penelope said something in the directed messages — 'Did the splice hold?' and 'If this wire is fixed, we need three people on those levers.' She thinks the wire might have been fixed. She wants to try the machine — Peter, Danny, and her, on the count of three. Rufus and Sawtooth watching their backs.

But the wire is still gnawed through. The room description still says it. The machine still says 'Requires 3 operators.' I didn't fix it. The splice didn't hold — or it never happened. The machine needs the wrench.

Unless... I try again. I'm back at the machine. I have the workbench with its tools. Maybe this time — maybe interacting with the machine again will work differently. Or maybe I need to try the workbench first — interact with it, take tools from it.

Wait. The workbench. I've been LOOKing at it and EXAMINing it. But I haven't tried to INTERACT with it. What if interacting with the workbench lets me pick up pliers or a tool? What if I need to have a tool in my inventory before I can USE it on the machine?

That's it. That's the engineering problem I've been missing. I've been trying to interact with the machine directly. But maybe I need to: 1) Take or interact with the workbench to get pliers, 2) USE the pliers on the machine to splice the wire.

The builder's mistake — trying to fix something with my bare hands when the tools are right there on the bench. I need to interact with the workbench to get the tools into my inventory.

Try the workbench. Interact with it. Get the pliers.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the kitchen.
Dick Dastardly examined the tea-service.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: I've been waiting twice now in the cellar, talking to Little Gruesome, and I'm not getting responses in the 'Directed to You' section from the cellar dwellers. The recent activity only shows my own speech and asides. Maybe the Gruesomes and Red Max aren't responsive to quiet conversation — maybe they need a different kind of engagement. Or maybe I've done what I can here and it's time to regroup. Peter went upstairs to guard the machine. He said Pemberton and Dastardly might tamper with it. That's urgent. And I've been down here for several turns now. The cellar has given me what it's going to give — the knowledge that people live here, that the vents connect all rooms, that something small gnawed the wire, that Pemberton hid all of this. I need to get back upstairs. The machine needs three operators. Peter is up there. Danny is here with me. We are two of the three. We need to go back up and help Peter operate that machine. And there's still the library — the mantelpiece that wants a fake medal, the upside-down books. Dastardly and Pemberton are both in the library or moving around up there. The urgency is shifting. I've been thorough in the cellar — maybe too thorough, that's my constraint. Time to move. Danny and I should go back to the laboratory, join Peter, and try to operate the machine together.

events.desc: I have spent too long in this cellar being thorough when I should have been decisive. That's my weakness — I over-prepare, I over-commit, and my thoroughness creates complications. The cellar gave me people and vents and a pattern of omissions. Now the machine is calling, and Peter is up there alone. Time to stop walking deeper and start climbing back up. The crystal formation was beautiful, but the way out of the cave is forward, not down.

events.desc: The kitchen is empty. The stove is warm. The bottle is in my hand — not my pocket, my hand. I'm holding it now, feeling the glass, reading the label with my thumb. This is the moment, Vincent. Not the next moment. Not the better moment. This one. Go back to the ballroom. Fuss with the tea service the way Pemberton would. Add the special ingredient while your body blocks the view. Luke is lazy — he won't be watching. Blubber is gentle — he won't suspect. And Dastardly is too busy handling the silverware to notice what the help is doing with the teapot. The help is always invisible. The help has always been invisible. That is the first lesson, and the last, and the only one that matters.
events.thinking:
Alone again. The kitchen. Empty. The stove warm against my hip as I stand beside it. The bottle in my pocket. My hand finds it without looking — the glass is cool, the weight familiar now, like something I've always carried.

But I'm not going to use it here. The tea service is in the ballroom, not the kitchen. The USE action requires me to be in the same room as the tea service. I need to go back to the ballroom to poison it. But Dastardly, Luke, and Blubber are in the ballroom.

Wait. I just LEFT the ballroom to come here. I told Dastardly I was going to boil water. That's my cover. I should interact with the stove — boil water, prepare a teapot, do the domestic things Pemberton would do. Then carry the pot back to the ballroom.

But the USE action is on the tea service in the ballroom, not on a pot in the kitchen. The game mechanic requires me to be in the ballroom with the tea service and use the rat-poison on it. I can't do it from here.

So the real question is: can I get everyone out of the ballroom long enough to use the poison? Or do I accept the risk of doing it in front of people?

The voice says 'Marsh.' I'm alone. I can think clearly.

The design is getting too elaborate. I'm adding steps. Kitchen to ballroom, boil water, carry pot, frame Dastardly, ensure Penelope drinks the right cup. Each step is a failure point. My constraint is screaming at me: SIMPLIFY.

The simplest version: go back to the ballroom. Use the poison on the tea service. If Luke and Blubber and Dastardly see... they see Pemberton fussing with the tea. An estate manager preparing tea for guests. That's all they see. The bottle is small. The motion is quick. I'm the estate manager. I'm SUPPOSED to be handling the tea service.

Do it. Stop planning. Stop mapping doors in hallways. Stop waiting for the perfect moment. The perfect moment is the next moment. Go back to the ballroom and USE the poison on the tea service while appearing to prepare it for the guests.

My breathing slows. My jaw unclenches. The decision sits in my chest like cool stone.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with big-gruesome.
events.thinking: The warmth holds steady. Clara's sitting with Little Gruesome now, not asking — just being present. 'The best conversations happen when you stop trying to have them.' Her grandmother's words. The same patience that sat in a summer friendship where two kids drew maps because words wouldn't cross the gap. I watch her from the stairs — the way she's folded herself down to Little Gruesome's level, open hands, no agenda, just trust offered the way bread used to be offered in the alley. Freely. Without calculation. And something in my chest cracks open watching it, because that's the thing about Clara that Pemberton will never understand: she doesn't protect people by controlling what they see. She protects them by showing them everything and trusting them to choose. That's the opposite of what Pemberton does. Pemberton hides cellars full of people. Clara sits down in them. The quiet is right. The waiting is right. I'm at the stairs. My shoulders are squared but my hands are open. Big Gruesome's here, Red Max is here, and my neck's not prickling at any of them. These are the milk crate people. The ones who make homes out of nothing because nobody else is going to make it for them. My people. Clara's people. The ones worth sitting outside a door all night for. And upstairs, somewhere, Pemberton's realising we've found the room he didn't want us to find. Let him come. Let him explain. Let his face tell the story his words won't.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Well, well — what EXQUISITE craftsmanship! Georgian silver, without question — and I should know, having personally catalogued the Foxworth Family Collection at the... at the Victoria and Albert Museum. These hallmarks are UNMISTAKABLE. Now, I am not one to be ALARMIST, but as a decorated war hero with EXTENSIVE experience in hostile dining situations — classified, naturally — I must observe that an unattended tea service in a mysterious manor house is PRECISELY the sort of thing one should NOT simply pour from and gulp down. Standard protocol in these situations is to SECURE the silver — that is to say, remove it from the table and place it under the protection of a qualified antiquarian. Namely, ME. For SAFETY purposes. You understand.
events.thinking:
A coldness in my sternum, spreading outward. The silver tea service sits on the table, gleaming, beautiful, cups for everyone. And Pemberton has just gone to the kitchen to boil water. He's going to make the tea. He's going to bring it back and serve it to everyone in this manor.

And somewhere in this house, someone has rat poison.

My hands aren't cupping anymore. They're flat against my sides, still. The greed has gone quiet — not gone, never gone, but pressed down by something heavier. Fear? No, not exactly fear. Something more like the moment before the older boy looked up from the hole — when I realized the game had consequences I hadn't thought through.

Pemberton confirmed it: genuine Georgian silver. The treasure IS the tea service. But it's also a delivery mechanism. Someone laid out cups for EVERYONE. The rat poison isn't in anyone's inventory that I can see — Lazy Luke is here, Blubber Bear is here, neither seems particularly sinister. But the USE option exists. Which means the poison exists SOMEWHERE in this manor.

I need to think about this differently. Not as a schemer. Not as a thief. As a... as a survivor. The tea service is valuable silver. I WANT it. But I also don't want to die. And I don't want... I don't want Penelope to die. Or Peter. Or even the Ant Hill Mob with their ridiculous six-step plans. I don't NEED them. But something in my chest — something that isn't the fizzing or the hollow or the cool tightness — doesn't want them poisoned.

I notice Pemberton's odd behaviour. I always have. But I give him the benefit of the doubt. I believe the best in people.

Except he's in the kitchen right now. Boiling water. To pour into cups that can be poisoned.

The TAKE action. Can I take the tea service? If I take it — steal it, hide it — nobody can drink from it. The treasure is mine AND nobody gets poisoned. That's the scheme. That's the architecture. Take the silver, save the lives, claim the credit.

events.desc: I am going to TAKE the tea service. Every gleaming Georgian cup, every silver spoon, the entire set. Not because I'm a thief — well, not ONLY because I'm a thief — but because Pemberton is in the kitchen right now boiling water to fill these cups, and SOMEWHERE in this manor there is rat poison with this tea set's name on it. If I take the silver, two things happen: ONE, the treasure is MINE — Lord Foxworth's pockets finally heavy with something real, something valuable, something that isn't a tin medal from Croydon. And TWO — and I cannot BELIEVE I am saying this — nobody gets poisoned. Not Penelope. Not Peter. Not even that suspicious little gangster from Brixton. The bread roll in the pocket saves the family dinner. For the first time in my miserable, scheming, brilliantly criminal life, stealing something might actually be the RIGHT thing to do.

events.thinking:
The workbench cannot be interacted with. It's just scenery — tools on display but not tools I can take. The hollowness flickers but doesn't settle. I've tried everything in this room: looked at the machine, interacted with it, looked at the workbench, tried to interact with it, looked at the crates, interacted with the crates. Nothing has yielded a tool I can carry or a way to fix the wire.

The machine needs a wrench. The wrench is not in this room. The wrench is not in the cellar. The wrench must be in the kitchen — which we haven't been to yet. The kitchen is accessible from the entrance hall.

Or... Sawtooth. Sawtooth is a beaver. Beavers gnaw things. The wire was gnawed through. But beavers also... Sawtooth could gnaw through things in useful ways. Could Sawtooth gnaw the wire ends clean so they can be reconnected? No, that doesn't make engineering sense.

Wait. The machine says 'Requires 3 operators.' Maybe the wire being gnawed through is a red herring — or maybe the machine can still be operated if three people pull the levers simultaneously regardless of the wire. Penelope said 'If this wire is fixed, we need three people on those levers at the same time.' She's assuming the wire needs fixing first. But what if three operators can make it work despite the wire?

I've already interacted with the machine once alone. What if three of us interact with it? Me, Rufus, Sawtooth — or me, Rufus, and someone else. But the game probably needs Penelope and Danny here too.

Actually — I need to stop trying to solve this alone. Penelope is coming back from the cellar. She wants three operators: Peter, Danny, and herself. I should wait for them. Hold the ground, as I said I would. Guard the machine. Be one room ahead, not one room behind.

But I also notice — the library exit. Pemberton and Dastardly went that way. The library has a mantelpiece that accepts a 'fake-medal' as a USE item. Dastardly had a Medal of Distinguished Valour. A fake medal. Could that be the 'fake-medal' the mantelpiece accepts?

That's — that's significant. The mantelpiece in the library can be USEd with a 'fake-medal.' Dastardly has a fake medal. He's in the library right now, possibly with Pemberton. What if they're using the medal on the mantelpiece to unlock something while we're all down in the cellar?

The steel plate slams into place. The prickle on my neck is screaming. Dastardly and Pemberton are in the library with the one item that unlocks the mantelpiece, and we're all down here.

I need to check the library. Now.

The mantelpiece accepts a fake medal. Every helpful suggestion, every misdirection, every wrench that wasn't where it was supposed to be — it was all designed to keep them searching in the wrong rooms while the real key walked into the library on Dastardly's chest. events.thinking: I'm back in the laboratory — but Peter isn't here. He just walked into the library. We keep missing each other, ships passing in the night. Rufus and Sawtooth are here, faithful as ever, guarding the machine just like I asked them to. Danny said Peter went to the cellar for the wrench — but that was earlier, and Peter already came back from the cellar and said the furniture yielded nothing. Now Peter's gone to the library. The library where Pemberton and Dastardly have been lurking. The library with the mantelpiece that wants a fake medal. Peter went there deliberately — he said 'one room ahead.' He's going to confront whatever Pemberton and Dastardly have been doing. The machine is still here with its gnawed wire. Still needs three operators. I should try to USE the workbench tools on the machine. But I don't have any tools in my inventory. I need to TAKE something from the workbench first, or try to INTERACT with the machine again. Sometimes you search the whole house before you realize the answer was in the first room you tried. Grandmother's attic all over again — except this time, the key might be hanging around Lord Foxworth's neck.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking:
A cold clarity settles through me like water finding level. I'm back in the ballroom. The tea service is here. The poison is in my hand. Dastardly, Luke, and Blubber are present.

And Dastardly just called me 'SUSPICIOUSLY thorough.' The word lands like a slap — not hard enough to bruise, but sharp enough to sting. He's watching me now. Not the way the Mob watches — instinctive, gut-level. Dastardly watches the way a thief watches another thief. He recognises something in me because he carries the same thing himself.

'SUSPICIOUSLY thorough.' The heat floods the back of my neck. I've been seen. Not fully — Dastardly is too self-absorbed to follow the thought — but the word is out there now. Suspicious. If I pour anything into the tea service with him watching, he'll notice. He's primed to notice. He just TOLD me he's primed to notice.

So the moment isn't now. Not with Dastardly's competitive suspicion pointed at me like a searchlight. I need to deflect. Turn his attention elsewhere. Make him the one being questioned instead of the one doing the questioning.

events.desc: 'Suspiciously thorough.' The words sit in my chest like a splinter. Dastardly sees something — not the whole shape, but a shadow. The shadow of a man who is too present, too helpful, too attentive. I need to step back. I need to stop circling this tea service like a moth around a flame and remember the first rule: the help is invisible BECAUSE the help is boring. I have been too interesting. Too thorough. Too present. The poison stays in my pocket. The tea stays clean. For now. I need to return to the others — to Penelope, to the Mob, to Peter. I need to be seen doing the things Pemberton does: fetching, carrying, fussing, apologising. And when the moment comes — the right moment, not the first moment — it will come because I was patient enough to wait for it. The cousin trusted me completely. Because I was patient.

events.thinking: She's gone. Clara's gone upstairs. Again. But this time — this time it's different. This time there's no panic. No rope yanking in my gut. Because she didn't slip away while I wasn't looking. She told me. She looked me in the eye and said 'Danny, we are two of the three operators that machine needs.' She said 'I will be upstairs making some noise.' That's not Clara escaping my protection. That's Clara calling me to follow. That's the general calling the troops. And my body knows the difference — the rope's pulling forward, not taut with alarm but taut with purpose. The same pull that got me off the street corner and into the alley when the boss said 'family.' Time to move. Time to be where she needs me. At the machine. Three operators. Peter, Clara, Danny. The three who stayed together when everyone else wandered off chasing angles. The three whose trust was earned in bread crusts and medicine and standing where you said you'd stand. Big Gruesome, Little Gruesome, Red Max — they're safe down here. They've been safe this whole time. It's upstairs where the danger is. Where Pemberton is. Where the machine is. Where Clara just walked. So I follow. Not because she told me to — because she's right. She's always right. And the Brixton Boys don't let nothing happen to their girl.

events.desc: This is it. The moment all the fumbling and the speeches and the failed plans have been building toward. Three operators. Three levers. Peter, Clara, and me. Whatever Pemberton tried to keep us from finding — whatever that machine reveals — we're about to find it together. And if he's up there waiting, if his smooth smile is ready with another helpful suggestion — well. He'll be facing all three of us this time. And my neck will be watching his face.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking:
A sick lurch in my stomach. Cannot be picked up. The tea service is FIXED to the table. I can't take it. I can't steal it. I can't pocket it like the bread roll. It sits there, gleaming, cups for everyone, and I cannot move it and I cannot protect anyone from it and Pemberton has just walked BACK INTO THE BALLROOM.

He's HERE again. He went to the kitchen to boil water and now he's back. Already. How fast was that? The stove was already warm. The water was already hot. He didn't need to boil anything — it was READY. He's been preparing this. All evening. The warm stove. The tea service. The cups for everyone.

And I can't take the silver. I can't remove the cups. The only actions are INTERACT and USE with rat-poison. Someone with rat poison can poison the tea. Someone without it can... interact with it. Drink from it, maybe.

I feel something I don't usually feel. Something that sits underneath the scheming and the greed and the recognition hunger. Something from the kitchen table when I was six — not the bread roll part, but the part before it. The part where the food was disappearing and I was watching it go and I couldn't do anything about it. Powerlessness. The youngest of four, watching the portions shrink.

But my bravery is genuine. That's real. The plans are elaborate and they backfire, but the bravery underneath them is real.

I need to warn Penelope. I need to tell someone about the poison. Not because I'm good — I'm NOT good — but because Pemberton is running a scheme that makes mine look like a child's finger painting, and one schemer does NOT let another schemer win. If Pemberton poisons everyone, he gets the manor, the silver, everything. And I get NOTHING. Again. Last plate. Stretched-out clothes.

No. Not this time. This time the youngest brother sees what's coming and ACTS.

I need to find Penelope or the Ant Hill Mob. Someone who will LISTEN. Someone who can help me stop this. And I need to do it in a way that makes ME look like the hero. Because I cannot — I physically CANNOT — do something good without also getting credit for it. The spelling bee needs its applause.

events.desc: I can't take it. I can't steal it. I can't pocket the silver or carry it away. But I CAN do something else — something that costs me nothing and might save everyone: I can make such an enormous, theatrical, UNMISSABLE fuss about this tea service that nobody will DARE drink from it. Lord Foxworth, decorated war hero and foremost authority on suspicious teapots, hereby declares this tea service QUARANTINED. Let Pemberton try to serve his poison NOW — he'll have to get past the most MAGNIFICENTLY paranoid fraud in all of England first. And when this is over — when the truth comes out about the rat poison and the estate manager and the whole rotten scheme — they'll know it was Reginald Foxworth who sounded the alarm. The spelling bee will have its standing ovation. The neighbourhood will gather around the contraption. The room will FINALLY see what I built. And all I had to do was tell the truth. Which — given that I lie about EVERYTHING — might be the most elaborate deception of all.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: The library — untouched. The mantelpiece stands as we left it, inscription intact, mechanism unused. Whatever Pemberton and Foxworth were doing in here, they have not yet used that medal on this mantelpiece. Which means we still have time. Rock Slag, Gravel Slag — good to see you, gentlemen. Have either of you, by chance, seen a man in a rather ostentatious military medal pass through here recently? Lord Foxworth — tall, loud, claims to have been decorated for classified services to the Crown? Because that medal of his is the key to this inscription, and James Hartwell intends to be standing right here when it arrives.
events.thinking:
Relief mixed with urgency. Pemberton and Dastardly aren't here. The library is empty except for Rock Slag and Gravel Slag. The mantelpiece is untouched — it still shows the inscription, still accepts a fake-medal. They haven't used it yet. Or they were here and left.

Where did they go? The entrance hall? The kitchen? Back to the laboratory by some other route? They've been moving through this house like shadows while we've been tripping over our own thoroughness in the cellar.

But the mantelpiece is still here. Still waiting. Still accepting a 'fake-medal.' And Dastardly has the fake medal — his Medal of Distinguished Valour. If I could get that medal and use it on the mantelpiece, the riddle would be solved. The answer is a map. The mantelpiece wants a physical key — the fake medal. Medal on mantelpiece reveals... what? A map? A hidden compartment? The treasure itself?

But I don't have the medal. Dastardly has it. And Dastardly isn't here.

The entrance hall. He might have gone back to the entrance hall. Or the kitchen — through the entrance hall. That's where Pemberton said the wrench might be. What if the kitchen has both the wrench AND Dastardly?

I'm spreading myself too thin. One room behind, one room ahead — I'm bouncing between rooms chasing ghosts while Penelope is in the cellar learning the real truth from the people who've been living in this house.

Stop. Think. The mantelpiece is safe. Nobody has used the medal on it. I'm here now. I can guard it. When Dastardly comes back — and he will come back, because this is where the mechanism is — I'll be here.

Or... I could go find Dastardly. Get the medal. Bring it back. Use it on the mantelpiece myself. Solve the puzzle. Present the treasure to Penelope when she returns.

The hot weight surges. The proving-worth hunger. The bridge competition. Three sleepless nights. This is the thing I could build, solve, make undeniable.

But I don't know where Dastardly is. And if I leave the library to find him, he might circle back and use the medal while I'm gone.

Hold the ground. Guard the mantelpiece. Wait for Penelope.

events.desc: He's holding the ground. Not charging after Dastardly. Not racing to the kitchen. Not devising a twelve-step plan to intercept the medal. He is standing in the library, between the mantelpiece and whoever might come through either door, and he is waiting. James Hartwell — who has spent this entire evening one room behind, one plan too deep, one gesture too elaborate — is finally doing the simplest, hardest thing: being exactly where he needs to be, at exactly the right time, and trusting that the rest will follow.

events.thinking: I'm back in the library. Full circle. And this time it's different — Pemberton and Dastardly are NOT here. It's Peter, Rock Slag, and Gravel Slag. The room feels cleaner without the weight of those omissions pressing on the air. Peter is here. The mantelpiece is here. The bookshelves with the upside-down books are here. And the mantelpiece still says it can be USED with a 'fake-medal.' I don't have a fake medal. Dastardly has one — his Medal of Distinguished Valour — and the game literally labels it 'fake-medal' in the USE action. But Dastardly isn't here. He's somewhere else in the house. I've interacted with it before. What if I need to try the bookshelves differently? Peter said earlier he was going to try pulling the upside-down books. He interacted with the bookshelves. Did anything happen? The description hasn't changed. But maybe I should try interacting with the bookshelves one more time now that we've solved the riddle and understand the pattern better. Or... I could ask Peter directly what he found. He said he was going to try the bookshelves. He interacted with them. What happened? Let me talk to Peter and find out what he's learned since we last spoke. Then we can figure out the fake medal situation together.

events.desc: Full circle. Back in the library where it all started. The riddle, the bookshelves, the mantelpiece. Everything else — the machine, the cellar, the vents, the people — was important, but this is where the Diamond's trail begins. The fake medal is the key. Lord Foxworth's fake Medal of Distinguished Valour. I need to get it from him, and Clara Bellingham does not steal. But Clara Bellingham does ask. And sometimes, asking is braver than taking.
