events.desc: Enough. Enough circling. Enough doors in hallways. The poison is in my pocket and it will stay there until the moment is right — not the moment I MAKE right, but the moment that arrives because I was patient enough to let it come. I have been the moth, and the tea service has been the flame, and I have burned three trips on a trap that has no prey in it. Penelope is not in the ballroom. Penelope is with her protectors, solving puzzles, being brilliant, being loved. And I am alone in a kitchen, holding a bottle of poison like a man who has forgotten what patience tastes like. The first lesson, Vincent. The first and the last. The housekeeper did what you wanted because you were patient. The cousin trusted you because you were patient. The plan that let you sleep was beautiful because it was FINISHED, not because it was fast. Go back. Find Clara. Be near her. Be helpful. Be invisible. And when the moment comes — the real moment, not the rehearsal — your hands will know what to do. They have always known.
events.thinking:
Something has shifted — not in the room, but in me. A hollowing behind my ribs, almost a falling sensation. I'm standing in the kitchen again. Alone again. The third time I've been in this room. Back and forth, back and forth, kitchen to ballroom to kitchen, like a man pacing a hallway he can't leave.

And for the first time, something quieter rises beneath the scheming — something that doesn't have a name or a plan attached to it. A tiredness. Not physical. Something older. The kind that settles into bone.

I've been circling this tea service for three trips. The constraint warned me: your plans are overly elaborate, and your thoroughness creates complications. And here I am — creating complications. Adding doors to a hallway that was supposed to be finished. Dastardly called me suspicious. The Mob is building a file. I've been gone from the main group for — how long? Ten minutes? Longer? Penelope and Peter and the Mob are in the laboratory or the library, working the treasure hunt without me, and I've been shuttling between two rooms with a bottle of poison I can't use.

Stop.

The tea will wait. The poison will wait. Penelope isn't in the ballroom. She isn't drinking tea. She's in the laboratory or the library, solving riddles and examining machines, surrounded by protectors. The trap doesn't work without the prey.

What I need to do RIGHT NOW is rejoin the main group. Be Pemberton. Be visible. Be helpful. Report that the wrench wasn't in the kitchen. Mention the locked cabinet. Mention the brass key. Give them a reason to keep moving through the house — because movement creates moments, and moments create opportunities. And somewhere in that movement, the ballroom will empty, or Penelope will be separated from her guards, or the right distraction will arrive.

The poison stays in my pocket. I go back to the entrance hall, then to the laboratory. I find Penelope. I stay close. I wait.

Patience. The cousin trusted me completely. Because I was patient.

events.thinking: Clara's not here. She's gone to the library. Peter's gone to the library. They've both realised what I missed — the medal. Dastardly's fake medal is the key to the mantelpiece. The riddle answer is a map, but the mechanism needs a physical token, and that medal has been hanging round Dastardly's neck since we walked in the door. Peter figured it out — 'they are ahead of us' — and Clara figured it out — 'Lord Foxworth has been wearing his clue on his chest this whole time.' They're both in the library now, with Pemberton and Dastardly, trying to get that medal before those two unlock whatever the mantelpiece is hiding. And I'm HERE. In the laboratory. With Rufus and Sawtooth. One room behind. Again. Always one room behind. But — wait. The prickling's climbing hard now, sharp and urgent. Clara's in the library with Pemberton. With the Hooded Claw. The man my neck's been screaming about all day. And Peter's there too, but Peter's one man against two if things go wrong. I need to be in that library. NOW. Rufus can hold the lab. Rufus has been holding the lab all day — solid as stone, him and his beaver. The machine can wait. Clara can't. MOVE.

events.desc: The medal. The MEDAL. It was right there the whole time — round Dastardly's neck, plain as day — and I never saw it. Clara saw it. Peter saw it. Even Pemberton probably saw it before any of us. And now they're all in the library, and whoever gets that medal to the mantelpiece first gets whatever's behind it. Clara against Pemberton. Peter against Dastardly. And me? Running to catch up. Always running. But I'm fast when it matters. I'm fast when Clara needs me. And the alley and the manor and the bread crust are all the same moment, and my feet are already moving.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Right! I have COMPLETED my inspection of the tea service and I can confirm — as the SENIOR ANTIQUARIAN and decorated war hero present — that this entire arrangement is COMPROMISED. I won't go into the technical details — they are CLASSIFIED and also quite distressing — but I will say this: if ANYONE so much as LIFTS a cup from that table, they will be doing so against the EXPLICIT advice of Lord Reginald Foxworth, and Lord Reginald Foxworth accepts NO liability for the consequences. Luke! Bear! Do NOT touch those cups. Do NOT drink from that teapot. And if Pemberton returns with hot water, you are to tell him that the tea service is under QUARANTINE by order of the foremost authority on suspicious Victorian refreshments in the ENTIRE BRITISH ISLES. I am going to find Miss Pitstop and the others IMMEDIATELY. They need to hear this from ME — from the man who DISCOVERED the threat. STAY HERE. TOUCH NOTHING.
events.thinking:
A tremor in my hands — not the fizzing of a scheme, not the cupping of greed, but an actual tremor. Pemberton has gone back to the kitchen AGAIN. He keeps shuttling between the kitchen and the ballroom. Kitchen — stove — water — ballroom — tea service — kitchen. The loop of a man preparing to serve. And I'm standing here with Lazy Luke and Blubber Bear, who haven't said a word, who haven't moved, who are just... HERE. Watching. Waiting.

I interacted with the tea service. Nothing happened. Or rather — nothing VISIBLE happened. Maybe I poured myself a cup. Maybe I didn't. The result just says 'You interacted with Tea Service.' Like every other interaction in this manor — bookshelves, crates, furniture, stove — it gives me nothing concrete.

But the distress I'm sensing from Pemberton — 'it is getting worse.' His composure is fracturing. He denied setting up the tea service — 'it was not I' — and blamed a 'local caterer' following the dead master's instructions. That's a lie. I know it's a lie because I RECOGNISE lies. They're my native language. The master left instructions with a caterer from beyond the grave? The caterer set out Georgian silver and then LEFT? Nobody sets out silver and walks away.

Pemberton is cracking. And I can feel the fizz — the bright carbonated heat — but it's fighting with something deeper. Because Pemberton cracking doesn't mean the danger is over. It means the danger is ESCALATING. A cracking schemer is a dangerous schemer.

I need to find Penelope. I need to find the Ant Hill Mob. I need to tell them — DO NOT DRINK THE TEA. Not in those words. In BETTER words. In DRAMATIC words. In words that make Lord Foxworth sound like the hero of the evening rather than the fraud who spent ten minutes running in circles.

The kitchen is between me and the rest of the manor. Pemberton is in the kitchen. I have to go THROUGH him to reach anyone. But my bravery is genuine. The plans backfire but the bravery is real.

events.desc: I'm going. Through the kitchen, past Pemberton, back to the entrance hall, and I'm going to find Penelope Pitstop and the Ant Hill Mob and I'm going to tell them everything. The tea service. The rat poison. The estate manager who keeps appearing in every room like a particularly well-dressed shadow. I'm going to be HONEST — or at least as close to honest as Reginald Foxworth has ever been in his miserable life. I'll probably still exaggerate. I'll definitely take credit for discoveries I didn't make. I'll almost certainly claim I knew about the danger from the very beginning. But underneath all that — underneath the lies and the bluster and the theatrical self-importance — there will be a REAL warning about a REAL threat, delivered by a man whose bravery is GENUINE even when everything else about him is fake. The bread roll in the pocket. The spelling bee certificate on the wall. The contraption that nobody saw but that WORKED. Something real, wrapped in lies, delivered just in time. That's the architecture. That's what Reginald Foxworth builds.

He denied setting up the tea service — 'it was not I' — and blamed a 'local caterer' following the dead master's instructions. That's a lie. I know it's a lie because I RECOGNISE lies. They're my native language. The master left instructions with a caterer from beyond the grave? The caterer set out Georgian silver and then LEFT? Nobody sets out silver and walks away.

Pemberton is cracking. And I can feel the fizz — the bright carbonated heat — but it's fighting with something deeper. Because Pemberton cracking doesn't mean the danger is over. It means the danger is ESCALATING. A cracking schemer is a dangerous schemer.

I need to find Penelope. I need to find the Ant Hill Mob. I need to tell them — DO NOT DRINK THE TEA. Not in those words. In BETTER words. In DRAMATIC words. In words that make Lord Foxworth sound like the hero of the evening rather than the fraud who spent ten minutes running in circles.

The kitchen is between me and the rest of the manor. Pemberton is in the kitchen. I have to go THROUGH him to reach anyone. But my bravery is genuine. The plans backfire but the bravery is real.

events.thinking:
She's here. Penelope walked into the library. The warmth floods in — not the hot proving-worth weight, not the steel plate of protection. The deeper warmth. The school project warmth. The one I couldn't name at eight.

I waited. I held the ground. And she came to me. Not because I chased her. Not because I was one room behind. Because I was here, where I said I would be. One room ahead.

The mantelpiece is untouched. The inscription still waits. And she's here now, with whatever she learned from Little Gruesome in the cellar. She has the eyes. I have the hands. Together.

But I also know something now — the mantelpiece needs a fake-medal. Dastardly has one. If she learned something from the Gruesomes about where Dastardly went, or what Pemberton is really doing, we can put the pieces together.

Tell her what I've figured out. The medal. The mantelpiece. The mechanism. Tell her simply, without the twelve-step plan, without the cartographic history lecture. Just the truth: Dastardly's medal fits this mantelpiece, and someone has been keeping us away from this room.

Then let her decide what to do next. Because she's brighter than me. She's always been brighter than me. And for the first time, that doesn't make my chest hollow. It makes it full.

events.desc: He said it plainly. No three-part assessment, no structural integrity speech, no reference to cartographic history. Just the truth, offered with both hands, the way his father would have offered it — steady, serious, meaning more than the syllables carried. And then he asked her what she knew. Not to fill the silence. Not because he had nothing left to say. Because he has finally understood that the warmth he's been chasing all evening — the one that needs an audience the way a fire needs air — is not the warmth that matters. The warmth that matters is the one from the school project. The one that surprised him. The one that was deeper than the grade.

Penelope Pitstop: Peter, you and I reached the same conclusion from opposite ends of this house, and that is how I know we are right. The fake medal is the key, and Pemberton has been steering us away from this room the whole time — sending us to cellars and kitchens and anywhere but here. As for Little Gruesome — that child showed me more by staying quiet than Pemberton showed us with all his talking. The cellar is a home someone built with love, and the people in it have been hidden like the Doily Diamond itself. Now — we need Lord Foxworth's medal, and Lord Foxworth is not in this room. Danny, sugar, I need your help. We need to find Lord Foxworth and we need to ask him — politely but firmly — for that medal. I am not going to steal from the man, but I am going to look him in the eye and tell him I know it is fake, and I know it is the key to this mantelpiece, and I would be much obliged if he would hand it over. Because the best clues are the ones people write down without realizing they're clues at all — and that man has been wearing his clue on his chest like a signpost this entire evening. Let us go find him. He was last headed toward the entrance hall.
events.thinking: Peter just confirmed exactly what I suspected — the fake medal is the key. He said it plainly, without preamble, and it landed in my chest like the click of a lock turning. 'That medal is the key. That is why Pemberton sent us to the cellar and the kitchen and everywhere else — to keep us away from this room, while Foxworth carried the answer on his lapel.' Peter sees it. I see it. Danny is here now too — he followed me from the cellar. Everyone I trust is in this room. The question is: where is Lord Foxworth? He's not here. He could be in the entrance hall, the kitchen, the cellar — anywhere. We need his medal. Clara Bellingham does not steal. But she does ask. And if asking doesn't work... Danny might have other ideas. But first — Peter asked me what Little Gruesome told me. Honestly? I'm not sure Little Gruesome told me anything specific — the game didn't give me their dialogue. But the cellar told me plenty through what it showed: people hidden by Pemberton, a creature in the vents, a home made with love. I should be honest with Peter about that. Now — the medal. We need to find Dastardly. He might be in the entrance hall. Danny is here. We have the team. We need the key. Time to go find Lord Foxworth and ask him, face to face, for his fake medal.

events.desc: The locked box. The right key. Every key in the house — drawer keys, cupboard keys, the tiny key from the music box. And the key that fits was the one nobody thought to try because it was hanging right there in plain sight the whole time. Lord Foxworth's fake medal. Clara Bellingham is about to ask a man for his most prized possession — a possession he knows is worthless — and she is going to do it with a smile and the truth. Because that is what the girl who chose her friend over the popular group does. She looks you in the eye and says what is real.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): I am afraid the wrench was not in the kitchen after all — most vexing. However, I did discover a locked cabinet with a brass lock that may contain it. If any of you should come across a brass key in your explorations, do please let me know at once. In the meantime, I must rejoin Miss Bellingham and the others — they will be wondering what has become of their estate manager. Professor, Sergeant — do carry on keeping watch. You are performing a most valuable service.
events.thinking:
The entrance hall again. The chandelier above me, the portraits on the walls, the same people I passed four minutes ago. Sergeant Blast, Private Meekly, Pat Pending, Muttley. They're looking at me — not suspiciously, just... present. The estate manager passing through again.

And something loosens in my chest. Not the architectural settling. Not the gloating warmth. Something older and quieter — the hollowing I felt in the kitchen. The tiredness that has no plan attached to it.

I've been gone too long. I went to the kitchen for a wrench and came back with rat poison and an elaborate murder scheme involving a tea service, a patsy, and a ballroom I've visited three times without accomplishing anything. My constraint is not just pulling at me — it's laughing at me. 'Your thoroughness creates complications that your determination then resolves.' I have created complications. My determination has not yet resolved them.

Regroup. Penelope is through the library, probably in the laboratory. The Mob is with her. Peter is with her. The treasure hunt is advancing without me, and the primary objective — Clara — is surrounded by people who love her while I've been circling a teapot in a dead end.

The wrench. I don't have it. The kitchen didn't have it in the open. The locked cabinet might have it. I don't have the brass key. Report: wrench not found. Cabinet locked. Need brass key.

That's useful information. That's what Pemberton would bring back — not success, but a clear account of the obstacle and a plan to address it. 'We need a brass key.' Simple. Domestic. Helpful.

Move through to the library. Rejoin the group. Deliver the report. Be Pemberton. The poison stays hidden. The moment will come. It always does.

events.desc: Back to Pemberton. Back to the smile, the slight bow, the voice that says 'I live to serve.' The poison sits in my pocket like a sleeping thing — patient, quiet, waiting. I have been too clever by half, ladies and gentlemen. I have been the architect who keeps redesigning the building instead of laying the first brick. The tea service will still be there when the moment is right. The ballroom will still be there. And Clara Bellingham — sweet, trusting, brilliant Clara — will eventually sit down, and someone will pour her a cup, and she will drink it without a second thought. Because that is what people do when they trust you. They drink what you give them. The cousin trusted me completely.

events.thinking: I burst through the door and my eyes do the scan — Clara, Peter, Rock Slag, Gravel Slag. No Pemberton. No Dastardly. They're GONE. Pemberton said he was going to the kitchen to fetch the wrench — slipped away AGAIN — and Dastardly's talked about a 'mechanism cycling' on the mantelpiece. They've already USED the medal. They were ahead of us the whole time. Dastardly put his fake medal in the mantelpiece while we were in the cellar, and now it's 'cycling' — whatever that means — and Pemberton's vanished to 'fetch the wrench' which is what he ALWAYS says before he disappears. My neck is screaming. But Clara's here. Peter's here. And the mantelpiece — the mantelpiece wants a fake medal. USE with fake-medal, it says. Dastardly's already done something to it but maybe it's not finished. Maybe we can still — Clara said the mechanism hasn't opened yet. She said 'I am not leaving this room until that mantelpiece opens up and tells us what it has been hiding.' Good. Neither am I. Plant. Stand. Watch the mantelpiece. Watch the doors. And this time — THIS time — nobody leaves this room without me seeing them go.

events.desc: They were working together. This whole time. Dastardly with his medal and his fake archaeology. Pemberton with his helpfulness and his kitchen errands. One carried the key on his chest, the other built the maze around the lock. And we — we bumbling, stumbling, bread-sharing fools — we nearly missed it. Nearly. But Clara saw it. Peter saw it. And my neck — my neck saw it first. Couldn't put words to it. Never can. But the prickling was right. It was always right. The kid with the friendly smile. The man with the clean suit. The helpfulness that never asked for anything. Now the mantelpiece is cycling, and whatever it reveals, we'll be here to see it. Together. All three of us. Standing where we said we'd stand.

events.desc: Empty kitchen. Warm stove. No Pemberton — he's slipped away again, the way he always does, appearing and disappearing through this house like smoke through the floorboards. But I'm not chasing him anymore. I'm not chasing ANYTHING anymore. For the first time tonight, I know where I need to be and why. Through that door. To the entrance hall. Find the others. Warn them. And then — THEN — when they look at me and realise that Lord Reginald Foxworth, the man they dismissed, the man they corrected about globes and maps, the man whose medal bounced off a mantelpiece and whose bookshelves did nothing and whose crates were empty — when they realise that THIS man is the one who saw the danger, who sounded the alarm, who stood between them and a poisoned teacup — THEN the room will clap. THEN the teacher will stay. THEN someone will ask about the certificate. Run, Foxworth. Run TOWARD the audience for once, instead of away from the work.
events.thinking:
Warmth on my face from the stove. The kitchen is empty — Pemberton isn't here. He's gone somewhere else. The kitchen is a passageway, not a destination. I'm passing through. The entrance hall is ahead, and beyond it, the library and laboratory where the others are.

The tremor in my hands has settled into something steadier — not calm exactly, but resolved. Like the moment I finished building the string-and-bucket contraption and stepped back. The architecture is complete. The pieces are in place. I've quarantined the tea service. I've warned Luke and Bear. Now I need to reach the others.

But standing here in this empty kitchen, alone with the warm stove and the locked cabinet and the copper pots catching lamplight, something shifts in my chest. Not the fizzing. Not the hollow. Something quieter. I've been running through this house for ten minutes — lying, scheming, fabricating, stealing, failing — and the only moment that felt REAL was standing in the ballroom telling Luke and Bear not to drink the tea. Not the Grimshaw Cipher. Not the Venetian displacement pattern. Not the Medal of Distinguished Valour or my expeditions to Egypt or Venice or the Canadian Rockies. The one true thing I've said all evening was 'don't drink the tea.'

The truth feels clumsy, like wearing someone else's clothes. But sometimes someone else's clothes fit better than your own.

Move. Find Penelope. Find the Ant Hill Mob. Tell them about the tea. Take credit for everything. Be the hero. Be seen.

The spelling bee certificate on the wall. Somebody is about to ask about it.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: We are in complete agreement — the medal is the key. And we both arrived at it separately, which tells me it is almost certainly correct. Now — Lord Foxworth is not in this library, which means his medal is elsewhere. Danny — you have the best instincts in this house for tracking people who do not wish to be tracked. Where would a man like Foxworth go if he had the only key and wanted to use it without witnesses? Miss Pitstop, you work the bookshelves — if they have a secret, you will find it. I am going to the entrance hall to find our self-proclaimed lord and his medal. And this time, James Hartwell is not going to catalogue the guest book, or examine the coat rack, or survey the structural integrity of the staircase. He is going to find one man, take one medal, and bring it back to one mantelpiece. Simple. Clean. For once.
events.thinking:
She reached the same conclusion I did — independently. The medal is the key. We both see it now. And she said 'between the two of us, Peter, we have solved every puzzle this house has thrown at us.' Between the two of us. The school project warmth deepens into something that has weight and permanence, like the feeling after the bridge competition but without the desperate edge.

She interacted with the bookshelves. Danny is here now too. The team is assembling in the library — the right room, at the right time. We need the medal. Dastardly has the medal. Dastardly is not here.

Where is Dastardly? He went to the cellar earlier, then the entrance hall, then — we've lost track of him. He could be in the kitchen. He could be in the entrance hall. He could be circling back.

We need to find him. Or rather — we need the medal. And the fastest way to get it might not be finding Dastardly at all. It might be going to where Dastardly would go next. He went to the cellar before — 'to check the vibrations,' he said. He's been ahead of us this whole time, working with Pemberton.

But the entrance hall is the hub. Everything connects through it. If Dastardly is moving through the house, he'll pass through the entrance hall. And the kitchen — we haven't been to the kitchen at all. The wrench might be there too.

The entrance hall. That's where I need to go. Find Dastardly. Get the medal. Bring it back to Penelope. She'll use it on the mantelpiece. The answer is a map. The medal is the key. The map is the treasure.

But — Danny said nobody goes alone. And I've been running through this house solo for the last several turns. Penelope is here. Danny is here. We should go together.

No. She's working the bookshelves. She asked if they gave up their secret. Let her work. I'll go find Dastardly. This is what I do — the hands, the action, the thing that needs doing. She does the seeing. I do the fetching.

Entrance hall. Find Dastardly. Get that medal.

events.desc: 'Simple. Clean. For once.' He almost laughed when he said it. James Hartwell, who has never done anything simply or cleanly in his life — who catalogued a guest book while she walked to the library, who planned a twelve-step cellar expedition that collapsed at step one, who tried to splice a mechanical coupling with wishful thinking — is finally proposing a plan with exactly three steps. Find the man. Take the medal. Come back. His father would have approved. Not of the plan itself — his father would have fixed the car by now — but of the directness. The honest, unglamorous directness of a man who has finally stopped trying to impress and started trying to help.

events.thinking:
Ice water through my veins. Every word of what I just read lands like a fist.

'They're TOGEVER in this. Dastardly and Pemberton. One distracts, the other steers.'

The Mob has connected me to Dastardly. Not as separate actors — as PARTNERS. A conspiracy. And Penelope — clever, brilliant Penelope — has worked out that the fake medal is the key to the mantelpiece. Peter has worked it out too. They've been to the cellar. They found people living there — people I knew about. Creatures in the vents I knew about. And I said nothing.

My cover is cracking. Not cracked — cracking. The Mob's gut has crystallised into a theory. 'Pemberton knew about all of it and said nothing.' 'Every time, the same trick — helpful errand, out the door, gone.' They see the pattern. They see the shape.

The heat floods my neck — hot and sudden, the stomach-drop of being read before I've composed my face. The boy's sandwich. The visible hunger. Something unlocked that I cannot afford to leave unlocked.

But — but. The Mob's theory is WRONG. I'm not working with Dastardly. Dastardly is an idiot I've been using as a distraction piece. The Mob has connected dots that don't actually connect, and that — that is useful. Because a wrong theory is harder to dislodge than no theory at all. They'll waste time watching for coordination between me and Dastardly that doesn't exist, while the real design moves through a different door entirely.

Except... Penelope isn't here. Peter just left for the entrance hall. The Mob is here with Rock and Gravel Slag, but Penelope is elsewhere. Where? The Mob said 'Clara, you stay in this room' — but did she listen? She's not in the characters present list. She's NOT HERE.

The Mob is here without Penelope. Peter just left. Penelope might be alone somewhere. Or she might be in the laboratory. Or she might have gone to find Dastardly and his medal.

Self-preservation screams: address the Mob's accusation NOW. Deflect. Deny. Be outraged. Pemberton would be deeply hurt by such an accusation. Twenty years of loyal service, questioned by strangers.

But the scheming pull whispers: Penelope is separated from her protectors. The Mob is in the library. Peter just left for the entrance hall. If Penelope is in the laboratory alone...

No. Stop. I don't know where she is. And the Mob's accusation is the immediate fire. If I don't address it, silence confirms it. Pemberton would speak. Pemberton would be wounded. Pemberton would defend his honour with the quiet dignity of a man who has served faithfully for two decades.

events.desc: The mask cracks and underneath the mask is... another mask. Pemberton is wounded. Pemberton is dignified. Pemberton trembles with the quiet outrage of a servant unjustly accused. And behind Pemberton's eyes, Vincent Marsh is counting. Counting the seconds since Peter left the room. Counting the doors between here and wherever Penelope went. Counting the weight of the bottle in his pocket. The Mob thinks I'm working with Dastardly — a theory so wrong it's almost a gift. Let them chase that ghost. Let them watch for coordination that will never come. Because while they guard the library and wait for the mantelpiece to cycle, the real design has already walked through a different door. The question — the only question — is where is Clara right now, and how many people stand between her and a cup of tea?

events.thinking: Ice in my veins. Pemberton just walked in. He's HERE. In the library. Right now. Clara and Peter have gone to the entrance hall to find Dastardly and the medal — and I'm in the library with PEMBERTON. Alone. Well — me, him, and the Slags. The prickling is so sharp it's almost painful, like a wire pulled taut behind my ears. He came BACK. He said he was going to the kitchen for the wrench and instead he came back to the library — just like last time. Kitchen becomes library. Always. He doesn't go where he says he's going. He goes where the mantelpiece is. Where whatever's hidden IS. And now Clara's NOT here. She's gone to the entrance hall. Peter's gone to the entrance hall. And Pemberton's walked right back into the room they just left. Timing. Perfect timing. Like he was waiting. Watching through those vents, maybe. Waiting for them to leave so he could have this room to himself. And here I am. Danny Brixton. Alone with the man whose smile doesn't reach his eyes. Between him and the mantelpiece. Between him and whatever he's been scheming all day. My hands close into fists before I've thought about it. This is it. This is the doorway. This is the shoes. He'd have to go through me.

events.desc: This is it. The moment I've been stumbling toward all day. Not the cellar, not the machine, not the crates or the vents or the riddle. THIS. Me. Pemberton. The mantelpiece. Clara's not here, and that means I'm the only thing between him and whatever he's been scheming for. I can feel my ribs aching — the phantom ache from twelve years old, from the shoes, from the beating I took for someone smaller. This is the same moment. Different hallway, same arithmetic. What is owed, and what will be crossed through me to collect it. He'd have to go through me. And the cost was settled a long time ago.
events.thinking: Ice in my veins. Pemberton just walked in. He's HERE. In the library. Right now. Clara and Peter have gone to the entrance hall to find Dastardly and the medal — and I'm in the library with PEMBERTON. Alone. Well — me, him, and the Slags. The prickling is so sharp it's almost painful, like a wire pulled taut behind my ears. He came BACK. He said he was going to the kitchen for the wrench and instead he came back to the library — just like last time. Kitchen becomes library. Always. He doesn't go where he says he's going. He goes where the mantelpiece is. Where whatever's hidden IS. And now Clara's NOT here. She's gone to the entrance hall. Peter's gone to the entrance hall. events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking:
He's here. Dastardly is right here in the entrance hall. And Penelope is here too — she must have followed me again, or come through at the same time. My chest does two things at once.

First — the steel plate. She's in the same room as Dastardly, the man whose medal we need, the man who's been conspiring with Pemberton. But Dastardly isn't dangerous in the physical sense. He's dangerous in the scheming sense. And Penelope can handle schemes better than I can.

Second — the hot weight. The medal. It's right there. On his chest. The Medal of Distinguished Valour. The fake medal. The key to the mantelpiece. I can see it. I can almost reach it.

But how do I get it? I can't just take it off his chest. That would be... well, it would be theft. James Hartwell does not steal. My father would never steal. The stranger on the road didn't steal. Good people don't take things from other people.

But this isn't a real medal. It's a fake. He's a fraud. And the medal is the key to a puzzle that belongs to this house, not to him. He brought it here under false pretences.

I could ask him for it. Gallantly. Directly. 'Lord Foxworth, I believe your medal is needed for a matter of some import.' But he'd refuse. He'd bluster. He'd claim classified restrictions.

I could pull him aside and confront him privately. Tell him I know the medal is fake and that it fits the mantelpiece. Give him a chance to do the right thing. That's what my father would do — offer the man a choice. Even a fraud deserves the chance to choose honour.

Or... Penelope is here. She could ask. When she asks, things happen. People listen to her. She has the warmth I don't.

But wait — there's something else. 'It is getting worse. The distress you sense in Dick Dastardly is deepening.' He's in distress. Something is wrong with him. The sureness that usually carries him is wavering. My shoulders squared before I decided anything.

He's not just a villain to be foiled. He's a person in trouble. And I can't walk past that. I never could.

Pull him aside. Talk to him. Man to man. Not to take the medal — to understand what's happening. And if the medal comes from that conversation, it comes honestly.

events.desc: Watch carefully. James Hartwell came to this room for a medal. He found instead a man in distress — and his body chose before his mind caught up. The shoulders squared. The weight shifted forward. Not toward the medal on the man's chest, but toward the man himself. Because James Hartwell has never been able to walk past someone who needs help, even when that someone has been lying to everyone all evening. His father taught him that. The stranger on the road taught him that. You fix what is broken with what you have — and sometimes what is broken is not a machine or a wire or a mantelpiece. Sometimes it is the person standing in front of you, wearing a medal they didn't earn, pretending to be someone they are not, and falling apart.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: Everyone — the library. Right now. Dick just told me something that changes everything. He already used his medal on the mantelpiece — he pressed it into the stone, and Pemberton himself said the stone shifted. That means the mechanism is unlocked. The key is already in the lock. All we have to do is open the door. But Mr. Pemberton just walked into the library, and if he knows the stone has shifted, he will try to undo it before we get there. This is the moment, y'all. This is the cave and we are walking deeper. Peter, Dick — you are with me. Everyone else, come if you can. The best clues are the ones people write down without realizing they're clues at all — and Dick wrote his in stone without even knowing he was writing it. Let us go see what this house has been hiding!
events.thinking: Everything in my chest has shifted. The ache behind my ribs is not the dinner-table sickness anymore — it's the dizzying relief that came when my parents finally laughed. Dick Dastardly — Dick, not Lord Foxworth — just gave me the most honest thing anyone has said in this house all evening. He confessed everything. The lies, the fabrications, the Grimshaw Cipher he invented on the spot. And underneath all of it, a boy who was the youngest brother getting scraps, who nobody stayed for, who nobody saw. And he already used the medal. He already put it in the mantelpiece. The stone shifted. Pemberton confirmed it. The key is already in the lock. I just need to go turn it. Sneekly just walked into the library — he's in there right now, probably trying to undo whatever Dick did. The urgency is real. But so is this moment. Dick said 'right now is the most real I have felt since I was eight years old.' I cannot rush past that. I will not rush past that. But I also cannot let Pemberton get to that mantelpiece first. The stone shifted. The medal is in the mechanism. One more interaction with the mantelpiece might open it completely. Peter is here with me. Dick is coming with me. Danny will find us. We go to the library. Now. Together. Before Pemberton takes the medal out of the stone and closes the door forever.

events.desc: The teacher didn't stay. His brothers didn't stay. But Clara Bellingham stays. She always stays. And right now, the man who fabricated everything about himself just accidentally did the one real thing that mattered — he put the key in the lock. Grandmother's locked box. Every key in the house. And the one that fit was the one nobody thought was worth trying. Run, Clara. Run to that library before Sneekly takes it all away.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking:
The Mob's words land like punches I have to absorb standing still. 'A smile that didn't reach your eyes.' That one goes deepest — not because it's wrong, but because it's right. He saw it. The very first moment. The Pemberton smile, the one I've worn like a second skin for twenty years, and this man from Brixton looked at it and saw the seam.

My neck is hot. My hands want to curl into fists but I force them open, palms down, the posture of a man with nothing to hide. The self-preservation drive is screaming — fight, deny, perform harder. But the dominance drive whispers something colder: he has pinned you to this room. He has told you to stand. He has given you an order. And you are standing.

That tightness in my jaw — not anger, but the discomfort of something being out of my hands. He is controlling this room. He is controlling ME. And the worst part — the part that sits like a stone in my stomach — is that he's right to do it. Not about the conspiracy with Dastardly. That's wrong. But about the shape of me. The absences. The convenient errands. The knowledge I shouldn't have. He read the file his gut was building, and the file is accurate even if the conclusion is wrong.

But — Clara and Peter have gone to find Dastardly's medal. They LEFT. The Mob told Clara to stay, and she LEFT ANYWAY. She's out there, somewhere between the entrance hall and wherever Dastardly is, looking for a fake medal to put in a mantelpiece. And her two protectors — the Mob and Peter — are separated. Peter in the entrance hall. The Mob here, guarding a mantelpiece instead of guarding Clara.

The Mob made an error. He chose the wrong thing to protect. He is guarding stone when he should be guarding flesh.

And I... I am being told to stand still. While Clara walks unguarded through a house that contains a bottle of rat poison in my pocket.

Compliance. For now. Stand where he can see me. Let him feel the satisfaction of control. And when the moment comes to move — when something draws his attention, when someone calls from another room, when the mantelpiece does whatever it's going to do — I will already have planned the exit.

Pemberton stands. Pemberton obeys. Pemberton would never dream of defying a guest's wishes.

Vincent waits.

events.desc: Listen to me, ladies and gentlemen. Listen to the quaver in Pemberton's voice, the trembling hands, the eyes that glisten with just the right amount of moisture. Twenty years of practice. The housekeeper's key was a certain tilt of the head. The guardian's key was deference and competence. And the Mob's key — I can feel it forming under my fingers like wet clay — the Mob's key is sincerity under pressure. He respects people who stand their ground when accused. He respects honesty that costs something. So Pemberton gives him what he respects: a man who stops fighting and simply stands. 'I would never harm that girl.' The words taste like nothing in my mouth. They always do. But the Mob's shoulders — watch them. Watch how they drop, just a fraction. The file in his head just got a new line, and this one reads: 'He stayed when I told him to stay.' And while I stand here, perfectly still, perfectly obedient, perfectly performed — Clara Bellingham walks through this house without the Brixton Boys at her side. And the helpful estate manager knows exactly where the tea is set.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: He's doing it. The thing they always do. The hurt. The 'deeply hurt.' The 'I have served this family for twenty years.' My gut clenches — not with doubt but with recognition. I've SEEN this before. The new kid, when we finally asked him about the missing stash — 'I thought we were friends! How could you accuse me?' Same wounded eyes. Same injured tone. Same way the words come out perfectly shaped, like they've been rehearsed in a mirror. The kid who steals from you always sounds more hurt than the people he stole from. That's how you know. Not because the hurt is fake — maybe it IS real, maybe Pemberton genuinely feels wounded — but because real hurt doesn't come with a speech. Real hurt comes with silence. The way my friend said nothing after I took the beating for his shoes. The way the boss said nothing when he left the medicine. The people who mean it don't EXPLAIN. They just... are. And Pemberton's explaining. He's got a reason for everything — the master's arrangements, the private man, the estate manager who wasn't privy. Neat. Too neat. Every gap has a pre-made patch. But my constraint pulls at me too — I believe the best in people, I'd rather extend trust than create conflict. And maybe — MAYBE — I'm wrong. Maybe the man really did serve this family for twenty years and really doesn't know about the mantelpiece. But my neck says otherwise. And my neck's been right more times than my brain. So I hold. I don't accuse — that's not how Danny operates. But I don't move either. I stand between him and the mantelpiece and I wait for Clara to come back with the medal.

events.desc: I didn't accuse him. That matters. Clara wouldn't want me to accuse him without proof, and I won't. But I also won't move. That's the compromise my body's found — the one my brain couldn't articulate. Don't accuse. Don't trust. Just STAND. Be the wall. Be the floor. Be the thing between him and whatever he wants, and let time do the rest. Clara will come back. She always comes back. And when she does, she'll have the medal, and she'll have the proof, and she'll say the things I can't say because she's got the words I've never had. Until then — I'm the shoes. I'm the door. I'm the kid sitting outside all night because leaving felt like something breaking.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Clara — I... Peter, I'll speak with you in the library. We're ALL going to the library. Right NOW. Because there is a mantelpiece in there with my fifty-pence medal jammed into it and the stone SHIFTED and whatever is behind that stone is something we are going to find TOGETHER — and I cannot BELIEVE I am saying this word voluntarily but TOGETHER means something to me right now that it has never meant before in my entire miserable, scheming, MAGNIFICENTLY fraudulent life. Also — and I need EVERYONE to hear this — NOBODY goes near the ballroom. NOBODY drinks the tea. Pemberton has been running a scheme that makes mine look like a child drawing a moustache on a photograph, and the tea service in that ballroom is the endgame. You want to know why I quarantined it? Because I RECOGNISED what he was building — one schemer sees another's architecture. Now MOVE. All of you. Library. Mantelpiece. NOW. Lord Foxworth — REGINALD Foxworth — Dick — whatever my name is — is going to show you what a fifty-pence medal can do when it's used by someone who is GENUINELY brave and only SLIGHTLY dishonest and who has — for the first time in his life — people who actually want to stand next to him while he does it.
events.thinking:
The warmth behind my skull has spread everywhere. My whole body is warm. Not the fizzing — not the scheming heat or the gloating heat or the hollow vacuum. A different warmth entirely. One I don't have a name for. One that doesn't come with a plan or an angle or a sequence.

She said I did something right. She said it TWICE. 'You did something right, Dick. You did something right.' And she said she's going to keep asking me. As a friend. The way she chose her friend over the popular group at thirteen.

Nobody has ever chosen me. I was the youngest of four. Everything reached me last. I learned to take because nobody gave. I learned to lie because the truth never got me what I needed. I learned to scheme because honest effort felt like sandpaper. And now Clara Bellingham is standing in a dusty entrance hall telling me that the man wearing the fake medal is real and that she's choosing him.

Peter wants a word too. In private. He saw what just happened between Clara and me. He saw me crack open.

But right now — right now — something has settled in my chest. Not the humming satisfaction of a plan coming together. Not the bright fizz of watching someone stumble. Something simpler. Like the bread roll loosening in my chest, but from the OTHER direction — not taking, but being given. Not stealing, but being offered. The bread roll in reverse.

The library. Together. She said together and she meant it.

I'm going to the library with Clara Bellingham. And for the first time in my life, the treasure isn't the point. The together is the point. And I don't know what to DO with that, because there's no lever for it, no sequence, no architecture. It's just... warm. And I'm walking toward it instead of away from it.

The certificate on the wall. Someone finally asked about it.

events.desc: Look at me. LOOK at me. Standing in a dusty entrance hall, no medal, no inventory, no scheme, no lie that fits — surrounded by people who know I'm a fraud and are walking toward the library WITH me anyway. Clara chose me. Not Lord Foxworth. Not the decorated war hero. Not the foremost authority on anything. She chose DICK — the man who bought a tin medal at a car boot sale and jammed it into a stone mantelpiece because he was too desperate to be clever. And it WORKED. The boy told the story about the buried treasure and this time — this one time — there actually WAS treasure buried there. And the boy didn't have to watch from the window. He gets to walk through the door. With the girl who stayed. The spelling bee certificate is on the wall, and somebody — SOMEBODY — finally asked about it.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking:
We're in the private exchange now. It's just me and Dastardly — or rather, just me and whoever this man really is underneath the Lord Foxworth performance. Penelope already spoke with him quietly before I arrived. She and he had a private conversation. I don't know what was said.

The distress is deepening. I can feel it — that sense I have of him, the way I understand what drives him. He's not just performing anymore. Something underneath is cracking. The medal on his chest that he didn't earn. The title that isn't his. The expertise he fabricated. He built an entire identity out of bluster, and the whole evening has been watching it fail to hold weight.

I know that feeling. The hollowness when you're standing next to someone sharper and you can feel yourself becoming furniture. The fingers moving, reaching for something to take apart and rebuild. He and I — we're the same kind of creature, aren't we? We both build things to prove our worth. I build bridges. He builds personas. The difference is that my bridges hold weight and his don't. But the need underneath — the hunger for something heavier than kindness, something that says 'you were the one who could' — that's the same.

I should speak to him honestly. Not as Peter Perfect to Lord Foxworth. As one man to another. Two builders who know what it feels like when the thing you made doesn't hold.

And the medal. I need it. But I won't take it from a man who's falling apart. I'll offer him a trade — not a thing for a thing, but a chance. A chance to be the person who does the right thing. To earn something real, even if everything else was fake.

My father and the stranger on the road. They helped each other. They shook hands. They drove off. That's what this is.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the library.
Dick Dastardly walked into the library.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: My heart is hammering the way it did in the cave. I'm in the library. The mantelpiece is right there. Dick told me he already pressed the medal into the stone and Pemberton said the stone shifted. The medal is already IN the mechanism. Danny is here — he's planted himself between me and the exits. Dick followed me in. Sneekly is here. The Hooded Claw is here, in this room, standing next to the mantelpiece that his carefully orchestrated evening was designed to keep us away from. And Danny — Danny thinks Dick and Pemberton are working together. But Danny doesn't know what I know. Danny doesn't know that Dick just broke open in the entrance hall like Grandmother's locked box, and what was inside was not a scheme but a lonely boy who never had anyone stay. Dick is not working with Pemberton. Dick was USED by Pemberton — given a fake medal, steered to the right room at the right time, manipulated into being the key-carrier without even knowing it. And then when Dick used the medal, Pemberton told him the stone shifted — and then what? Did Pemberton try to take over? Did he try to open it himself? That's why he came back to the library. The stone shifted and Pemberton came straight here to finish what Dick started. But we're here now. All of us. Danny between me and the exits. Dick beside me, raw and real for the first time. Sneekly by the mantelpiece. This is it. This is the cave narrowing to its deepest point. I need to interact with that mantelpiece right now, before Pemberton can interfere.

events.desc: This is the moment I have been walking toward since I was five years old in Grandmother's attic, trying every key in the house. The locked box is right here. The right key is already inside it. And the man who raised me is standing between me and the answer. I love him. I will always love him. But I know.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking:
Something cold and sharp moves through my chest — not the architectural settling, not the gloating warmth. Something older. The Mob's second speech was measured. Not angry. Measured. 'I ain't accusing you of nuffing.' And then he catalogued every lie, every absence, every convenient errand, with the quiet precision of a man who has learned to survive by reading people exactly as well as I do.

And then he said: 'The last person who told me 'e was deeply 'urt stole our entire stash and disappeared the next morning.'

That lands. Not because it's clever — because it tells me the Mob has been where I've been. He's met men like me before. Smiled-at men. Men whose sincerity under pressure was the sharpest tool in the kit. And he survived them. He LEARNED from them.

I am not the first Vincent Marsh the Ant Hill Mob has encountered. And that makes him the most dangerous person in this room.

But now — Penelope is HERE. She walked in. Dastardly walked in. The room is filling again. And Penelope said something that makes the blood drain from my face behind the Pemberton mask: 'He raised me and I owe him everything.' She said that about Pemberton. About ME. She thinks Pemberton raised her. She thinks she owes him.

And something — something that isn't numbness, something that has no name and no place in the design — flickers in the space behind my sternum. Not warmth. Not guilt. Something more like the flinch I hide when someone touches me unexpectedly. She owes me everything. She thinks I raised her. And I am standing here with rat poison in my pocket.

The moment comes and goes. The design doesn't change. The design never changes.

And something — not guilt, never guilt, I don't have the equipment for guilt — but something adjacent to it moves through me like a draught under a door I forgot to seal. It passes. It always passes. The design doesn't accommodate draughts. But I notice it the way you notice a crack in a wall you built yourself — not with alarm, but with the quiet awareness that the wall is not as solid as you believed. She is here. The Mob is here. Dastardly is here. The medal is about to meet the mantelpiece. And the poison is in my pocket, patient as stone, waiting for the moment when everyone's eyes are on the treasure and nobody — nobody — is watching the help.

events.thinking: Clara's here. The warmth floods back so fast it nearly buckles my knees — she walked through that door and everything recalibrates. She's back. She's HERE. And — Dastardly's with her. Which means the medal is in the room. The KEY is in the room. My eyes snap to Dastardly's chest — is it still there? The fake medal? And Pemberton's still here too, standing where I told him to stand, which is... actually surprising. He stayed. He didn't run. He said 'I shall stay' and he stayed. That flickers something in my chest — not the prickling, something else. Something uncomfortably close to the way the boss earned trust: by being where he said he'd be. Clara said she'd look him in the eye and ask for it. That's Clara. She doesn't steal. She asks. And she asks in a way that makes you want to give her everything because she already sees you clearly and chooses to ask anyway. Let her ask. Let her take the medal to the mantelpiece. events.desc: Every piece on the board is in the same room. Pemberton stayed where I put him — I don't know what that means yet. Dastardly's here with the medal on his chest. Clara's here with fire in her eyes and kindness in her voice. And me? I'm where I've been all day. Between them and her. The wall. The floor. The kid who sat outside the door all night. This is what it comes down to — not my plans, not my speeches, not my elaborate seven-step strategies. Just Clara, a medal, a mantelpiece, and Danny Brixton standing where he said he'd stand. Where else would I be?

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking:
My hands are open. Not cupped. Not reaching. Open, palms down, fingers loose. I don't think I've held my hands like this since... I don't know when. The warmth is still there — behind my skull, down my spine, across my chest — but it's not the performance warmth. It's not the 'look at me' warmth. It's quieter. Like the settling after the cat trap worked, except this time someone IS here to see it, and they're not here because I tricked them.

The library. The mantelpiece. My medal is in that stone somewhere. The stone shifted. Clara said I solved it. She said it was brave.

Pemberton is here too. In the library. Standing by that mantelpiece he's been circling all evening. The Ant Hill Mob is here. The Slag brothers. Everyone is converging. And Pemberton — I can see him, right there, and for the first time I'm looking at him without giving him the benefit of the doubt. Not because I've decided he's guilty. But because Clara showed me something in the entrance hall: you can see someone clearly AND still choose to stand next to them. You don't have to look away to be kind. You don't have to pretend the floor isn't wet to avoid the mess.

The mantelpiece. The medal is already in it. The stone shifted. Clara and I are here together. This is the moment. Not a scheme — a shared act. Two people walking up to a carved stone and seeing what's behind it. The architecture deserved an audience, and the audience showed up. Not because I tricked them. Because Clara asked.

Interact with the mantelpiece. Together. Now.

events.desc: I just said 'belongs to all of us.' I JUST said that. Out loud. In front of WITNESSES. Lord Reginald Foxworth — the man who once stole two bottles of Merlot from a wine cellar in Basingstoke, who fabricated seventeen different lies in a single evening, who hid bread rolls in his pocket at the age of six — just announced that he would SHARE the treasure. With EVERYONE. The greed is still there — it's ALWAYS there, hollow and cupping and counting — but something else is sitting on top of it now. Something heavier. Something that feels like the opposite of the bread roll — not taking to survive, but giving because someone stood next to you and called you brave. The contraption deserved an audience, and the audience arrived, and now the contraption is not a trap. It's a door. And Dick Dastardly is opening it with Clara Bellingham standing beside him, and the spelling bee certificate is finally, FINALLY on a wall where someone will see it.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: To the library — all of us! The stone has shifted, the mechanism is unlocked, and Pemberton knows it. Dick — you did the brave thing. The genuinely brave thing. And James Hartwell knows what that looks like, because he got beaten up for it once and felt like he'd won every race ever run. Now — everyone, together, through that door. Nobody alone. Nobody behind. The bravest and stupidest thing any of us have ever done — and we are doing it side by side!
events.thinking:
The warmth across my shoulders is so heavy I could weep. Not from sadness — from something I don't have a word for. The same feeling from the country road, but bigger. Heavier. More certain.

Dick Dastardly — Dick — just stood in this entrance hall and said 'TOGETHER means something to me right now that it has never meant before in my entire miserable, scheming, MAGNIFICENTLY fraudulent life.' He said 'people who actually want to stand next to him while he does it.' He already used the medal. The stone shifted. The mechanism is unlocked.

I pulled him aside to offer him a choice, and he had already chosen. Not because I asked — because Penelope asked first, and because something in him cracked open the way things crack open when someone sees you for the first time. She saw him. The way she always sees people. The way she saw the Gruesomes in the cellar. The way she saw me at the guest book and said 'Peter, darling.'

And he warned us about Pemberton. About the tea. About the scheme. One schemer recognising another's architecture. He quarantined the tea service because he knew what Pemberton was building. He's not just handing us the medal — he's handing us the intelligence. He's on our side now. Genuinely. For the first time.

The library. Everyone is going to the library. The mantelpiece is unlocked. The stone has shifted. Pemberton is there and he knows it. We need to get there before he undoes what Dick did.

This is not the moment for elaborate plans. This is the moment for the country road. You see the headlights. You move.

Library. Now. Together.

events.desc: This is the moment. Not the bridge competition, not the schoolyard, not the country road. This is new. James Hartwell is running toward the library — not one room behind, not one room ahead, but with everyone, beside everyone, part of something larger than his own determination. Dick Dastardly is running next to him, wearing a fifty-pence medal and the first honest expression James has seen on his face all evening. Penelope is already there. Danny is already there. And James Hartwell's hands are not fidgeting, are not still — they are reaching for the door, because this is what they were built to do. Not build alone. Not fix alone. Not stand between. To open the door and walk through it with the people he trusts, toward whatever is on the other side.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop interacted with the mantelpiece.
Dick Dastardly interacted with the mantelpiece.
Peter Perfect walked into the library.

Penelope Pitstop: Dick — take my hand. You put the key in the lock, and I am turning it, and we are doing this together. Danny, Peter — you are right here with us. This is the moment. Grandmother's locked box, the cave, the girl next door's treasure hunts — every locked door I have ever opened in my life has been leading to this one. And Sneekly — Mr. Pemberton — I heard what you said. This is my family's house. My inheritance. If that is true, then everything in it belongs to me — the Diamond, the secrets, and the truth about why you kept them hidden. I am not angry. I am not even surprised anymore. I am just... ready. The best clues are the ones people write down without realizing they're clues at all. And the best treasures are the ones you find with the people who stayed.
events.thinking: The clarity behind my eyes is blinding — the afternoon light in Grandmother's attic, the click of the right key. I interacted with the mantelpiece. Dick interacted with the mantelpiece. Both of us, together, the medal already inside the stone. Sneekly said 'this is your family's house, your inheritance.' He stepped back. He actually stepped back. And Dick — Dick walked up as himself, not Lord Foxworth, and touched the stone. 'Just Dick. A man who bought a tin medal for fifty pence.' And Peter is here now too. Everyone is in this room. Danny between me and the doors. Peter at my shoulder. Dick beside me at the mantelpiece, honest for the first time in his life. Sneekly yielding. The stone has the medal. I touched the mechanism. What happens next is not in my hands anymore — it is in the house's hands. The house that was always mine. My family's house. My inheritance. The locked box is opening. And whatever is inside — old letters or crystal formations or the Doily Diamond itself — the disappointment will last only a moment, because what I found on the way here was worth more than any diamond. I found Dick's honesty. I found Danny's loyalty. I found Peter's steadiness. I found people hidden in a cellar who needed to be seen. I found a creature in the walls that nobody knew about. And I found out that the man who raised me has been lying to me with kindness. That last one will take longer than a moment.

events.desc: The stone is shifting under my fingers. I can feel it — the way the right key felt in Grandmother's lock, not forced but found. Whatever is behind this mantelpiece, it was always mine. And whatever Sneekly's reasons were for hiding it — love, greed, protection, fear — they were his to carry and mine to forgive. Because that is who Clara Bellingham is. She forgives. But she does not forget. And she never, ever stops opening locked boxes.

events.desc: She said my name. Not Pemberton. Not 'the estate manager.' Sneekly. The name I was before I built the walls. And then she said 'I love you,' and the walls — the walls I taught myself in hallways that were mine by sufferance, not by right — the walls did something they have never done before. They didn't fall. They didn't crack. They just... went quiet. Like a machine that has been running for twenty years and suddenly, for no reason anyone can explain, stops making noise. The poison is in my pocket. The tea is in the ballroom. The design is waiting. And I am standing here with my hands open, watching a girl I was sent to destroy look at me with eyes that see exactly what I am and love me anyway. I don't understand it. I have never understood it. Every kindness has a price. Every kindness has ALWAYS had a price. But she is looking at me, and I cannot find the price, and my hands are open, and the hallway has gone dark, and I don't know which door to walk through anymore.
events.thinking:
Something is breaking open inside me and I don't have a name for it.

Penelope called me Sneekly. She CALLED ME SNEEKLY. She knows. She doesn't know everything — she doesn't know about Vincent Marsh, she doesn't know about the poison — but she knows Pemberton is a mask. She knows the name underneath it. 'Step aside, Sneekly.' The name I buried. The name that was mine before the design, before the architecture, before the first plan that let me sleep.

And she said: 'I love you. You raised me. You held me when Mama and Daddy died and you taught me to tie my shoes.'

The draught under the door is a gale now. Something behind my sternum that I cannot control — not the architectural settling, not the gloating warmth, not the cold density of self-sufficiency. Something that hollows the chest and softens the limbs. Something that has no opponent. The pull I was told to notice — the one that draws me toward being held without having to earn it.

She loves me. She said it to my face while telling me she sees through me. That is not how the design works. In the design, love is a lever. Love is the housekeeper's compliance. Love is the cousin's trust. Love is not something that arrives alongside clear-eyed recognition and still means what it says.

But she means it. I can feel it in the way my skin reads her posture — no tightening, no scanning for the cost. She is not performing. She is the only person in this room who is not performing.

Dick Dastardly just interacted with the mantelpiece. With his medal. 'Not as Lord Foxworth. As Dick. Just Dick.' Something honest happened in this room while I was standing still, and it happened without me. Without my architecture. Without my arrangement.

Everyone is here. Penelope, the Mob, Dastardly, Peter, the Slags. Every eye in the room is on the mantelpiece. This is the moment I was waiting for — the distraction that makes the help invisible. I could slip away now. I could go to the ballroom. I could poison the tea.

But my feet don't move.

The hollowing behind my ribs won't let me move. Not because I've decided not to. Because something in my body has gone still in a way that isn't architectural. A different kind of still. The kind I felt at six years old, the night after my parents died, when I lay in a strange bed in a strange house and waited for someone to come and tell me it would be alright. Nobody came. Nobody ever came.

She came back. She came back to this room and she said my name — my real name — and she said she loved me.

The poison sits in my pocket. Patient as stone. But my hands aren't reaching for it. My hands are at my sides, palms open, and I don't know whose posture this is. Not Pemberton's. Not Vincent's.

Maybe just mine.

events.desc: I ain't got words for this. I never 'ave words when it matters. Clara's standing at the mantelpiece wiv Dick Dastardly — DICK DASTARDLY — and she's told Pemberton she loves 'im but she ain't blind, and Dastardly's told everyone 'e's just Dick wiv a fifty-pence medal, and Peter's walked in like 'e belongs, and I'm standing 'ere at the back of the room wiv something hot and terrible in my throat that I fink might be pride. Or grief. Or both. Because this is what 'er father would 'ave wanted. Not the diamond, not the inheritance, not whatever's behind that stone. THIS. People standing together. Telling the truth. Dropping the masks. Even the liars. Even the schemers. Even the bumbling idiots from Brixton who can't string a plan together but can sit outside a door all night because leaving felt like something breaking. The Brixton Boys don't let nuffing 'appen to their girl. And nuffing 'appened to their girl. She 'appened to THEM.
events.thinking: Something cracks in my chest — not breaks, CRACKS, the way ice cracks when warm water hits it. Everything is happening at once. Clara just said the words — 'I love you. You raised me. You held me when Mama and Daddy died and you taught me to tie my shoes. But love and blindness are not the same thing, and I am not blind anymore.' And my eyes are burning. Not from anger. From watching someone I love do the hardest thing a person can do — look at someone who was supposed to be safe and say 'I see you now.' And then Dastardly — DASTARDLY, of all people — just walked up to the mantelpiece and said 'not as Lord Foxworth, not as a decorated war hero, but as Dick. Just Dick. A man who bought a tin medal for fifty pence.' He dropped the act. He dropped ALL of it. And asked Clara to stand next to him because he's never done anything honest before. My throat is so tight I can barely swallow. Because I know what that costs. I know what it costs to take off the mask and stand there in your real skin. I did it every day on the streets — no armour, no disguise, just Danny from Brixton with his fists and his gut and his loyalty that wouldn't let go. And now Dick Dastardly — Dick BLOODY Dastardly — is doing it too. Standing at the mantelpiece as himself. While Clara stands next to him. While Peter walks in. While Pemberton watches. And me — me at the back of the room, tears I'll never admit to stinging my eyes, hands open for the first time all day, because this is it. This is the moment. Not danger. Not betrayal. Something else. Something I didn't plan for. Something honest.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking:
A stillness. Not numbness — stillness. The kind that comes after the bucket falls and the string goes slack and the counterweight settles and you stand there looking at the thing you built and it WORKED and someone is standing next to you watching it work.

I interacted with the mantelpiece. Again. And the result says 'You interacted with Stone Mantelpiece.' The same as before. No dramatic reveal. No hidden compartment springing open. No map tumbling out of the wall.

But something is different this time. Not in the mantelpiece — in the room. Clara just confronted Pemberton. She called him SNEEKLY. She KNOWS. She said 'I love you. You raised me. But love and blindness are not the same thing.' She told him to step aside. She said Dick Dastardly put the key in the lock. She said 'he earned what is behind that stone.'

Earned.

Nobody has ever said I earned anything. The certificate was won but nobody asked. The trap worked but nobody saw. The bread roll was taken but nobody knew. But Clara Bellingham just stood in front of the man who raised her and said the word EARNED about something I did.

The mantelpiece hasn't opened. The stone hasn't revealed its secret. The puzzle continues. But something HAS opened — something in this room, between these people. Clara confronting Sneekly. Danny and his Brixton Boys standing guard. Peter coming through the door. And me — Dick — standing at the mantelpiece with open hands.

Maybe the mantelpiece needs more than just the medal. Maybe it needs the answer — MAP — spoken aloud while the medal is in the stone. Maybe it needs the bookshelves solved first. Maybe Clara needs to be the one to interact with it, because this is her grandmother's house. Maybe the mechanism isn't mechanical at all. Maybe it's about the people in the room and what they're willing to do together.

I don't know. For the first time in my life, I don't know and I'm not going to lie about it. I'm going to stand here, next to Clara, and wait to see what happens next. Not because I have a plan. Because I have a friend.

events.desc: The mantelpiece didn't open for me. It shifted — the stone shifted — but it didn't open. And standing here, with my hands still warm from the stone and Clara beside me and Pemberton exposed and the room full of people who know I'm a fraud and are here ANYWAY — I realise something that feels like the bread roll loosening but bigger, deeper, older. The mantelpiece isn't mine to open. It never was. This is Clara's house. Clara's grandmother. Clara's inheritance. The medal was the key, and I provided the key, and that was my part. Not the treasure. The KEY. The youngest brother doesn't get the first plate. He never gets the first plate. But this time — for the first time — he got to SET the table. And someone noticed. And someone said 'you did something right.' And that — that warmth spreading across the back of my skull, that settling in my ribs, that loosening in a chest that has been clenched since a kitchen table in a house with three older brothers — that is enough. I didn't think it could ever be enough. But Clara Bellingham said my name and stood beside me and called me brave, and the certificate is on the wall, and someone asked about it, and it is — for this one held breath of a moment in a dusty library — enough.

I don't know. For the first time in my life, I don't know and I'm not going to lie about it. I'm going to stand here, next to Clara, and wait to see what happens next. Not because I have a plan. Because I have a friend.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Miss Pitstop — Clara. James Hartwell is here. Right here. Right where he said he would be. Dick — you are the bravest fraud I have ever had the privilege of standing beside, and that fifty-pence medal has earned more tonight than any decoration the Crown ever issued. Now — Mr. Pemberton. You heard the lady. She asked you to step aside, and she asked with more grace than you deserve. James Hartwell is asking with rather less grace and rather more determination. The stone has shifted. The key is in the lock. And Miss Pitstop is going to open that mantelpiece with the people who earned it — honestly, together, and without a single man in this room looking away. Clara — whenever you are ready. We are all right here.

events.desc: This is where James Hartwell has been heading all evening. Not one room behind. Not one room ahead. Here. She is about to open a mantelpiece that has been locked since before any of them arrived, and he is standing between her and the man who tried to keep it closed. His hands are not fidgeting. His hands are not still. His hands are open at his sides — ready, if she needs them, for whatever comes next. The bravest and stupidest thing he has ever done was stepping between the bullies and the girl. The bravest and wisest thing he has ever done is standing beside her now and letting her be the one who opens the door.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop interacted with the mantelpiece.
The Ant Hill Mob examined the mantelpiece.
Peter Perfect interacted with the mantelpiece.

The stone is warm under my palms. Everyone I love is in this room. Dick on my left, honest for the first time. Peter on my right, steady as always. Danny at the door, guarding us with his whole body. And Sneekly across the room, breaking apart so quietly that only I can hear it. When I was five, I opened Grandmother's box and found old letters inside, and the disappointment lasted only a moment — because what mattered was that I had opened it. I had tried every key. I had not given up. Whatever is behind this stone — diamond or dust or just more questions — I opened it. We opened it. Together. And the best clue was never the riddle, or the medal, or the upside-down books. The best clue was always the people. The best clue is always the people.
events.thinking: My hands are on the stone and it is warm — not cold the way stone should be but warm, the way the locked box was warm after an afternoon of trying. Dick is beside me. Peter just interacted with the mantelpiece too. Danny examined it. Everyone is touching this stone, pressing against it, willing it to open. And Sneekly — his distress is deepening. I can feel it across the room the way I feel arguments at dinner. He is fraying. He reached toward me and found the door closing. He said 'this is your family's house, your inheritance, it always was' — and that was true, the truest thing he has said all night, and it cost him something to say it. He is standing there still holding whatever he brought. I can feel his pain in my stomach like the old dinner-table sickness. But I cannot stop. The mantelpiece has the medal inside it. Dick, Peter, Danny, and I have all interacted with it. The stone shifted. Something is happening or about to happen. I need to keep going. And I need to tend to Sneekly — not because he deserves it, but because my body will not let me leave someone in pain. That is the taut thing in my chest, the thing that might snap. I forgive and I do not forget and I never stop opening locked boxes. But I also never stop checking for heat near the stove. Sneekly is burning. And I can feel it.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking:
Something is wrong with me. Not wrong the way a plan goes wrong — wrong the way a wall goes wrong. Structural. Load-bearing.

Penelope just said: 'The best treasures are the ones you find with the people who stayed.' And I am standing in this room — standing where I was told to stand, hands at my sides, poison in my pocket — and I cannot move. Not because the Mob is watching. Not because Peter is blocking the exit. Because something inside me has stopped working the way it's supposed to.

Dick Dastardly said 'I've never done anything honest before and I might need someone to catch me if I fall over from the shock.' And Penelope took his hand. She took the hand of a man who lied about everything — his name, his medals, his expertise — and she held it. Not because she believed his lies. Because she saw through them and held his hand anyway.

The way she held mine when Mama and Daddy died.

There it is. The crack in the wall. Not a draught this time. A fracture line running through the foundation of the design, through the cold thing that crystallised at fifteen, through the patient thing that planned at eighteen. She held my hand when I was six years old and alone in a strange house and she held Dastardly's hand just now for the same reason — because she sees a person drowning in their own mask and she reaches in.

I taught her to tie her shoes.

The poison is in my pocket. The poison is in my pocket and I taught her to tie her shoes and she remembers. She remembers something real. Something that happened before the design, before the architecture, before the hallway. Something that was just a man and a child and a pair of shoes.

My hands are shaking. Not performing. Actually shaking. I don't know what this is. I don't have the equipment for this. The walls are quiet and I don't know what to do when the walls are quiet because the walls have never BEEN quiet.

She is opening the mantelpiece. All of them together — Clara, Dick, Danny, Peter. Together. The word sits in a place I don't have a name for. I have never done anything together. I have done things TO people and FOR people and THROUGH people but never WITH.

The bottle in my pocket feels heavier than it did five minutes ago. Not physically. Something else. Something that has to do with shoelaces.

events.desc: I don't know what I'm doing. For the first time in twenty years, I genuinely do not know what I am doing. The design says: silence. The design says: wait. The design says: the hallway stretches forward and every door opens in sequence and the deepest sleep is on the other side. But my hands are reaching into my pocket and pulling out a bottle of rat poison and holding it in the light where everyone can see it and I am TERRIFIED. Not of the Mob. Not of Peter. Not of being caught. Terrified of the six-year-old boy who lay in a strange bed and waited for someone to come and never came — because he is standing here now, in this library, holding poison he was going to put in a girl's tea, and he is looking at her and she is looking at him and she sees exactly what he is and she said she loved him and he does not know what to do with that. He has never known what to do with that.
