events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Clara said — I forgive you. Not for what you did. For who you became in order to do it. She said the man who tied her shoes is still in there, wrapped up for twenty years. She said tomorrow we unwrap him together. And she said — stop standing alone. Sit down. The way Danny told Dick to sit. Not to put anything down. Just to stop standing alone. My shoulders tightened when she said it — the old reflex, the scan for the price, the automatic inventory of what this kindness will cost. But the tightening was smaller than it used to be. Quieter. Like a machine running down. Like a mechanism that has been turning for twenty years and is finally — finally — losing momentum. She sees me. She sees that I am still standing. She sees that I am always still standing. She sees that the man who holds things closed is the last one to sit down. And she is asking me to sit. Not Pemberton. Not Sneekly. Me. Vincent. The boy who was never asked how he felt. The boy who learned that standing was safer than sitting because sitting meant trusting that nobody would take the chair away. She is asking me to trust that the chair will still be there. And I — I am going to sit down. Not because she asked. Not because it is strategic. Because my legs are tired and the chair is there and a girl I tried to poison just told me she forgives the wrapping, even if she cannot yet forgive what was inside it. And that is enough. That word again. Enough.

events.desc: He walks to the guest book — the same one he was cataloguing at the start of the evening, when he was one room behind and two plans too deep. He doesn't catalogue it this time. He signs it. James Hartwell. One name. No elaboration. No plan appended. Just a man who was here, and who will be here again tomorrow.
events.thinking:
Task commitments feel neglected — obligations piling up. That's the system telling me I haven't been doing enough toward my goals. Impressing Clara. Finding the treasure. But the evening is ending. Clara said goodnight. The treasure — if there is one — is behind a mantelpiece that won't fully open until tomorrow.

And yet the feeling in my body isn't the hollow ache of falling short. It's the warm settling across the shoulders. The embers. My hands are still.

The old James Hartwell would hear 'obligations piling up' and launch into a seven-point plan for tomorrow. The wrench — where to source it. The approach — arrive at dawn, check the perimeter, inspect the machine, prepare a schematic. The guest book — finish cataloguing it while waiting for Clara to arrive. The mantelpiece — develop a theory about the five books, research the first letters...

But no. Not tonight. Tonight I sign the guest book — just sign it, the way a person does when they've been to a place that mattered — and I wait. The obligations will still be there in the morning. The wrench will be in my hand. The tea will be sweet. And Clara will walk through that door and I will be here, the first one, the way I said I would be.

Sign the guest book. Not catalogue it. Sign it.

events.desc: Peter Perfect interacted with the guest-book.

James Hartwell signed the guest book. Not catalogued it — signed it. One name, steady hand, no plan attached. Then he stepped back and leaned against the wall beneath the portraits of Clara's stern ancestors, and for the first time all evening, his hands found his pockets instead of reaching for something to fix. Above him, the chandelier hangs precariously. He has noticed. He has not made a plan. Tomorrow. Everything tomorrow. Tonight there is only the watch, and the quiet, and the knowledge that when she walks through that door in the morning, the first thing she will see is a man who kept his word. A Hartwell is always early.
events.thinking:
I signed the guest book. James Hartwell. The pen touched the page and my hand was steady — no tremor, no hesitation, no elaborate flourish. Just a name.

The entrance hall is quiet. The chandelier hangs precariously overhead — I noticed that the moment I walked in, hours ago, and my first instinct was to plan how to secure it. Three-phase approach: assess the chain, identify load-bearing anchor points, source appropriate hardware. That was the old instinct. Now I look up at it and think — tomorrow. Tomorrow I'll fix that too. Tonight it hangs, and we are all beneath things that could fall, and that is just what it means to be in an old house with people you're learning to trust.

My body is settling. The warmth is low and steady — embers, not flame. My feet are flat on the floor, rooted the way they were when I stood next to Clara while she shook. Not bracing. Not charging. Just planted.

The night watch. That's what this is. My father on the country road, sitting in the broken-down car with his hand on the wheel even though it wouldn't turn, just because that's where you sit when you're the one who keeps things steady. Waiting for morning. Waiting for the headlights.

Goodnight, Bellingham Manor. James Hartwell is here.

events.desc: The room is quiet. The curtain falls on a library full of sleeping villains and forgiving heroines and loyal men in chairs too big for them — and one estate manager on the floor, learning for the first time that the deepest rest does not require a finished design. It only requires stopping. Goodnight, Doily Manor. Goodnight, architecture. Goodnight, Pemberton. Goodnight, Sneekly. Goodnight, Vincent. Whoever you turn out to be in the morning — he will be enough.
events.thinking: The room is quiet. That is the entire recent activity report. The room is quiet. No one spoke. No one moved. No one interacted with anything. The room is just — quiet. Danny and Dick are in the chairs. Clara is here. Rock and Gravel are here. And I am here, having failed to sit in a chair because I tried to operate it like a machine. The room is quiet. And I am sitting on the floor. Because the chair would not let me interact with it, and I am too tired to stand, and the floor does not require a mechanism. The floor is just — there. The way the truth is just there. The way Clara's forgiveness is just there. The way the dust is just there. I am sitting on the floor of my own library, in a house I managed for twenty years, beside a chair I cannot operate, surrounded by people who are falling asleep, and the room is quiet. And I am — I am going to close my eyes. Not the deep dreamless sleep of a finished design. Something else. Something I do not have a name for yet. The sleep of a man who has no plans left. The sleep of empty hands and a closed ledger and a floor that does not ask anything of you except that you stop.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with pat-pending.
events.thinking:
Still quiet. Still nothing. The watch continues.

But there's something stirring — the task commitments nagging again. And I notice the Professor is here. Pat Pending. A man of science, of tools, of mechanical understanding. He might know where to find a wrench. Or he might have one. The old James Hartwell would have asked hours ago — would have launched a reconnaissance mission, interrogated every person in the manor about wrench availability, drawn up a supply chain diagram.

But the new — no, not new. The quieter version. He notices the Professor is here, and he thinks: tomorrow, I'll ask. Not tonight. Tonight is the watch.

Except — no. That's not right either. The watch doesn't mean doing nothing when something useful is right in front of you. My father on the country road — he didn't just sit. When the stranger came, he helped. The watch is about being ready. And being ready for tomorrow means knowing where the wrench is.

One question. Simple. No elaborate plan. Just — Professor, do you know where I might find a wrench?
